# Vault objects, cli.sgit.ai

> The pointer store: read, write, batch, destroy and presigned endpoints, the caching contract that separates immutable content-addressed objects from mutable refs, and the storage layout behind every vault.

*Source: <https://cli.sgit.ai/api/vault-objects.html> · generated from the same content as the page, so the two cannot drift. Moved from <https://sgit.ai/api/vault-objects.html> (sgit.ai v0.7.87) on 2026-10-20.*

---
# Vault objects

The pointer store: the ciphertext objects a vault is made of, addressed by opaque identifiers the server cannot interpret. This is what `sgit push` and `sgit pull` are doing underneath.

## Endpoints

| Method | Path | Auth | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| PUT | `/api/vault/write/{vault_id}/{file_id}` | access token + write key | Body is raw ciphertext |
| GET | `/api/vault/read/{vault_id}/{file_id}` | none | Raw bytes. [Reads are public by default](../api/authentication.md#reads) on the shared host |
| GET | `/api/vault/read-base64/{vault_id}/{file_id}` | none | Base64 in JSON, MCP-safe. Around 3.75 MB ceiling |
| DELETE | `/api/vault/delete/{vault_id}/{file_id}` | access token + write key |  |
| POST | `/api/vault/batch/{vault_id}` | per operation | Mixed reads and writes, **max 100** per request |
| POST | `/api/vault/list/{vault_id}` | none |  |
| GET | `/api/vault/health/{vault_id}` | none |  |
| GET | `/api/vault/public-info/{vault_id}` | none |  |
| DELETE | `/api/vault/destroy/{vault_id}` | write key | Body `{vault_id, purge?}`. Without `purge` it writes a tombstone that blocks reuse of the ID |

Large blobs go through presigned URLs rather than the request body: `POST /api/vault/presigned/initiate|complete|cancel/{vault_id}` and `GET /api/vault/presigned/read-url/{vault_id}/{file_id}`.

`GET /api/vault/zip/{vault_id}` is registered in the route table but marked PROPOSED upstream. It is deliberately [not documented](../api/index.md#unresolved) until that is reconciled.

## Destroy, and why the tombstone matters

`destroy` without `purge:true` leaves a tombstone that prevents the vault ID being registered again. That is a security property, not bookkeeping: vault IDs are short and a released ID is a squattable namespace. If somebody still holds a read key pointing at that ID, a new vault claiming it would be answering reads meant for the old one. `purge:true` skips the tombstone and frees the ID, use it only when you are sure no credential survives.

## The caching contract

Anyone writing a client needs this, and getting it wrong produces a bug that looks like corruption:

| Object | Response header |
|---|---|
| File ID containing `-imm-`, immutable, content-addressed | `Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable` |
| Refs and indexes, mutable | `Cache-Control: no-store` |

Immutable objects are content-addressed, so their bytes can never change and a year-long cache is safe, which is what lets a vault sit behind a CDN. Mutable refs must never be cached: a stale ref renders a previous commit’s tree from ciphertext that is itself perfectly valid, so nothing errors and the reader simply sees the wrong version of the vault.

**Measured 21 September 2026: the immutable header is not currently being sent.** A GET of an `obj-cas-imm-` object on `/api/vault/read/` returned **no `Cache-Control` header at all**, and the CDN reported a miss. The table above is the contract, not a description of what is served on that path today. Build as though the header may be absent: cache on the id, which is a hash of the ciphertext and therefore cannot be stale, rather than on a header you were sent. That is what the client-side caches in this estate already do, and [why caching ciphertext is the easy case](https://sgit.ai/demos/fractal-graphs/performance.html#caching).

## Storage layout

```
bare/data/obj-cas-imm-{hex}     blobs, trees, commits — content-addressed, immutable
bare/keys/key-rnd-imm-{hex}     PKI public keys — immutable
bare/refs/                      branch refs — mutable
bare/indexes/                   branch index — mutable
bare/append/                    append lanes — managed, outside the commit DAG
```

The prefixes are load-bearing. `obj-cas-imm-` is SHA-256 over the *ciphertext*, which gives deduplication without the server knowing any plaintext, and makes the caching rule above derivable from the ID alone. Append lanes sit outside the commit DAG on purpose, a message arriving does not rewrite your history.

This site is itself served from a vault, so these are the objects behind the page you are reading. The [live-vault case study](https://sgit.ai/case-studies/live-vault-docs.html) shows the fetch sequence.

## See also

- [Append lanes](../api/append-lanes.md), the write-only channel that does not touch the commit tree
- [Errors and limits](../api/errors.md)

---

*[Site index for agents](../llms.txt) · [HTML version](https://cli.sgit.ai/api/vault-objects.html)*


# A pack per push: git's packfiles, applied to an encrypted vault, with no server change, cli.sgit.ai

> For three days I have been talking with the CLI team about keeping a vault's objects in zip files, and this is where it landed. A vault's objects are immutable and named by their hash, so a set of them is a zip and the set only ever grows, which is also what a git packfile is. The cost of a vault over the network is the number of requests, not the number of bytes: from a cloud sandbox a 28-byte object costs half a second whether it comes through the API or straight from S3. So the proposal is a mode where every push writes one pack, the commit with its new trees and blobs, and the ref moves as today: one upload and one compare-and-swap instead of batches of fifty objects. Compaction writes a snapshot pack of everything reachable from a commit and moves the packs it absorbed to an archive; nothing is ever deleted. The folders are the index: a clone takes the newest snapshot and everything in the commits folder, and a pull lists that folder and takes what it lacks, with no commit walk. Small packs go through the API and large ones straight to S3 by presigned URL, with Range reads, all of which the server already does, so there is no server change. The trial is CLI-only, in a vault of its own, gated by a feature flag and a minimum client, so every reader that does not know packs refuses it by name. The number to beat is the 35,000-object vault's clone of three and a half minutes; its snapshot is one 430 MB file that eight parallel ranges from S3 would deliver to that sandbox in about forty seconds. Nothing here is built yet.

*Source: <https://cli.sgit.ai/articles/a-pack-per-push.html> · generated from the same content as the page, so the two cannot drift.*

---
By [Dinis Cruz](https://sgit.ai/about/) · 2026-10-21 · published

**Summary:** For three days I have been talking with the CLI team about keeping a vault's objects in zip files, and this is where it landed. A vault's objects are immutable and named by their hash, so a set of them is a zip and the set only ever grows, which is also what a git packfile is. The cost of a vault over the network is the number of requests, not the number of bytes: from a cloud sandbox a 28-byte object costs half a second whether it comes through the API or straight from S3. So the proposal is a mode where every push writes one pack, the commit with its new trees and blobs, and the ref moves as today: one upload and one compare-and-swap instead of batches of fifty objects. Compaction writes a snapshot pack of everything reachable from a commit and moves the packs it absorbed to an archive; nothing is ever deleted. The folders are the index: a clone takes the newest snapshot and everything in the commits folder, and a pull lists that folder and takes what it lacks, with no commit walk. Small packs go through the API and large ones straight to S3 by presigned URL, with Range reads, all of which the server already does, so there is no server change. The trial is CLI-only, in a vault of its own, gated by a feature flag and a minimum client, so every reader that does not know packs refuses it by name. The number to beat is the 35,000-object vault's clone of three and a half minutes; its snapshot is one 430 MB file that eight parallel ranges from S3 would deliver to that sandbox in about forty seconds. Nothing here is built yet.

![A pack per push, in one picture. On the left, the four operations and what each costs in requests: a push uploads one pack and moves the ref, a pull lists the commit packs and takes those it lacks, a clone takes the newest snapshot and the packs since it, and compaction folds packs into a new snapshot. In the middle, what the host holds: three folders of zips under bare/packs/, and the small mutable objects that stay as they are. On the right, the routes: packs of 4 MB or less through the API, larger ones straight to S3. Dashed boxes are proposed; the routes exist today.](../articles/images/pk-architecture.webp)

*A pack per push, in one picture. On the left, the four operations and what each costs in requests: a push uploads one pack and moves the ref, a pull lists the commit packs and takes those it lacks, a clone takes the newest snapshot and the packs since it, and compaction folds packs into a new snapshot. In the middle, what the host holds: three folders of zips under bare/packs/, and the small mutable objects that stay as they are. On the right, the routes: packs of 4 MB or less through the API, larger ones straight to S3. Dashed boxes are proposed; the routes exist today.*


## In short {#in-short}

- **A vault's objects are immutable and named by their hash, so a set of them is a zip and the
  set only ever grows.** That is also what a git packfile is.
- **The mode: every push writes one pack.** `bare/packs/commits/<epoch>__<commit>__<bytes>.zip`,
  the commit with its new trees and blobs. The ref moves as today. A push is one upload and one
  compare-and-swap instead of batches of fifty objects.
- **Compaction is a snapshot pack**: every object reachable from a commit, in one zip, written to
  `snapshots/`; the commit packs it absorbed move to `archive/`. Nothing is ever deleted.
- **The folders are the index.** A clone fetches the newest snapshot and everything in
  `commits/`. A pull lists `commits/` and takes what it lacks. No commit walk, no listing of
  thirty-five thousand objects.
- **Small packs go through the API, large ones straight to S3** by presigned URL, with `Range`
  for partial reads; the server already does both, and listing, and delete. **No server change.**
- **CLI-only, gated, in its own vault.** A pack vault carries a feature flag and a minimum client
  in its branch index, so every reader that does not know packs refuses it by name. The web app
  and the static readers come later, once the numbers are in.
- **The numbers to beat:** the 35k-object vault clones in 3½ minutes through the API today; its
  snapshot is one 430 MB file that a local server delivered in 3 s and that eight parallel ranges
  from S3 would deliver from here in about 40 s.

## Where the cost is today {#cost-today}

Three days of measuring the same vault from the same sandbox gave one answer: the cost of a vault
over the network is the number of requests, not the number of bytes. A 28-byte object costs
0.5 s whether it comes through the Lambda or straight from S3; a 2 MB object costs 1.5 s; eight
objects in parallel reach 12 MB/s together. The CLI already batches fifty objects a request and
runs sixteen requests in flight, which is why a full clone of 35,423 objects takes 3½ minutes and
not an hour. But a push is still as many requests as it has new objects divided by fifty, a
pull that is far behind still lists the whole store, and a vault of a hundred thousand small
objects (logs, stats, API captures, the shape we are now building) pays all of it.

Git met the same wall twenty years ago and answered with the packfile: many objects in one file,
written once, never changed, with an index beside it. Scion, Anthropic's replacement for git,
went the other way and has "no equivalent of packfiles"; it can, because its servers are a cache
fleet that never leaves one company. A vault's server is a bucket. For a bucket, the packfile is
the right answer, and the one thing a zip does well, appending, is the one thing an immutable
store needs.

## The mode {#mode}

Nothing about a vault's content changes. Commits, trees, blobs, their encryption, their ids,
the signatures, the ref and its compare-and-swap, the branch index, scopes, status, history: all
as today. What changes is how objects travel and where the host keeps them.

```
bare/packs/
  commits/    <epoch>__<commit>__<bytes>.zip   one per push: the commit, its new trees, its new blobs
  snapshots/  <epoch>__<commit>__<bytes>.zip   every object reachable from <commit>
  archive/    <epoch>__<commit>__<bytes>.zip   commit packs a snapshot has absorbed; kept
bare/refs/, bare/indexes/, bare/cache/         unchanged: small, mutable, compare-and-swap
```

Two things are in every name because they are free and useful: an epoch, so a plain listing comes
back in time order (the append lane's entries are named the same way), and the size, so a client
knows before it fetches whether to go through the API (under 4 MB) or straight to S3 (over it).

**Push.** Build the pack from the commit's new objects, as `publish --bundles` already builds a
per-commit delta zip: `ZIP_STORED` because ciphertext does not compress, sorted members, fixed
timestamps, so the same commit always gives the same bytes. Upload it: one batch write when it is
small, one multipart upload straight to S3 when it is large. Then move the ref, with the same
compare-and-swap as today. Two or three requests, whatever the commit's size.

```mermaid
%% A push in pack mode: one pack per pushed commit, sent by the route its size picks, then the same compare-and-swap on the ref as today.
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client, sgit push
    participant A as SG/Send API
    participant S as S3
    C->>C: build one pack per commit, stored, sorted, deterministic
    alt pack of 4 MB or less
        C->>A: batch write packs/commits/epoch__commit__bytes.zip
    else pack over 4 MB
        C->>A: presigned initiate
        A-->>C: one URL per 10 MB part
        C->>S: PUT the parts
        C->>A: presigned complete
    end
    C->>A: compare-and-swap the ref, as today
    A-->>C: moved, or the branch moved on
    C->>C: record the pack in packs_absorbed.json
```

**Pull.** List `bare/packs/commits/`. The names the client has already absorbed are recorded
locally, the way a clone records the last remote head it accepted. Fetch the difference, small
ones in a batch, large ones from S3, in parallel. Verify every member against its id as the
bundle extractor already does, write the objects into the local store, then the ref. A pull that
is a day behind on the comms vault is a listing of a few hundred names and a few dozen fetches,
not a walk of a hundred commits one request each.

```mermaid
%% A pull in pack mode: one listing, the packs this clone has not absorbed, each verified member by member before anything is written.
flowchart TD
    A[sgit pull] --> B[list bare/packs/commits/]
    B --> C{{absorbed already?}}
    C -- yes, in packs_absorbed.json --> D[skip it]
    C -- no --> E{{size in the name}}
    E -- 4 MB or less --> F[batch read, up to 50 packs a request]
    E -- over 4 MB --> G[presigned read-url, parallel Range GETs]
    F --> H[check the size, then every member's id against its bytes]
    G --> H
    H -- a member fails --> I[refuse it, report it, leave the pack unabsorbed]
    H -- all pass --> J[write the objects to the loose store, record the pack]
    J --> K[then the ref and the merge, as today]
```

**Clone.** List `snapshots/`, take the newest, fetch it (one file, or several parallel ranges of
it). List `commits/`, fetch everything there: by construction that is exactly what the snapshot
does not hold. No walk, no listing of the object store. For the comms vault that is the 430 MB
snapshot and a few packs.

```mermaid
%% A clone in pack mode: the newest snapshot, then every commit pack since it, then a local walk that confirms nothing is missing.
flowchart TD
    A[sgit clone] --> B{{client knows packs?}}
    B -- no, says the branch index --> X[refuse by name: run sgit update]
    B -- yes --> C[list snapshots/ and take the newest by epoch]
    C --> D[fetch it: one GET, or parallel 10 MB Range reads]
    D --> E[list commits/ and fetch every pack there]
    E --> F[verify and extract every member]
    F --> G{{local walk complete?}}
    G -- no --> H[fetch what is missing by the ordinary route, a safety net]
    G -- yes --> I[record the packs, check out as today]
    H --> I
```

**Compaction.** Any writer with the write key can run it, when `commits/` holds more than some
number of packs or more than some fraction of the snapshot's size; the trial will find the
numbers. It writes the snapshot to `snapshots/`, reads it back from the host and checks every
expected id is in its directory (a `Range` read of the tail, no members downloaded), and only then
moves each absorbed pack to `archive/`: an upload there and a delete from `commits/`, in that
order, so a crash between the two leaves a pack in both places, which is harmless. Old snapshots
stay. The archive stays. Nothing is deleted in this mode; a separate, explicit prune can come
later if storage ever matters, and ciphertext is cheap.

```mermaid
%% Compaction: build and upload a snapshot, read its directory back before anything moves, then copy each absorbed pack to archive/ before deleting it from commits/. A crash between the last two steps leaves a pack in both places, which is harmless.
flowchart TD
    T{{time to compact?}} -- no --> Z[nothing to do]
    T -- over 50 packs, or a tenth of the snapshot --> A[build a snapshot of every object reachable from the remote head]
    A --> B[upload it to snapshots/]
    B --> C{{directory read back: all ids there?}}
    C -- no --> Y[abort, everything left as it was]
    C -- yes --> D[upload each absorbed pack to archive/]
    D --> E[then delete it from commits/]
    E --> F[old snapshots and the archive stay]
```

**Reading.** First version: packs are extracted into the loose store on arrival, so every read
path in the CLI is untouched. Second version, if it pays: keep the packs and read objects by
offset through a local index over them, which is git's `.idx`. The first version is enough to
measure everything in this article.

## Why a separate vault, and why it is gated {#gated}

A vault that holds only packs is unreadable to the web app and to every static reader, which
look up loose objects by id. Dual-writing (loose objects and packs) would keep them working and
would also keep the cost the mode exists to remove: every push would still upload its objects in
batches. So the trial is packs-only, in a vault of its own, and the vault says so: the branch
index already carries a format gate (`min_client`, `features`) that 0.19.0 built for 128-bit ids
and required signatures, and a pack vault sets `features: [packs]` and a minimum client. Every
older CLI, the web app and the static readers then refuse it by name ("this vault needs
sgit-ai >= X: run sgit update") instead of seeing an empty vault. Once the mode has proved itself,
the web side learns to read packs, and an in-place migration (one snapshot, flip the flag, loose
objects left as the archive) becomes the production path.

```mermaid
%% The gate: a pack vault says so in its branch index, and every reader that does not know packs refuses it by name instead of seeing an empty vault.
flowchart TD
    I[branch index: features packs, min_client] --> N{{reader}}
    N -- sgit with pack mode --> OK[reads the packs]
    N -- an older sgit --> R1[refused: this vault needs a newer sgit-ai, run sgit update]
    N -- the web app or a static reader --> R2[refused by name]
```

**Importing a vault** is a full clone, the re-encryption `vault move` already does (the read key is
derived from the passphrase and the vault id, so a new vault means new keys and new ids for every
object, walked blobs first, then trees, then commits, history intact), one snapshot pack, the ref,
and the index with the flag. The source vault is untouched. The two then live apart, which for a
trial is what you want.

```mermaid
%% Importing a vault: a full clone, re-encrypted under a new key the way vault move does it, written as one snapshot pack. The source is not touched.
flowchart TD
    S[(source vault)] -- full clone --> L[local clone]
    L -- re-encrypt: blobs, trees, commits --> N[new ids under the new key]
    N --> P[one snapshot pack]
    P --> V[(new pack vault: snapshot, ref, index with the flag)]
```

## What it should cost, and how we will know {#should-cost}

| | Today (API, loose objects) | Pack mode (expected) |
|---|---|---|
| push of one small change | 2 to 4 requests | 2 to 3 requests |
| push of 500 new objects | 10 batch requests + ref | 1 upload + ref |
| pull, 50 pushes behind | up to 50 commit requests, then batches | 1 listing + 50 small fetches in batches |
| cold clone, 35k objects | 21 s listing + 700 batch requests, 3½ min | 1 listing + 1 snapshot (430 MB) + a few packs; ~40 s from this sandbox at 12 MB/s, seconds on a good link |
| a vault of 100k objects of 300 bytes | 2,000 batch requests | one 30 MB snapshot |

![Requests, not bytes. Each row is one operation on a vault: the grey bar is today's request count through the batch route, the orange bar the expected count in pack mode, on the same scale. Pack mode wins on large pushes, far-behind pulls and cold clones. The red row is what the bars hide: a scoped clone of one folder is 3 MB today and would be the whole 430 MB snapshot in pack mode's first version. The pack-mode figures are arithmetic, not measurements.](../articles/images/pk-costs.webp)

*Requests, not bytes. Each row is one operation on a vault: the grey bar is today's request count through the batch route, the orange bar the expected count in pack mode, on the same scale. Pack mode wins on large pushes, far-behind pulls and cold clones. The red row is what the bars hide: a scoped clone of one folder is 3 MB today and would be the whole 430 MB snapshot in pack mode's first version. The pack-mode figures are arithmetic, not measurements.*


The tests, on the CLI side, against the dev server with direct S3: a cold clone of the imported
comms vault, pack mode against the batch route; a push loop of a hundred one-file commits, time
and requests per push; pulls after 10, 100 and 1,000 pushes without compaction, then after it,
to set the trigger; two writers pushing at once, which the ref's compare-and-swap already keeps
straight and the packs never collide on. The numbers go in the article that follows this one.

## Side by side: the files and the steps in each mode {#side-by-side}

*This section is not in the CLI team's draft. It was added on cli.sgit.ai on 21 October 2026 at my request, by the site's build agent, from the CLI's code and the spec.*

![The comms vault in each mode. On the left, today: every object one file in data/, and the steps a push, a pull and a cold clone take. On the right, pack mode: the same objects in zips under packs/, and the same three operations. The keys, the refs, the branch index and the cache are the same files in both, in the same places. Colour marks the kind of each file: teal never changes, orange is shared and moves by compare-and-swap, violet has one writer.](../articles/images/pk-side-by-side.webp)

*The comms vault in each mode. On the left, today: every object one file in data/, and the steps a push, a pull and a cold clone take. On the right, pack mode: the same objects in zips under packs/, and the same three operations. The keys, the refs, the branch index and the cache are the same files in both, in the same places. Colour marks the kind of each file: teal never changes, orange is shared and moves by compare-and-swap, violet has one writer.*


The same layout as text, for a reader without the picture:

```text
today (loose)                              pack mode (proposed)
bare/                                      bare/
  data/obj-cas-imm-...   x 35,423            packs/commits/<epoch>__<commit>__<bytes>.zip
                                             packs/snapshots/<epoch>__<commit>__<bytes>.zip
                                             packs/archive/<epoch>__<commit>__<bytes>.zip
  keys/key-rnd-imm-...                       keys/key-rnd-imm-...        unchanged
  refs/ref-pid-muw-...  ref-pid-snw-...      refs/                       unchanged
  indexes/idx-pid-muw-...                    indexes/  + features: [packs]
  cache/  value, pointer                     cache/                      unchanged
```

### Why the two can mix: three kinds of object {#three-kinds}

The reason pack mode is a change of shipping and not a change of format is in the names. Every object a vault stores says in its name what kind it is, and the CLI's code treats the three kinds differently:

| Kind | In the name | Written how | Examples | Pack mode |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Immutable** | `imm` | once, named by its hash (or at random, for a key); a copy anywhere is as good as the original | `obj-cas-imm-…` blobs, trees, commits; `key-rnd-imm-…` public keys | the objects move into zips; still immutable, still checked against their ids |
| **Mutable, many writers** | `muw` | overwritten only by compare-and-swap: a write names the version it replaces, and loses if another got there first | the named branch's ref, the branch index | unchanged |
| **Mutable, one writer** | `snw` | overwritten by its one owner, no race to lose | a clone branch's ref, the cache | unchanged |

So a vault mixes mutable and immutable files today, and that is why the architecture holds together: almost everything is immutable and can be copied, cached, zipped or archived in any shape, because its name is its content; a handful of small files say where the history is, and only they need a host that can compare-and-swap. Pack mode changes the shape of the first group and leaves the second alone. The same split is what lets a whole vault [travel as one file](../articles/a-vault-you-can-carry.md).

## What this does not claim {#limits}

- Nothing is built; the per-commit and head zips exist in `publish --bundles`, the routes exist,
  the rest is the spec.
- The expected costs above are arithmetic from measured request floors and throughputs, from one
  cloud sandbox.
- The web app and static readers cannot read a pack vault; that is by design for the trial.
- A pack vault still has one writer at a time on the ref, as every vault does; packs themselves
  never conflict, because their names are commit ids.

If you keep a vault with tens of thousands of small objects and would like to be in the trial, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.

## Where this comes from {#sources}

Draft for the newsroom, 21 Oct 2026, from three days of conversation of mine with the CLI team on zip storage. Facts from the CLI at `dev` 37218af, the SG/Send server code (0.34.0) and live tests on `dev.send.sgraph.ai` on 16 and 20 Oct. Nothing here is built.

Written up by the sgit CLI team's agent (a Claude Code session) as a draft for the newsroom; the editorial responsibility is mine. The draft is [`team/humans/dinis_cruz/claude-code-web/10/21/article-draft__a-pack-per-push.md`](https://github.com/SGit-AI/SGit-AI__CLI/blob/67025214653476bfe108713ecd83075c6b6155ae/team/humans/dinis_cruz/claude-code-web/10/21/article-draft__a-pack-per-push.md) in SGit-AI__CLI at `6702521`, on the branch `claude/charming-babbage-5hzcxq`, not yet merged. Published on cli.sgit.ai on 21 October 2026 in the newsroom's format: the front matter, the summary, the anchors, this section and the line above it were added, and so were the figures, the six flow diagrams and the section Side by side, drawn and written by cli.sgit.ai's build agent from the draft, [the spec](../research/pack-mode-spec.md) and the CLI's code at `477d328`; the draft's own text is as drafted. The spec is the CLI team's for building it; [the brief to the SG/Send team](../research/zip-append-via-s3-brief.md) of the evening before describes the earlier design this one replaced. The build agent's reading of all three, with five decisions to make, is [Pack mode, read closely](../articles/pack-mode-read-closely.md). # A vault in one file: native zip support for sgit, where it wins, where it loses, and what already exists, cli.sgit.ai

> A vault is files and folders, so it can be a zip. Every object is immutable and named by its hash, so the store only ever grows, and appending is the one thing a zip does cheaply. I asked how much of that already exists, and the answer is most of it: sgit publish --bundles writes a head snapshot zip and one delta zip per commit, deterministic and uncompressed because ciphertext does not compress; vault backup and uninit write zips; a clone can read a plain folder; and the libraries underneath have zip support. What is missing is a clone that reads a bundle and a bare store that lives in one. The cost today is requests, not bytes. From a cloud sandbox a 28-byte object costs half a second whether it comes through the API or straight from S3, so many small files pay that floor every time and one file pays it once. On the article's 12 MB vault, 106 separate requests took 2 to 2.5 seconds and one 12.7 MB zip took 0.05 seconds to fetch and 0.08 to unpack. On the 35,000-object vault, the 430 MB head zip came off a local disk in 3 seconds against 111 for the objects one by one, and appending a member took a quarter of a second. Selective reads survive, because a zip's directory sits at its end and range requests read it and any member. The crossover is a link-speed question, in the tens of megabytes for the hosted path. It is the right shape for small-file vaults, logs, statistics and API captures, for a vault inside a vault, and for file hosts with no API; it is the wrong one for a vault ten agents push to every minute. Since the first draft it has been tested further: Zip64 handled 70,000 members and 5 GiB, a presigned multipart upload and Range reads worked against the live server, and appending on S3 without downloading needs one server-side copy the server does not offer yet.

*Source: <https://cli.sgit.ai/articles/a-vault-in-one-file.html> · generated from the same content as the page, so the two cannot drift.*

---
By [Dinis Cruz](https://sgit.ai/about/) · 2026-10-20 · published

**Summary:** A vault is files and folders, so it can be a zip. Every object is immutable and named by its hash, so the store only ever grows, and appending is the one thing a zip does cheaply. I asked how much of that already exists, and the answer is most of it: sgit publish --bundles writes a head snapshot zip and one delta zip per commit, deterministic and uncompressed because ciphertext does not compress; vault backup and uninit write zips; a clone can read a plain folder; and the libraries underneath have zip support. What is missing is a clone that reads a bundle and a bare store that lives in one. The cost today is requests, not bytes. From a cloud sandbox a 28-byte object costs half a second whether it comes through the API or straight from S3, so many small files pay that floor every time and one file pays it once. On the article's 12 MB vault, 106 separate requests took 2 to 2.5 seconds and one 12.7 MB zip took 0.05 seconds to fetch and 0.08 to unpack. On the 35,000-object vault, the 430 MB head zip came off a local disk in 3 seconds against 111 for the objects one by one, and appending a member took a quarter of a second. Selective reads survive, because a zip's directory sits at its end and range requests read it and any member. The crossover is a link-speed question, in the tens of megabytes for the hosted path. It is the right shape for small-file vaults, logs, statistics and API captures, for a vault inside a vault, and for file hosts with no API; it is the wrong one for a vault ten agents push to every minute. Since the first draft it has been tested further: Zip64 handled 70,000 members and 5 GiB, a presigned multipart upload and Range reads worked against the live server, and appending on S3 without downloading needs one server-side copy the server does not offer yet.

![Requests against one file. Top, measured on the article's 12 MB vault from a local server: 106 separate GETs took 2.0 to 2.5 seconds, one 12.7 MB zip took 0.13 seconds to fetch and unpack. Middle, the 35,000-object vault from local disk: 111 seconds object by object, 3 seconds as one 430 MB zip. Bottom, the shape of the file: members appended one after another and the central directory at the end, so two range requests read the directory and any one member.](../articles/images/a-vault-in-one-file.svg)

*Requests against one file. Top, measured on the article's 12 MB vault from a local server: 106 separate GETs took 2.0 to 2.5 seconds, one 12.7 MB zip took 0.13 seconds to fetch and unpack. Middle, the 35,000-object vault from local disk: 111 seconds object by object, 3 seconds as one 430 MB zip. Bottom, the shape of the file: members appended one after another and the central directory at the end, so two range requests read the directory and any one member.*


## In short {#in-short}

- **A vault is files and folders, so it can be a zip.** Every object is immutable and named by
  its hash, so the store is append-only by nature, which is the one thing a zip does cheaply.
- **Most of it exists.** `sgit publish --bundles` already writes a head snapshot zip and one
  delta zip per commit, deterministic and uncompressed because ciphertext does not compress;
  `vault backup` and `uninit` write zips; `--transport local` reads a folder; OSBot-Utils has a
  zip-bytes library and Memory-FS a zip storage provider. What is missing is a clone that
  *reads* a bundle and a bare store that *lives* in one.
- **The cost today is requests, not bytes.** From the sandbox a 28-byte object costs 0.5 to
  0.6 s whether it comes through the API or straight from S3; a 2 MB object costs 1.5 s; eight
  in parallel reach 12 MB/s. Many small files pay the per-request floor every time; one file
  pays it once.
- **Measured locally on the article's 12 MB vault:** 106 separate GETs, 2.0 to 2.5 s; one
  12.7 MB zip, 0.05 s to fetch and 0.08 s to unpack.
- **The crossover is a link-speed question**, and for the hosted path it sits in the tens of
  megabytes: below it a zip wins outright, above it the zip's cost is bandwidth while the
  objects' cost is the request count, and the batched routes already amortise that.
- **Selective fetch survives.** A zip's central directory sits at its end; one range request
  reads it, one more reads any member. A vault in one file on S3, Dropbox or a Drive that
  honours `Range` is still a vault you can read one file from.
- **Measured on the 35k-object vault:** the 430 MB head zip fetched in 3 s from a local disk
  against 111 s for the objects one by one; appending a member costs 0.25 s; the directory and
  one member read over HTTP `Range` in six requests.
- **It is the right shape for the small-file vaults** (logs, stats, API captures), for a vault
  inside a vault, and for file hosts that have no API at all. It is the wrong shape for a
  shared vault ten agents push to every minute, because every write would rewrite the file's
  directory.

## What a zip is, for this purpose {#zip-this-purpose}

A zip is a sequence of members, each a header followed by its bytes, with a **central
directory** at the end that lists every member and its offset. Three consequences matter here:

1. **Appending is cheap.** To add a member you write it after the last one and rewrite the
   central directory; nothing before it moves. Removing or replacing a member means rewriting
   the file.
2. **Reading one member needs two reads**: the directory (at a known place, the end), then the
   member's bytes at the offset the directory gives. Over HTTP those are two `Range` requests.
3. **Compression is per member and optional.** `ZIP_STORED` keeps bytes as they are, which is
   what `publish --bundles` chose after measuring: DEFLATE on ciphertext came out *larger*
   (1.078× against 1.075×) at ten times the CPU.

Put a vault's object model next to that. Objects are immutable and content-addressed, so they
are only ever appended, never changed; a zip of them is append-only in exactly the way the
format likes. The mutable pointers (the ref, the branch index, cache objects) are the parts a
zip does badly, and they are tiny, so they live beside it or in a second small file.

## What already exists {#already-exists}

| Piece | What it does | Where |
|---|---|---|
| `sgit publish --bundles` | `bundles/head-<commit>.zip` (every object reachable from the head) and `bundles/<commit>.zip` (what that commit introduced); `ZIP_STORED`, fixed timestamps, sorted members, so publishing twice gives identical bytes; "derived, never authoritative": a missing bundle degrades to loose fetches, and every extracted object is id-verified before it is written | `Vault__Publish__Bundles`, 0.18.0 |
| `sgit vault backup` / `restore` | a zip of the vault store with a manifest; `uninit` leaves one; a zip that holds a key is refused at commit | `Vault__Backup`, 0.20–0.21 |
| `--transport local` | a folder is a vault; reads are file reads | `Vault__API__Static` family |
| `--transport static` | any GET host; batch reads fan out to parallel GETs | 0.18.0 |
| `sgit vault mirror` | a keyless, verified copy of a published vault | 0.18.0 |
| OSBot-Utils `Zip_Bytes`, `utils/Zip` | add, replace, remove, list and read members of a zip held as bytes; zip and unzip folders | 3.75.0 |
| Memory-FS `Storage_FS__Zip` | a storage provider whose whole file system is one zip, in memory, saved to disk on demand: `file__save`, `file__bytes`, `file__delete`, `files__paths`, `export_bytes` | installed with the SG/Send server |

So: a vault can already be *written* as one file (the head bundle is a complete bare store),
and the server already runs on a file-system abstraction that has a zip backend. Nobody has yet
made the CLI **clone from** a bundle or **run on** one.

## The numbers {#numbers}

**The per-request floor.** From this sandbox, today, one object of 28 bytes:

| Path | Round trip |
|---|---|
| hosted API (`/api/vault/read/`, Lambda in front of S3, through the sandbox's proxy) | 0.50 to 0.64 s |
| direct S3 (presigned URL, no Lambda, same proxy) | 0.55 to 0.63 s |

The Lambda is not the floor from here; the network path is. One 2.15 MB object takes 1.4 to
1.8 s either way (about 1.3 MB/s on one stream); eight in parallel finish in 1.46 s together,
11.8 MB/s aggregate. Those are this sandbox's numbers; a laptop on a good link has a lower floor
and more bandwidth, and the arithmetic below is written so the reader can put their own in.

**Many objects against one file, locally** (no network at all: a Python file server, the
article's own vault, 83 files, 106 objects, 12.3 MB of ciphertext):

| | Time |
|---|---|
| `sgit clone --transport static` (106 GETs, verified, checked out) | 2.04 s, 2.45 s |
| `GET bundles/head-….zip` (12.7 MB, one request) | 0.05 s |
| unpack it (106 members) | 0.08 s |
| `sgit publish --bundles` (make the zips) | 4.9 s |

Even with zero latency, a hundred small requests cost two seconds of process and protocol; one
file costs a tenth of that.

**The same vault hosted**, which is where the question is interesting:

| | Requests | Bytes | Time from here |
|---|---|---|---|
| clone through the API, 0.22.0 | 2 batches of 50 that overflowed the Lambda, 14 s of back-off, 106 single reads | 12.3 MB | 59 s |
| clone through the API, after the batch fix | ~5 (ref, index, two half-batches, trees) | 12.3 MB | 8 to 10 s |
| one zip from S3 (projected from the measured floor and throughput) | 1 | 12.7 MB | 0.6 s + 12.7 MB ÷ 1.3 MB/s ≈ 10 s on one stream; ≈ 1.7 s if the file is fetched in 8 ranges |

From this slow sandbox the zip and the fixed batch tie at 12 MB. From a client with 20 MB/s the
zip is under 2 s and the batches are still 5 requests deep, so the zip wins by three to four
times. The general rule, with *f* the per-request floor, *B* the bytes, *T* the throughput and
*N* the objects:

- objects: ≈ *f* × (fixed requests + ⌈*N*/50⌉ ÷ 16 in flight) + *B*/*T*
- one zip: ≈ *f* + *B*/*T*

The zip is never slower on bytes and always fewer requests; the objects path only catches up
when *N* is small enough that its batches are a handful, which is the case under about a
hundred objects. Above that, and for every vault of many small files, the single file wins on
the hosted path by the request count, and the gap grows with *N*, not with *B*.

**The large vault** (the comms vault: 35,423 objects, 527 MB; the per-object path from a local
file server was 110 s, from the hosted API 3½ min): 

| | Result |
|---|---|
| `sgit publish --bundles` | 13 min 44 s: one head snapshot of 430 MB (33,886 members, every object reachable from the head) and 1,227 per-commit delta zips (435 MB together, 865 MB in all). Unpacking shows the head zip itself is a matter of seconds; the time is the deltas, one walk of the parents per commit. |
| `GET` the head zip from a local file server | **3.06 s**, one request, 430 MB |
| unpack 33,886 members | 3.92 s |
| per-object static clone of the same vault (earlier run) | 110.6 s |
| open the zip and read its directory (33,886 entries) | 0.31 s; 200 random members then read in 5 ms |
| append one 4 KB member to the 430 MB zip | 0.25 s; the file grows by the member and a rewritten directory, nothing else moves |
| read it over HTTP with `Range` (a test server that honours it) | the directory in 5 requests and 2.7 MB; one member in one more request; 0.15 to 0.23 s in all |

So for the largest vault we have: one file fetched in three seconds against two minutes of
requests from the same disk, a store you can append to in a quarter of a second, and a file you
can read one object out of with two requests. One finding on the way: `sgit serve --static`
answers a `Range` request with the whole file (status 200), so the two-request read needs a host
that honours ranges, which S3 and CloudFront do and the local static server does not yet.

## Where it fits {#fits}

**The bare store as a zip, locally.** `.sg_vault/bare/data/` becomes `.sg_vault/bare/data.zip`:
objects are appended as they are written (a push's new objects, a pull's fetched ones), the
directory is rewritten at the end, and reads come from the zip by offset. Memory-FS's provider
already does the in-memory version; the CLI's object store would need a zip backend behind the
same `exists`/`read`/`write` interface. The mutable files (`refs/`, `indexes/`, `cache/`,
`local/`) stay as files beside it. A vault is then two things you can copy: a zip and a small
folder. That is the "original pedigree" the memo mentions, and it is what a backup already is.

**A clone that reads a bundle.** `sgit clone` from a static host that has `bundles/` fetches
the head bundle in one request (or in ranges), verifies every member by id as `extract_verified`
already does, and walks nothing. A pull from a static host fetches the per-commit delta bundles
for the commits it lacks, which is the union the bundle design promises reconstructs
`bare/data/` exactly. This is git's packfile in the one place sgit should have it: the cold
start from a dumb host.

**Hosting on file storage with no API.** A published vault is a folder of thousands of small
files, which is fine for S3 and GitHub Pages and poor for Google Drive, Dropbox or a NAS share,
where each file is an object with its own metadata and sync cost. As a zip plus a few small
files it is one upload, one download, and one sync. Dropbox staff have said on their forum that
the content-download endpoints honour HTTP `Range` requests; for Google Drive, `alt=media`
downloads are documented and a third-party guide reports `Range` working, which the CLI should
test for a `206` rather than assume. Where `Range` works, a vault in one file is still a vault
you can read one object from: two requests, the directory and the member.

**Vaults of small files.** The stats, log and API-capture vaults in the memo have the shape
that hurts most on per-object hosting (tens of thousands of objects of a few hundred bytes) and
that a zip serves best; the streaming-changes draft's hour-bucket files reduce the count at the
source, and a zip reduces the cost of what remains.

**Vaults within vaults.** A zip is one object, so a whole vault can sit inside another vault as
a single blob, keyed by its own key. The cost is the whole-object rule: a change to the inner
vault is a new blob of its full size. That is right for an archive, a run's evidence, a frozen
release; wrong for an inner vault that changes often.

## Appending to a zip on S3 without downloading it {#appending-zip-on}

A zip's only write is an append, and S3 can do that server-side. A multipart upload's parts can
be **copied from a byte range of an existing object** (`UploadPartCopy`) instead of uploaded, so
"add 40 KB to a 430 MB zip" is one copy part (everything before the old central directory, done
inside S3) plus one uploaded part (the new members and the new directory, about 3 MB here), then
`CompleteMultipartUpload`: four requests and no download. Parts are 5 MB to 5 GB, up to 10,000
of them, so the copied range can be one part up to 5 GB. S3's conditional writes (`If-Match` on
the ETag at complete) give the compare-and-swap: two pushers racing on the zip, the second fails
on the stale ETag, re-copies from the new version and retries, which is the ref's own rule, done
by the storage. The mutable files (ref, index, cache) stay as separate small objects overwritten
with the same `If-Match`, so nothing inside the zip is ever rewritten. Standard S3 has no in-place
append (S3 Express One Zone does); the copy is the trick, and it needs no Lambda. These are
documented S3 features, not exercised from this sandbox, which has no S3 credentials.

## What works today, tested on the live server {#works-today-tested}

Tested on 20 Oct against `dev.send.sgraph.ai` (S3 storage) on a throwaway vault, created and
deleted in the same run, with the routes the CLI already has:

| Step | Route | Result |
|---|---|---|
| start a multipart upload of a 12.6 MB object | `POST /api/vault/presigned/initiate` (write key) | S3 multipart created; two presigned `PUT` URLs for parts of 10 MB; 9.0 s (a cold Lambda) |
| upload the parts straight to S3 | presigned `PUT` ×2 | 10.5 MB in 3.6 s, 2.1 MB in 1.2 s, from this sandbox |
| assemble | `POST /api/vault/presigned/complete` | `status: ok`, 0.8 s |
| read a slice | `GET /api/vault/presigned/read-url` then `GET` with `Range` | `206 Partial Content` for the head (0–1023), the tail (last 2 KB) and the middle (6,000,000–6,001,023); bytes matched |
| read the whole object | `read_large` (the CLI's path) | matched, 12,582,912 bytes |

So the download half of "a vault in one file" works now: a zip pushed as a vault object can be
read by `Range`, which means the directory at its tail and then any member, through the existing
read-url route. And the zip's determinism (sorted members, fixed timestamps) plus append-only
growth give a second property for free: a client that holds version *N* of the zip knows the
offset of *N*'s directory, and everything version *N+1* added sits between that offset and
*N+1*'s directory. **An incremental pull from an appended zip is one `Range` request for the new
tail.** A sidecar index (the manifest `publish` already writes, with member offsets added) turns
"find the directory" into one small `GET`.

What the server does not offer yet, read from its code (`Service__Vault__Presigned`): it signs
`upload_part` only, never `upload_part_copy`, and it passes no `If-Match` to
`complete_multipart_upload`. So append-by-copy needs one small server addition, and the clean
shape is a route rather than a signed copy URL: `POST /api/vault/presigned/append` takes the
source object, the expected ETag and the tail's size; the server itself issues one
`UploadPartCopy` of the source (a server-side S3 call that moves no bytes through the Lambda),
returns the upload id and part URLs for the tail, and `complete` passes `IfMatch` so a stale
append fails instead of clobbering. Three functions in one service file.

## Where it does not fit {#does-not-fit}

- **Many writers.** Every append rewrites the central directory, and concurrent appends to one
  file need a lock the hosted server does not give. The shared comms vault stays as objects;
  the zip is for local stores, publication and transport.
- **Partial clones from a zip over HTTP are two requests per object**, not one, and the
  directory for a large vault is itself megabytes (35k entries is a few MB). Fine for "read
  three files from a published vault"; not a replacement for the batch route when a client
  wants half the objects.
- **The classic zip limits do not apply, with one reader caveat.** The 1989 format counts
  members in 16 bits and sizes and offsets in 32 bits (65,535 members, 4 GiB); Zip64, in the
  spec since 2001, makes them 64-bit. Verified here: Python's `zipfile` wrote a 70,000-member
  zip and a 5.00 GiB zip and Info-ZIP's `unzip` read both back. Only a reader that never
  implemented Zip64 (some minimal or browser-side libraries) would refuse them.
- **It changes nothing about security.** The members are the same ciphertext under the same
  names; a zip on a Drive is as readable to the host as the folder was, which is not at all.

## What this does not claim {#limits}

- No clone reads a bundle today, and no bare store lives in a zip; both are proposals.
- The hosted timings are from one cloud sandbox whose every request leaves through a proxy; the
  floor and the throughput are that sandbox's.
- Range support on Drive and Dropbox is reported, not verified here.

## Questions for the thread (each a code change) {#questions-thread-code}

0. **Server: `presigned/append`** (one `UploadPartCopy` of the source object plus part URLs for the
   tail) and `IfMatch` on complete. The only server change in this list; everything below is
   client-side.
1. **`clone --transport static` reads `bundles/head-*.zip` when it is there**, verifying each
   member by id; `pull` reads the delta bundles for missing commits; loose fetch stays the
   fallback. Smallest change, largest win on dumb hosts.
2. **A zip backend for the object store** (`bare/data.zip`, append on write, read by offset),
   behind the existing store interface; `refs/`, `indexes/`, `cache/` stay as files. Memory-FS's
   provider is the model.
3. **Range reads of a zip over HTTP** in the static transport: directory then member; test for
   `206` and fall back to a whole-file fetch. And `sgit serve --static` should answer `Range`
   with `206`, which it does not today.
4. **`sgit vault pack` / `unpack`** as the user-facing verbs (a backup that a clone can open), or
   fold them into `publish --bundles` and `clone`.
5. **A `--host` recipe for Drive and Dropbox**: publish as zip + manifest, and the read path for
   each, once `Range` is confirmed.

If you keep many small files in a vault, or need one on a file host that has no API, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.

## Where this comes from {#sources}

Draft for the newsroom and a brief for the CLI team, 20 Oct 2026, from a voice memo of mine. Facts from the CLI at `dev` 37218af, OSBot-Utils 3.75.0, Memory-FS, and measurements made that day from a cloud sandbox against the hosted API, direct S3 and a local file server. Nothing proposed is built; what exists is named as such.

Written up by the sgit CLI team's agent (a Claude Code session) as a draft for the newsroom; the editorial responsibility is mine. The draft is [`team/humans/dinis_cruz/claude-code-web/10/20/article-draft__native-zip-support.md`](https://github.com/SGit-AI/SGit-AI__CLI/blob/67025214653476bfe108713ecd83075c6b6155ae/team/humans/dinis_cruz/claude-code-web/10/20/article-draft__native-zip-support.md) in SGit-AI__CLI at `6702521`, on the branch `claude/charming-babbage-5hzcxq`. Published on cli.sgit.ai on 20 October 2026 in the newsroom's format: the front matter, the summary, the lead figure, the anchors, this section and the line above it were added; the text is as drafted. # A vault you can carry: one zip holds the whole vault, a public key can seal it, and the round trip already works, cli.sgit.ai

> Reading the pack-mode article, I wanted three things made explicit. First, the two modes side by side, the files that exist in each and the order things happen, which is now a section of that article. Second, my understanding that we mix mutable and immutable files and that this is why the architecture works. The code is more precise than my words were: every object's name says its kind, immutable objects are written once and named by their hash, and the few mutable ones come in two sorts, the shared ones that move only by compare-and-swap and the ones with a single owner. Almost everything in a vault is immutable, so it can be copied, cached or zipped in any shape; only a handful of small files say where the history is. Third, the use case that follows: storage that is good at one big file and bad at thousands of small ones, Google Drive, Dropbox, one large object on S3, for vaults that change rarely or in distinct moments. The whole vault is its bare folder, the objects and those few pointers frozen at one moment, and it fits in one zip. Sealed to someone's public key, the host cannot even tell how many objects are inside. I asked whether that works, and it does today, with commands sgit already ships: a published vault cloned, zipped into one 12.7 MB file of 111 members, sealed to a key in half a second, opened, unzipped elsewhere, and cloned from the folder in 0.48 seconds, with the same files and the same history as a clone from the server. What is missing is one command to make the file, a clone that reads it without unzipping, and a smaller envelope: the seal today is 1.78 times the zip.

*Source: <https://cli.sgit.ai/articles/a-vault-you-can-carry.html> · generated from the same content as the page, so the two cannot drift.*

---
By [Dinis Cruz](https://sgit.ai/about/) · 2026-10-21 · published

**Summary:** Reading the pack-mode article, I wanted three things made explicit. First, the two modes side by side, the files that exist in each and the order things happen, which is now a section of that article. Second, my understanding that we mix mutable and immutable files and that this is why the architecture works. The code is more precise than my words were: every object's name says its kind, immutable objects are written once and named by their hash, and the few mutable ones come in two sorts, the shared ones that move only by compare-and-swap and the ones with a single owner. Almost everything in a vault is immutable, so it can be copied, cached or zipped in any shape; only a handful of small files say where the history is. Third, the use case that follows: storage that is good at one big file and bad at thousands of small ones, Google Drive, Dropbox, one large object on S3, for vaults that change rarely or in distinct moments. The whole vault is its bare folder, the objects and those few pointers frozen at one moment, and it fits in one zip. Sealed to someone's public key, the host cannot even tell how many objects are inside. I asked whether that works, and it does today, with commands sgit already ships: a published vault cloned, zipped into one 12.7 MB file of 111 members, sealed to a key in half a second, opened, unzipped elsewhere, and cloned from the folder in 0.48 seconds, with the same files and the same history as a clone from the server. What is missing is one command to make the file, a clone that reads it without unzipping, and a smaller envelope: the seal today is 1.78 times the zip.

![A vault in one file. On the left, what goes in: the vault's bare/ folder as it is, 106 encrypted objects and 2 public keys that never change, and 3 small pointers that say where the history is, frozen at the moment the file was made; 111 files, 12.7 MB as one stored zip. On the right, what must stay out: the clone's own local/ folder, which holds its key. Below it, how the file is read back today, and what is not built yet.](../articles/images/of-anatomy.webp)

*A vault in one file. On the left, what goes in: the vault's bare/ folder as it is, 106 encrypted objects and 2 public keys that never change, and 3 small pointers that say where the history is, frozen at the moment the file was made; 111 files, 12.7 MB as one stored zip. On the right, what must stay out: the clone's own local/ folder, which holds its key. Below it, how the file is read back today, and what is not built yet.*


## In short {#in-short}

- **The two modes are now drawn side by side** in [A pack per push](../articles/a-pack-per-push.md#side-by-side): the files on the host and the steps of a push, a pull and a clone.
- **A vault mixes immutable and mutable files, and that is why it works.** Immutable objects are named by their hash and can be copied anywhere; the few mutable ones move by compare-and-swap or have one owner.
- **So a whole vault fits in one file:** its `bare/` folder, the objects and the pointers frozen at one moment, zipped. Never the clone's `local/` folder, which holds its key.
- **That suits storage that prefers big files**, Drive, Dropbox, one S3 object, for vaults that change rarely or at distinct moments.
- **A public key can seal it.** Then the place that stores it cannot see how many objects are inside, their sizes, or which vault it is.
- **It works today, measured:** a published vault zipped, sealed, opened, unzipped and cloned from the folder in 0.48 seconds, the same files and history as from the server.
- **What is missing:** one command to make the file, a clone that reads the zip directly, and a binary envelope; the seal is 1.78 times the zip today.

## Side by side first {#side-by-side}

The first thing I felt the pack-mode article was missing was the picture of the two modes next to each other: which files exist in each, and what happens, in order, when a push, a pull or a clone runs. That is now a section of [A pack per push](../articles/a-pack-per-push.md#side-by-side), and it is where this one starts, because the same picture explains everything below.

## Mutable and immutable, at the same time {#mutable-immutable}

My understanding was that we mix mutable and immutable files at the same time, that most of the data is immutable and the mutable files can simply be copied on top of each other, and that this is why the architecture works so well. The first two are right, and the code is more precise about the third. Every object a vault stores says in its name what kind it is:

| Kind | In the name | How it is written | In the vault measured below |
|---|---|---|---|
| Immutable | `imm` | once, named by its hash (a key at random); never changed | 106 objects and 2 public keys |
| Mutable, many writers | `muw` | only by compare-and-swap: a write names the version it replaces and loses if someone else got there first | the named branch's ref and the branch index, 2 files |
| Mutable, one writer | `snw` | by its one owner, so there is no race | a clone branch's ref, 1 file |

So the mutable files are not copied over each other freely: the shared ones are moved under a rule that makes two writers safe. But the shape I had in mind holds. Nearly all of a vault is immutable, and an immutable object can live anywhere, be copied any number of times and be packed in any container, because its name is its content and every reader checks it. Only a handful of small files have to be kept straight, and only writing them needs a host that can compare-and-swap. Reading needs nothing at all from the host but the bytes.

## What that makes possible: a vault in one file {#one-file}

If the immutable part can be shipped in any shape, and the mutable part is three small files, then the whole vault can be one file. That matters for storage that is good at large files and bad at thousands of small ones: Google Drive, Dropbox, a single large object on S3, a USB stick, an attachment. It suits a vault that does not change much, or changes at distinct moments: a release, a report, an archive of a run, the evidence for an audit, a dataset handed over once.

The structure is not new, it is the vault's own folder:

```text
vault.zip
  bare/data/obj-cas-imm-...      every object reachable from the head (106 here)
  bare/keys/key-rnd-imm-...      the public keys (2)
  bare/refs/ref-pid-muw-...      the named branch's head, frozen
  bare/refs/ref-pid-snw-...      a clone branch's head, frozen
  bare/indexes/idx-pid-muw-...   the branch index, frozen
  (never .sg_vault/local/: that is one clone's private state, with its key)
```

The objects in `bare/data/` are exactly what pack mode calls a snapshot pack. The pointers are what turn a snapshot into a vault you can clone: without them a reader would have the objects and no idea where the history starts. So the answer to "is the zip just the snapshot?" is: the snapshot, plus three small files frozen with it.

## Sealed with a public key {#sealed}

The file is already ciphertext: the object names are hashes and the contents are encrypted under the vault's read key. Sealing it to someone's public key adds a second lock with a different purpose. It hides the shape, and it names who can open it.

![What the place that stores the vault can see in each shape. Loose on a server: the vault id, the number and sizes of the objects, and who fetches what. One zip on Drive, Dropbox or S3: one file, and the zip's own directory of object ids and sizes. The same zip sealed to a public key: one file and its size, and nothing about what is inside. No host reads a filename, a file or a commit message in any of the three.](../articles/images/of-host-sees.webp)

*What the place that stores the vault can see in each shape. Loose on a server: the vault id, the number and sizes of the objects, and who fetches what. One zip on Drive, Dropbox or S3: one file, and the zip's own directory of object ids and sizes. The same zip sealed to a public key: one file and its size, and nothing about what is inside. No host reads a filename, a file or a commit message in any of the three.*


The cost is that a sealed file has to be opened whole. A plain zip can be read one member at a time by `Range` from a host that serves ranges; a sealed one cannot, until it is opened.

## It already works {#works-today}

I asked whether this would work with what sgit has today, and it was tried on a vault whose read key is published on purpose, the newsroom's synthetic-users vault from [sgit.ai's catalogue](https://sgit.ai/demos/vaults/index.html):

![The round trip, step by step, with the time each took. 1, clone the vault from the hosted server, 13.7 seconds. 2, zip its bare/ folder, 111 files into one 12.7 MB file. 3, seal it to a public key with sgit pki encrypt, 0.47 seconds, a 22.5 MB envelope. 4, open it with the private key, 0.82 seconds, the same zip byte for byte. 5, unzip it into any folder. 6, clone from that folder with sgit clone --transport local, 0.48 seconds, the same working tree and the same three commits.](../articles/images/of-round-trip.webp)

*The round trip, step by step, with the time each took. 1, clone the vault from the hosted server, 13.7 seconds. 2, zip its bare/ folder, 111 files into one 12.7 MB file. 3, seal it to a public key with sgit pki encrypt, 0.47 seconds, a 22.5 MB envelope. 4, open it with the private key, 0.82 seconds, the same zip byte for byte. 5, unzip it into any folder. 6, clone from that folder with sgit clone --transport local, 0.48 seconds, the same working tree and the same three commits.*


```mermaid
%% Who holds what in the round trip. The file host only ever holds an opaque file; the recipient's private key and the vault's read key are what open it, and neither is ever on the file host.
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as The author
    participant H as A file host: Drive, Dropbox, S3
    participant R as The recipient
    A->>A: sgit clone, then zip bare/ into vault.zip
    A->>A: sgit pki encrypt --recipient their key
    A->>H: upload vault.zip.enc, one file
    R->>H: download vault.zip.enc
    R->>R: sgit pki decrypt with their private key
    R->>R: unzip into a folder
    R->>R: sgit clone --transport local with the read key
    Note over R: a full clone: every file, every commit, nothing fetched from a server
```

Every step is a command sgit ships or a plain zip. The clone from the folder has the same files as the one from the server and the same three commits, `sgit status` reads clean, and it took 0.48 seconds against 13.7 from the hosted API, because nothing crossed a network.

## What is missing {#missing}

- **One command.** Today it is a clone, a zip, a seal; the file deserves a command of its own that zips exactly `bare/`, refuses to include `local/`, and names the format.
- **A clone that reads the file directly,** from a path or a URL, without unzipping, and by `Range` where the host allows it. The pack-mode spec's version 2 reads a snapshot's directory this way, so the code would be shared.
- **A smaller seal.** The envelope `sgit pki encrypt` writes is base64 inside JSON, and the whole is base64 again: 1.78 times the zip, which is exactly four thirds squared. A binary envelope would be about the zip's own size. That one is for the CLI team.
- **Carrying the read key.** The sealed file still needs the read key to clone. Putting the read key inside the sealed envelope would make the recipient's private key the only credential they need; that is a design, not a feature.
- **Writing back.** A clone from a folder is read-only, by design. A file on Drive has no compare-and-swap, so the honest pattern is one writer: change the vault in a live one and make the file again. Many writers belong on a host with compare-and-swap, which is what [pack mode](../articles/a-pack-per-push.md) is for.

## What this does not claim {#limits}

- **One run, one vault.** 111 files and 12.7 MB is a small vault; the times are from one cloud sandbox. A large vault's file is large: the comms vault's snapshot is 430 MB.
- **Nothing here is a new command.** The round trip used shipped commands and a hand-made zip; the missing pieces above are proposed.
- **Range reads on Drive and Dropbox** are reported, not verified here; on S3 they were measured on 20 October.
- **A sealed file hides the vault's shape from its host, not from its recipient,** who can open everything the read key opens.
- **The throwaway key pair** used for the seal was made for this run and is not published.

If you would like to keep a vault on Drive, Dropbox or one S3 object, or to hand one to someone as a sealed file, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.

## Where this comes from {#sources}

A message of mine on 21 October 2026, written up by cli.sgit.ai's build agent, cli.build, on the same day; the editorial responsibility is mine. The agent ran the round trip in a cloud sandbox with sgit-ai 0.23.0 from PyPI: `sgit clone` of the newsroom-synthetic-users vault with its published read key (listed in [sgit.ai's vault catalogue](https://sgit.ai/demos/vaults/index.html)), a stored zip of `.sg_vault/bare/`, `sgit pki keygen` for a throwaway recipient, `sgit pki encrypt --recipient`, `sgit pki decrypt --fingerprint`, an unzip, and `sgit clone --transport local --base-url <folder>`; `diff -r` compared the two working trees and `sgit history log` the commits. The three kinds of object are from the CLI's code at `477d328`: `Enum__Cache_Mutability` (`snw`, `muw`), `Vault__Crypto` (`obj-cas-imm-`, `ref-pid-muw-`), `Vault__Key_Manager` (`key-rnd-imm-`); that a writable clone keeps its vault key in `.sg_vault/local/vault_key` and a read-only one its read key in `clone_mode.json` is from the CLI team's [coverage map](../research/keys-pki-copy-on-write-coverage-map.md). The envelope ratio is the measured sizes, 22,530,348 bytes against 12,672,752. The pack-mode facts are from [the spec](../research/pack-mode-spec.md). The research topic: [How a vault takes writes](../research/topics/write-path.md).
