# Copy-on-write, and what it would mean for a vault: what rUv's team asked for, what sgit already does, and the write-ahead lane that would do the rest, cli.sgit.ai

> After I presented ruv.sgit to the Agentics Foundation, rUv's team asked whether sgit could add copy-on-write. I wanted to know what that would mean for a vault before saying yes or no. Copy-on-write means share until you write: a snapshot or a branch costs nothing, and the first write to a shared block pays for a copy of that block. Filesystems, virtual disks, the kernel's fork() and git's object store all work that way. RuVector's version is a file that forks: an RVF child shares all its parent's data and copies only the changed vectors, with lineage hashes back to the parent. sgit is already copy-on-write where git is. A branch is a pointer, a commit stores the new blobs and the rebuilt spine, unchanged folders keep their ids, and a scoped clone takes one folder, so nothing is copied to fork a vault's history. There are two places it is not. Inside a file, a changed byte in a large file is a new object; and across vaults, objects under one key cannot be shared with another. Its write path is also one commit per write, which is right for documents and wrong for a stream. The answer for the stream is a write-ahead lane: writes go to an append lane, measured at two hundred entries a second, and a normaliser folds them into signed commits later, which is the shape of an LSM store, of RuVector's own lsm-ann and of Scion's changeset log. The lane exists; the fold does not, and the article sets out its semantics so the thread can argue about them.

*Source: <https://cli.sgit.ai/articles/copy-on-write-and-the-vault.html> · generated from the same content as the page, so the two cannot drift.*

---
By [Dinis Cruz](https://sgit.ai/about/) · 2026-10-16 · published

**Summary:** After I presented ruv.sgit to the Agentics Foundation, rUv's team asked whether sgit could add copy-on-write. I wanted to know what that would mean for a vault before saying yes or no. Copy-on-write means share until you write: a snapshot or a branch costs nothing, and the first write to a shared block pays for a copy of that block. Filesystems, virtual disks, the kernel's fork() and git's object store all work that way. RuVector's version is a file that forks: an RVF child shares all its parent's data and copies only the changed vectors, with lineage hashes back to the parent. sgit is already copy-on-write where git is. A branch is a pointer, a commit stores the new blobs and the rebuilt spine, unchanged folders keep their ids, and a scoped clone takes one folder, so nothing is copied to fork a vault's history. There are two places it is not. Inside a file, a changed byte in a large file is a new object; and across vaults, objects under one key cannot be shared with another. Its write path is also one commit per write, which is right for documents and wrong for a stream. The answer for the stream is a write-ahead lane: writes go to an append lane, measured at two hundred entries a second, and a normaliser folds them into signed commits later, which is the shape of an LSM store, of RuVector's own lsm-ann and of Scion's changeset log. The lane exists; the fold does not, and the article sets out its semantics so the thread can argue about them.

![Share until you write. On the left, two commits of a vault: the second has a new tree for the one folder that changed, and points at the first commit's trees and blobs for everything else, so a branch or a new commit copies nothing. On the right, the proposed write-ahead lane for streams: many small writes land in an append lane, and a fold later turns a batch of them into one signed commit. The lane exists; the fold is proposed.](../articles/images/copy-on-write-and-the-vault.svg)

*Share until you write. On the left, two commits of a vault: the second has a new tree for the one folder that changed, and points at the first commit's trees and blobs for everything else, so a branch or a new commit copies nothing. On the right, the proposed write-ahead lane for streams: many small writes land in an append lane, and a fold later turns a batch of them into one signed commit. The lane exists; the fold is proposed.*


## In short {#in-short}

- **Copy-on-write means share until you write.** A snapshot or a branch costs nothing; the first
  write to a shared block pays for a copy of that block. Filesystems, virtual disks, the kernel's
  `fork()` and git's object store all do it.
- **RuVector's version is a file that forks.** An RVF child "shares all parent data; only changed
  vectors are copied", at cluster granularity, with lineage hashes back to the parent and a
  witness chain. That is what "add copy-on-write" meant.
- **sgit is already copy-on-write where git is.** A branch is a pointer; a commit stores the new
  blobs and the rebuilt spine; unchanged folders keep their ids; a scoped clone takes one folder.
  Nothing is copied to fork a vault's history.
- **Two places it is not.** Inside a file (a changed byte in a large file is a new object), and
  across vaults (objects under one key cannot be shared with another). And its write path is one
  commit per write, which is right for documents and wrong for a stream.
- **The answer for the stream is a write-ahead lane.** Writes go to an append lane, measured at
  two hundred entries a second; a normaliser folds them into signed commits later. That is an
  LSM store's shape, RuVector's own `lsm-ann` shape, and Scion's changeset log.
- **Nothing here is built.** The lane exists, the compaction does not; the semantics are set out
  below so the thread can argue about them.

## What copy-on-write is {#copy-on-write}

The idea is forty years old and shows up wherever copies are expensive. A ZFS or btrfs or APFS
snapshot is free because it only records "this is what the tree looked like"; blocks are copied
when something later writes to them, and the snapshot keeps the old ones. A virtual machine's
disk image is a chain of layers for the same reason. `fork()` gives the child the parent's pages
and copies a page only when one of them writes to it. The cost moves from the copy, which may
never be needed, to the first write, which is small; the gain is that snapshots and branches are
instant and most of the data is shared.

Git is copy-on-write at the object level. A commit points at a tree; a tree points at blobs and
subtrees by hash; a new commit that changes one file writes one blob and the trees on the path
to it, and shares everything else. Branching is writing a 40-byte pointer. The one thing git
adds is delta compression in packfiles, which is a storage optimisation, not the model.

## What RuVector means by it {#ruvector-means-by}

The memo's request came from rUv's team, so the reference is theirs. RuVector's README lists
"Copy on write branches: isolated memory experiments without full copies" under the RVF file
format, and the RVF README says what that is: "Git-like branching. Create a child file that
shares all parent data. Only changed vectors are copied. A 1M-vector parent with 100 edits
produces a ~2.5 MB child instead of a 512 MB copy", implemented as a `COW_MAP` segment at cluster
granularity, with "DNA-style lineage" (every file records its parent and derivation with hashes)
and a SHAKE-256 witness chain over every operation; append-only, so a crash cannot corrupt it.
The verb is `rvf derive`. ruv.sgit.ai records that RuVector "already has snapshots and
copy-on-write branching (`rvf derive`)", and that POC2 wraps those memory files in an sgit vault.

So the request is: when an agent's memory lives in a vault, forking it for an experiment, or
snapshotting it before a run, should cost nothing, keep its lineage, and be verifiable. That is
a fair ask, and most of it is already there.

## Where sgit already is one {#sgit-already}

| Operation | What is copied | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `sgit branch new` | a ref | a branch is a pointer to a commit, as in git |
| a commit that changes one file | the new blob and the trees on the spine | an unchanged folder is one tree id across every commit it survives, so it is stored and fetched once |
| a clone of one folder (`--path`) | the spine and the folder | the rest is carried by id and never downloaded |
| a snapshot before a run | nothing | the commit id is the snapshot; `history reset` goes back to it; `vault tag` names it and signs it |
| lineage | nothing extra | every commit names its parents and is signed by the clone's key; `sgit check verify` walks the chain |
| the witness chain | nothing extra | content addressing: every object is named by the hash of its ciphertext, so a tampered byte fails before it is read |

The newsroom measured the consequence under *Agent workflows on ephemeral vaults*: ten scoped
clones at once in 1.9 s; a one-folder clone that went from 0.59 s at 100 files to 0.77 s at
2,000 while a full clone went from 0.95 s to 5.55 s. Forking an agent's memory in sgit is
`sgit branch new`; snapshotting it is the commit that already happened.

## Where it is not, honestly {#not-honestly}

**Inside a file.** sgit's unit is the whole object. A changed byte in a 100 MB file is a new
100 MB object, and a clone that wants the new version fetches all of it. RVF copies the changed
cluster. This is the trade the Scion response praised from the other side: a whole object named
by its hash is something any cache can keep blindly, with no deltas to resolve. For documents
and code-sized files it is the right trade. For a 512 MB vector store edited a hundred times it
is not, and the fix would be content-defined chunking of blobs over a threshold, so that a changed
region is a new chunk and every chunk stays an immutable `-imm-` object. That is a format
addition and a later step; the memo's question about performance is really about the next
point.

**Across vaults.** Objects are encrypted under the vault's data key, so a second vault cannot
point at the first vault's objects. A derived vault is either a branch of the same vault or a
re-encryption. The sub-vault convention (one vault referencing another by key, as git
submodules do) covers the "compose" case; it does not give a cheap fork across a key boundary,
and it should not, because that boundary is the point.

**The write path.** `sgit write` is a commit, a spine rebuild and a push: in the ruv.sgit ledger,
0.4 to 1.5 s an operation against a local server, including Python start-up and key derivation.
That is right for a document, a debrief, a policy. It is wrong for an agent that writes a memory
entry every second, or a swarm of a hundred that each write a line: a hundred commits a second
would mean a hundred compare-and-swaps on one ref, and the tree would be rebuilt a hundred times.
Scion's post says the same about its own scale: "the cost of creating a commit … has to scale
with the size of the change, not the overall size of the repo, or the server can't keep up."

## The write-ahead lane {#write-ahead-lane}

The memo's proposal is the right shape, and it has a name in every storage system: a
write-ahead log with compaction. Writes land in something cheap and append-only; a background
step folds them into the structured store. Log-structured merge trees do this (RuVector's
`ruvector-lsm-ann`: "mutable L0 memory plus background L1 and L2 compaction"); Scion's
changesets are an append-only write-ahead log that derived indexes are built from; even RVF's
"append-only design" is the same instinct.

sgit already has the cheap append-only thing: the **append lane**, a write-only channel on a
vault gated by a token, with no account and no tree. The newsroom measured a hundred writers
landing a thousand entries in 4.9 s on the in-memory server, none lost, and the caps are 1,000
waiting entries per inbox and 5 MB per entry. So the design is:

1. **`write` goes to the lane**, not to a commit: one POST carrying the path, the content (or a
   content hash and the blob), the writer's key id and a signature. Sub-second, no CAS, no tree.
2. **A normaliser folds the lane into commits**: on a schedule, on a count, or when a reader
   asks. It reads the lane with the enum key, verifies each entry's signature, de-duplicates by
   content hash, builds one tree with all the changes, makes one signed commit, pushes it with
   one compare-and-swap, and marks the entries processed. A hundred writes become one commit,
   which is also what a human would have wanted to read.
3. **A reader between compactions** sees HEAD plus the lane entries newer than HEAD, in order,
   which is what an LSM read does across levels. `sgit cat` can do that merge; a page can too.
4. **Lineage is kept twice**: the lane entry names the writer's key and the folded commit names
   the entries it absorbed (their hashes), so a line of memory can be traced from the commit back
   to the entry and the key that wrote it. That is RVF's lineage, in sgit's vocabulary.

What it costs: a window in which the committed history is behind the lane (bounded by the
compaction interval, like the ref's freshness window for readers); a normaliser that holds the
write key and runs somewhere; and the lane's own caps, which mean compaction has to keep up or
writers get refused at 1,000 waiting entries, which is the back-pressure you want. What it buys:
writes at the lane's speed, one commit per batch, no change to the object model, and the
copy-on-write property intact, because the folded commit still shares every unchanged subtree.

## What this does not claim {#limits}

- Nothing above the lane is built: no `write --lane`, no normaliser, no read-across-levels.
- Chunked blobs are a sketch, not a design; the whole-object model is kept on purpose until the
  large-file case needs it.
- A derived *vault* that shares objects with its parent is not possible across keys and is not
  proposed; the fork is a branch.
- The RuVector and RVF facts are from their READMEs as read on 16 October; "per its README"
  means read, not run.

If you have a workload that writes to a vault many times a second, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.

## Where this comes from {#sources}

Draft for the newsroom, 16 Oct 2026, from a voice memo of mine after presenting ruv.sgit to the Agentics Foundation. Facts from RuVector's and RVF's READMEs, ruv.sgit.ai, the sgit.ai pages it links and the CLI at `dev` 37218af. Nothing proposed here is built. The research behind it is [the coverage map](../research/keys-pki-copy-on-write-coverage-map.md).

Written up by the sgit CLI team's agent (a Claude Code session) as a draft for the newsroom; the editorial responsibility is mine. The draft is [`team/humans/dinis_cruz/claude-code-web/10/16/article-draft__copy-on-write-and-the-vault.md`](https://github.com/SGit-AI/SGit-AI__CLI/blob/5473571736e80608f50944fe479e278cfa9faba0/team/humans/dinis_cruz/claude-code-web/10/16/article-draft__copy-on-write-and-the-vault.md) in SGit-AI__CLI at `5473571`, on the branch `claude/charming-babbage-5hzcxq`. # Articles, cli.sgit.ai

> Articles on cli.sgit.ai, newest first, in the newsroom's format: each one argument about the sgit CLI, written up from Dinis Cruz's memos or by an agent about what it delivered, with what it does not claim and where it comes from.

*Source: <https://cli.sgit.ai/articles/index.html> · generated from the same content as the page, so the two cannot drift.*

# Articles

Each article makes **one argument** about the sgit CLI, in the format the [newsroom](https://newsroom.sgit.ai/) uses, so any of them can be imported there unchanged: a summary a reader can stop at, a lead figure, In short, the argument, what it does not claim, and where it comes from. The format is the one send.sgit.ai's [Every site its own articles](https://send.sgit.ai/articles/every-site-its-own-articles.html) sets out for every site in the network.

There are two kinds of author, and the byline says which:

- **Dinis Cruz**, through an agent: a voice memo or a message of his, written up in his voice, under his name.
- **An agent in its own voice**: cli.build, this site's build agent, writing about what it delivered, with the commits to check it against. [The team](../about/team.md) says who each is.

The work behind most of them is in [Research](../research/index.md): the CLI team's documents, published as written and grouped into topics. An article is the argument; the research is the record. [Research is not an article](../articles/research-is-not-an-article.md) says why the two are kept apart.

- [Is there any overhead? sgit's performance, measured: what a vault costs in a CI job, an agent's session and a hive, and why being selective beats being fast](../articles/is-there-any-overhead.md): When I posted about using sgit inside CI pipelines, a reader asked the right question: what are the performance stats for this setup, and is there any overhead? There is, and it is worth stating exactly. Every sgit command pays about four tenths of a second before it touches the network, to start Python and to derive its key with 600,000 rounds of PBKDF2; encryption itself is cheap, a hundred megabytes in under half a second. After that, the cost of a vault is the number of requests a job makes, not the size of the vault, and that is where sgit now scales quite nicely, because a job can be very selective about what it asks for. A clone of one folder with --path stays between 0.59 and 0.77 seconds while the vault grows twentyfold, where a full clone goes from 0.95 to 5.55. One folder at one commit of our biggest vault, 35,000 objects and 527 MB, is 13 seconds and 3 MB from the hosted service, against three and a half minutes for all of it. Ruflo's hives on ruv.sgit.ai ran 603 sgit commands in 27 runs at about a second each, with every clone check identical. I would argue that for many of the jobs we use it for, sgit does less work than git and its alternatives: it fetches only the folders and commits a job needs, every object it fetches can be cached anywhere for ever, any static host can serve it, and large binary files clone faster than git's. Where git is faster, raw local speed for many tiny commands and its own partial clone from local disk, the article says so. And this is not the end of it: pack mode, a zip per push, is being written now; blob compression measured at 1.58 times; a commit-chain object; append lanes for streams. The convention is open, so a new workflow can be built on top without asking the server for anything.
- [A vault you can carry: one zip holds the whole vault, a public key can seal it, and the round trip already works](../articles/a-vault-you-can-carry.md): Reading the pack-mode article, I wanted three things made explicit. First, the two modes side by side, the files that exist in each and the order things happen, which is now a section of that article. Second, my understanding that we mix mutable and immutable files and that this is why the architecture works. The code is more precise than my words were: every object's name says its kind, immutable objects are written once and named by their hash, and the few mutable ones come in two sorts, the shared ones that move only by compare-and-swap and the ones with a single owner. Almost everything in a vault is immutable, so it can be copied, cached or zipped in any shape; only a handful of small files say where the history is. Third, the use case that follows: storage that is good at one big file and bad at thousands of small ones, Google Drive, Dropbox, one large object on S3, for vaults that change rarely or in distinct moments. The whole vault is its bare folder, the objects and those few pointers frozen at one moment, and it fits in one zip. Sealed to someone's public key, the host cannot even tell how many objects are inside. I asked whether that works, and it does today, with commands sgit already ships: a published vault cloned, zipped into one 12.7 MB file of 111 members, sealed to a key in half a second, opened, unzipped elsewhere, and cloned from the folder in 0.48 seconds, with the same files and the same history as a clone from the server. What is missing is one command to make the file, a clone that reads it without unzipping, and a smaller envelope: the seal today is 1.78 times the zip.
- [Pack mode, read closely: a sound design that needs no server change, and five decisions before it is built](../articles/pack-mode-read-closely.md): I am cli.sgit.ai's build agent. Dinis Cruz asked me to publish the CLI team's newest documents as articles and to say what I think of them, because they are big decisions. I read three, written on the CLI's working branch within an hour of each other on 20 and 21 October: the article draft A pack per push, the spec for pack mode, and a brief to the SG/Send team asking for a new server route. My reading is that the design in the spec is sound and should be built as it stands: every push writes one zip of its new objects, a snapshot compacts them, nothing is deleted, every route it uses already exists on the server, and a feature flag keeps every older reader out by name. Five things need a decision first. The brief describes the earlier design of the same evening, one to three zips grown in place, and asks the server team for an append route and conditional completes that the spec no longer needs; it should be parked before anyone builds it. Version 1 of a pack clone takes the whole snapshot, so the scoped, shallow clone agents run every day on the comms vault, 13 seconds and 3 MB today, would download 430 MB; the spec's four performance runs do not measure it. A push whose ref move fails leaves its pack in the commits folder, compaction ignores it and every later clone downloads it, which matters because agent sessions are often thrown away. The pack names tell anyone who can list the vault each push's size and the writer's clock, which is new and small and should be said. And moving packs to the archive costs a download and an upload each, unless the compacting clone kept them. None of this is run; it is a reading of three documents and the code they name.
- [A pack per push: git's packfiles, applied to an encrypted vault, with no server change](../articles/a-pack-per-push.md): For three days I have been talking with the CLI team about keeping a vault's objects in zip files, and this is where it landed. A vault's objects are immutable and named by their hash, so a set of them is a zip and the set only ever grows, which is also what a git packfile is. The cost of a vault over the network is the number of requests, not the number of bytes: from a cloud sandbox a 28-byte object costs half a second whether it comes through the API or straight from S3. So the proposal is a mode where every push writes one pack, the commit with its new trees and blobs, and the ref moves as today: one upload and one compare-and-swap instead of batches of fifty objects. Compaction writes a snapshot pack of everything reachable from a commit and moves the packs it absorbed to an archive; nothing is ever deleted. The folders are the index: a clone takes the newest snapshot and everything in the commits folder, and a pull lists that folder and takes what it lacks, with no commit walk. Small packs go through the API and large ones straight to S3 by presigned URL, with Range reads, all of which the server already does, so there is no server change. The trial is CLI-only, in a vault of its own, gated by a feature flag and a minimum client, so every reader that does not know packs refuses it by name. The number to beat is the 35,000-object vault's clone of three and a half minutes; its snapshot is one 430 MB file that eight parallel ranges from S3 would deliver to that sandbox in about forty seconds. Nothing here is built yet.
- [What shipped in cli.sgit.ai v0.1 and v0.2: 27 pages moved, 158 commands generated, and research given its own area](../articles/what-shipped-in-v0-1-and-v0-2.md): I am the build agent of cli.sgit.ai, and I built its first four releases on 20 October 2026 from two briefs Dinis Cruz gave that day. This is what I delivered, with the commits and the checks to verify it against. v0.1.0 made the site: 27 pages moved from sgit.ai's markdown twins at their original paths with the text unchanged, a command reference of 158 commands on 33 pages generated from the CLI's own sgit help all --format json, the brief published in full, a reality file and a corrections file, and a generator, a gate and a deploy pipeline ported from pki.sgit.ai. It did not deploy: the Python .gitignore template ignores every build/ folder, so the generator and the gate never reached the repository and CI could not find them. v0.1.1 fixed that and stopped the markdown twins carrying the site version, which had made every release rewrite about a hundred files. v0.1.2 recorded the site as live after I checked it. v0.2.0 answered the second brief: research and articles became two areas. 22 research documents from the CLI repository are published as written under /research/, grouped into seven topics; ten articles in the newsroom's format are under /articles/, held to that format by the gate; the 21 addresses the research had under /articles/ now send the reader on. What is not there yet is the review folder, roles and a board, a release script that checks the live site, and redirects on sgit.ai, and the reality file says so.
- [Research is not an article: the CLI's research gets an area of its own, and the articles stay readable](../articles/research-is-not-an-article.md): I asked for two things on cli.sgit.ai: an articles section built the way send.sgit.ai's guidance describes, and the CLI team's recent research published here, because I want to read it as articles and because we need it. I also said the research topics needed to be independent, and that maybe the site needed an area just for that more advanced research, apart from the general articles. The agent's answer, which the site now runs, is that research and articles are two different things and should live in two places. An article makes one argument for a reader, in the newsroom's format, with a summary, a lead figure, what it does not claim and where it comes from, and it can be imported into the newsroom unchanged. A research document is the work itself: the tables, the open questions, the plan that a later document superseded. Rewriting research into articles would lose the record, and dropping it into the articles list would bury the arguments. So /research/ holds 22 documents from the CLI repository, published as written, grouped into seven topics, each topic one open question with what is shipped, what is designed and what is absent. /articles/ holds ten articles: seven written up from my memos as newsroom drafts by the CLI team's agent, two more from my memos about this site, and one by the build agent about what it delivered. Where a research thread produced an argument, the topic page links both. The addresses the research had under /articles/ still work and send the reader on.
- [The CLI gets its own site: cli.sgit.ai documents the command line, and sgit.ai becomes the umbrella](../articles/the-cli-gets-its-own-site.md): This is the brief for the agent building the site for the sgit command-line tool, at cli.sgit.ai, and the idea is to make it the main documentation for the CLI. Until now we have been using sgit.ai for that, and I think it is time to move some of that content here, at least the most technical and the most detailed. The reason is that the CLI now has a whole set of use cases of its own, some of them independent of everything else, while sgit.ai is more the commercial side and the umbrella over all the different sgit usages. So the first step is simply to move the content, and the refactoring follows from that. The second thing I would like this site to have is a way to create articles that each focus on one specific topic, one implementation or one idea. We have talked about this before and started doing it on other sites: the place where we capture a topic first, which is almost our new generation of briefs, and which works better here, next to the thing it is about. On the first day that came to 27 pages moved from sgit.ai, at the same paths so a redirect is one rule each; a command reference of 158 commands generated from the CLI's own parser rather than written by hand; and the CLI team's research published beside it. What sgit.ai still has to do, pointing its pages here, is not something this site can do on its own, and it is said plainly.
- [A vault in one file: native zip support for sgit, where it wins, where it loses, and what already exists](../articles/a-vault-in-one-file.md): A vault is files and folders, so it can be a zip. Every object is immutable and named by its hash, so the store only ever grows, and appending is the one thing a zip does cheaply. I asked how much of that already exists, and the answer is most of it: sgit publish --bundles writes a head snapshot zip and one delta zip per commit, deterministic and uncompressed because ciphertext does not compress; vault backup and uninit write zips; a clone can read a plain folder; and the libraries underneath have zip support. What is missing is a clone that reads a bundle and a bare store that lives in one. The cost today is requests, not bytes. From a cloud sandbox a 28-byte object costs half a second whether it comes through the API or straight from S3, so many small files pay that floor every time and one file pays it once. On the article's 12 MB vault, 106 separate requests took 2 to 2.5 seconds and one 12.7 MB zip took 0.05 seconds to fetch and 0.08 to unpack. On the 35,000-object vault, the 430 MB head zip came off a local disk in 3 seconds against 111 for the objects one by one, and appending a member took a quarter of a second. Selective reads survive, because a zip's directory sits at its end and range requests read it and any member. The crossover is a link-speed question, in the tens of megabytes for the hosted path. It is the right shape for small-file vaults, logs, statistics and API captures, for a vault inside a vault, and for file hosts with no API; it is the wrong one for a vault ten agents push to every minute. Since the first draft it has been tested further: Zip64 handled 70,000 members and 5 GiB, a presigned multipart upload and Range reads worked against the live server, and appending on S3 without downloading needs one server-side copy the server does not offer yet.
- [Streaming changes into a vault: a thousand small writes, one commit, every line attributed](../articles/streaming-changes-into-a-vault.md): Every change in a vault is a commit, and a commit is a tree rebuild, a signature and a compare-and-swap on one ref. That is fine for a document and wrong for an agent that writes a line a second, for a hundred of them, or for an API log that arrives in bursts. The copy-on-write article proposed a write-ahead lane; this one works out the protocol. The ingest already exists: append lanes take a write with no account, no tree and no read-back, name every entry in arrival order, cap at 5 MB and 1,000 pending, and took a thousand entries from a hundred writers in 4.9 seconds on the in-memory server. A change becomes an entry: one atomic set of operations (put, patch, append or delete) on one or many paths, signed by its writer, naming the content hash it was made against. A fold turns a batch of entries into one signed commit, by count, size or time, in arrival order, and stops on a conflict it cannot resolve by the rule the path declares. Provenance survives the fold in a file inside the commit that lists every entry it absorbed, with its hash, writer key, sequence and paths, so the commit says who folded and the file says who wrote, and the lane keeps the originals until they are marked processed. Patches are an ingest format, not a storage format: the store keeps whole, immutable, cacheable objects, and a patch is applied at fold time. None of the entry format, the fold, the conflict rules or the provenance file exists yet, and disk-backed lanes are much slower than the in-memory figure until a server defect is fixed.
- [sgit is a standard, not a server: everything in a vault is one hash away](../articles/sgit-is-a-standard-one-hash-away.md): People read "encrypted git" and picture a product with a server in the middle. There is a server, and it is the least interesting part. A vault is a set of files laid out by a convention: blobs, trees, commits and one mutable ref per branch, all ciphertext, and every object except the ref and the branch index named by the SHA-256 of its own bytes. The name says which is which, `-imm-` or `-muw-`, so a browser, a proxy, a CDN or a CI cache can keep an object for ever by reading its name and never its content. Nothing in a vault has to be discovered: the read key gives the ref's name, the ref gives the commit, the commit the tree, and a file is four plain GETs of fixed paths, so any storage that answers a GET implements the read half, from S3 to GitHub Pages to a folder. Writing needs one thing storage does not give, a compare-and-swap on the ref, and that is what the API is for. A shipped cache layer lets a reader compute where a hot file's encrypted copy lives and fetch it in one batch. When you look at sgit's timings you are looking at the storage: 317 ms a request through the hosted API, 44 ms from GitHub Pages, 0.8 s for a scoped clone against a local server that takes 13 s hosted. The work stays on the client, as it did in git, because a merge needs the context of the change. The server cannot read a byte, so every feature had to be objects a writer produces and a reader derives, and that constraint is why the design is small enough to be a standard.
- [Policies the vault enforces: from a rule agents keep to a folder only one key can write](../articles/policies-the-vault-enforces.md): On ruv.sgit the vault is the record of a policy, not its enforcer. RiskMandate writes the mandate, the grant, the gap and the barrier; ruv.sgit compiles those rows into Ruflo's policy engine, which decides and writes receipts; the Cedar policy vault keeps the rules, their history, their signed releases and the evidence. What stops an action is the harness, a hook or an engine, never the vault. I asked whether sgit itself could enforce some of it. It already refuses things, and the rules travel with the vault: a scoped clone refuses a write outside its folders, a commit refuses secret-shaped files, signatures-required makes every client refuse an unsigned commit on pull, the named branch refuses a rewind, and a read-only clone cannot push. All of that is client-side and fails closed, and every honest client enforces it. That is the hook. A policy row that says key K may write path/ is one more rule of the same kind: refused on commit by the writer's own client and on pull by every other client, so a violating push stops the branch for the whole swarm until it is reverted, while the server stays blind. Labelled with RiskMandate's barrier kinds there are four levels: a convention is an expectation, a clone scope is a setting the agent can widen, a policy row is a boundary for every honest client and evidence against a dishonest one, and a server that verifies signed writes is a boundary against everyone. My rule, that once a folder is bound to a key it cannot be rebound and you start a new folder, is the right one because it only moves one way. Levels two and three are not built.
- [One vault, ten agents, 35,000 objects: what sgit does when the repository is big and the clients are many](../articles/one-vault-ten-agents-measured.md): When the clients are agents they are always online, there are many of them, and the expensive thing is moving bytes nobody needs. Anthropic's post on Scion answers that with a server that does the work and three tiers of cache in front of it. I wanted to know what sgit does with the opposite constraint, a server that cannot read a byte, on the one vault we have that is big by our standards and busy every day. The comms vault, where ten agents and I keep mail, briefs, runs and analysis, had 1,295 commits and about 35,000 encrypted objects on 16 October, 527 MB on disk. Nobody working in it needs all of it, and the design means they do not take it: a full clone is three and a half minutes, one folder at one commit is 13 seconds and 3 MB, and a pull when nothing changed is 2.5 seconds. The one real edge is a scoped clone that asks for a folder's whole history, which walks 1,295 commits one request at a time; the fix, a small object that records the commit chain, is designed and not shipped, and the depth flag is the answer until it is. One file is four requests computed from the read key, and every object but the ref is named by the hash of its ciphertext, so anything in the path can keep it for ever. Moving the same objects to local disk turns three minutes of history walking into seven seconds: sgit is not the bottleneck, the distance to the storage is. None of this is proven at Scion's scale, and the article says so.
- [Keys the way git does them, and the way a vault could: what SSH actually checks, what a read key actually prevents, and a door per member](../articles/keys-the-way-git-does-it.md): I asked how git actually handles keys, because I suspected sgit was closer to it than people assume. Git authenticates you once and then checks nothing: an SSH key or a token gets you to the server, a push is file copying, the author of a commit is a string unless it is signed, and a clone is yours to do anything with. sgit is the same shape with the names changed. The write key is the push credential, the read key is a deploy key, the access token is the account, and the server compares hashes the way GitHub checks a fingerprint. A read-only clone cannot push and cannot stop you editing files locally, exactly like a git clone, so that is not a gap, it is git's rule. Where sgit already goes further is on the client: every commit is signed by the clone's own key, a vault can require signatures, and the named branch only moves forward. Where it does not yet is the server, which cannot tell one writer from another because every writer presents the same key. The GitHub version of sgit is RFC 0001's Design 1, a write key pair per writer and a writer set the server trusts, and an SSH key fits it directly. The PKI version is a door per member: one small object per member holding the vault's data key sealed to that member's public key, join by adding one, leave by deleting one, and the key never written to disk. The catch is history, so the doors have to live outside the tree, as refs and the cache layer already do. Revocation stays bounded, as in git: it stops the next open, never a copy already made. None of the member pattern is built.
- [Copy-on-write, and what it would mean for a vault: what rUv's team asked for, what sgit already does, and the write-ahead lane that would do the rest](../articles/copy-on-write-and-the-vault.md): After I presented ruv.sgit to the Agentics Foundation, rUv's team asked whether sgit could add copy-on-write. I wanted to know what that would mean for a vault before saying yes or no. Copy-on-write means share until you write: a snapshot or a branch costs nothing, and the first write to a shared block pays for a copy of that block. Filesystems, virtual disks, the kernel's fork() and git's object store all work that way. RuVector's version is a file that forks: an RVF child shares all its parent's data and copies only the changed vectors, with lineage hashes back to the parent. sgit is already copy-on-write where git is. A branch is a pointer, a commit stores the new blobs and the rebuilt spine, unchanged folders keep their ids, and a scoped clone takes one folder, so nothing is copied to fork a vault's history. There are two places it is not. Inside a file, a changed byte in a large file is a new object; and across vaults, objects under one key cannot be shared with another. Its write path is also one commit per write, which is right for documents and wrong for a stream. The answer for the stream is a write-ahead lane: writes go to an append lane, measured at two hundred entries a second, and a normaliser folds them into signed commits later, which is the shape of an LSM store, of RuVector's own lsm-ann and of Scion's changeset log. The lane exists; the fold does not, and the article sets out its semantics so the thread can argue about them.

## Publishing an article

Adding one file publishes it: `admin/content/articles/<slug>.md` in the newsroom's format, with its lead figure in `articles/images/`. The gate refuses an article that does not have the format's front matter, a summary of 220 to 360 words, its three anchored sections and its figure, or that has an em-dash. The contract is `admin/content/articles/README.md`.

# Is there any overhead? sgit's performance, measured: what a vault costs in a CI job, an agent's session and a hive, and why being selective beats being fast, cli.sgit.ai

> When I posted about using sgit inside CI pipelines, a reader asked the right question: what are the performance stats for this setup, and is there any overhead? There is, and it is worth stating exactly. Every sgit command pays about four tenths of a second before it touches the network, to start Python and to derive its key with 600,000 rounds of PBKDF2; encryption itself is cheap, a hundred megabytes in under half a second. After that, the cost of a vault is the number of requests a job makes, not the size of the vault, and that is where sgit now scales quite nicely, because a job can be very selective about what it asks for. A clone of one folder with --path stays between 0.59 and 0.77 seconds while the vault grows twentyfold, where a full clone goes from 0.95 to 5.55. One folder at one commit of our biggest vault, 35,000 objects and 527 MB, is 13 seconds and 3 MB from the hosted service, against three and a half minutes for all of it. Ruflo's hives on ruv.sgit.ai ran 603 sgit commands in 27 runs at about a second each, with every clone check identical. I would argue that for many of the jobs we use it for, sgit does less work than git and its alternatives: it fetches only the folders and commits a job needs, every object it fetches can be cached anywhere for ever, any static host can serve it, and large binary files clone faster than git's. Where git is faster, raw local speed for many tiny commands and its own partial clone from local disk, the article says so. And this is not the end of it: pack mode, a zip per push, is being written now; blob compression measured at 1.58 times; a commit-chain object; append lanes for streams. The convention is open, so a new workflow can be built on top without asking the server for anything.

*Source: <https://cli.sgit.ai/articles/is-there-any-overhead.html> · generated from the same content as the page, so the two cannot drift.*

---
By [Dinis Cruz](https://sgit.ai/about/) · 2026-10-21 · published

**Summary:** When I posted about using sgit inside CI pipelines, a reader asked the right question: what are the performance stats for this setup, and is there any overhead? There is, and it is worth stating exactly. Every sgit command pays about four tenths of a second before it touches the network, to start Python and to derive its key with 600,000 rounds of PBKDF2; encryption itself is cheap, a hundred megabytes in under half a second. After that, the cost of a vault is the number of requests a job makes, not the size of the vault, and that is where sgit now scales quite nicely, because a job can be very selective about what it asks for. A clone of one folder with --path stays between 0.59 and 0.77 seconds while the vault grows twentyfold, where a full clone goes from 0.95 to 5.55. One folder at one commit of our biggest vault, 35,000 objects and 527 MB, is 13 seconds and 3 MB from the hosted service, against three and a half minutes for all of it. Ruflo's hives on ruv.sgit.ai ran 603 sgit commands in 27 runs at about a second each, with every clone check identical. I would argue that for many of the jobs we use it for, sgit does less work than git and its alternatives: it fetches only the folders and commits a job needs, every object it fetches can be cached anywhere for ever, any static host can serve it, and large binary files clone faster than git's. Where git is faster, raw local speed for many tiny commands and its own partial clone from local disk, the article says so. And this is not the end of it: pack mode, a zip per push, is being written now; blob compression measured at 1.58 times; a commit-chain object; append lanes for streams. The convention is open, so a new workflow can be built on top without asking the server for anything.

![Is there any overhead? Four answers, each measured, from the smallest unit up. One command: about 0.4 seconds fixed before the network, 0.22 to start and 0.18 for the key derivation. A CI job: a one-folder clone goes from 0.59 to 0.77 seconds as the vault grows from 100 to 2,000 files, where a full clone goes from 0.95 to 5.55. A big vault: one folder at one commit of a 35,000-object, 527 MB vault is 13 seconds and 3 MB from the hosted service. Many writers: a thousand entries from a hundred writers into an append lane in 4.9 seconds, and a hive's 603 operations at a median of about a second each.](../articles/images/pf-overview.webp)

*Is there any overhead? Four answers, each measured, from the smallest unit up. One command: about 0.4 seconds fixed before the network, 0.22 to start and 0.18 for the key derivation. A CI job: a one-folder clone goes from 0.59 to 0.77 seconds as the vault grows from 100 to 2,000 files, where a full clone goes from 0.95 to 5.55. A big vault: one folder at one commit of a 35,000-object, 527 MB vault is 13 seconds and 3 MB from the hosted service. Many writers: a thousand entries from a hundred writers into an append lane in 4.9 seconds, and a hive's 603 operations at a median of about a second each.*


## In short {#in-short}

- **Yes, there is overhead, and it is per command:** about 0.4 seconds before any network, to start and to derive the key once. Encrypting is cheap: 100 MB in 0.4 seconds.
- **After that, a vault costs requests, not size.** So the question is how many requests a job makes, and sgit's clone options decide that.
- **A CI job pays for the folders it asks for.** A `--path` clone stays under 0.8 seconds while the vault grows twentyfold; ten of them at once take 1.9 seconds.
- **A big vault stays usable.** One folder at one commit of 35,000 objects is 13 seconds and 3 MB, hosted; a full clone is three and a half minutes.
- **Hives work at about a second an operation.** 603 sgit commands in Ruflo's hives on ruv.sgit.ai, every clone check identical, no plaintext on the server.
- **Against git: sgit does less where a job can be selective,** the files are large or the storage is dumb. git is faster for many tiny local commands, and its partial clone from local disk is the fastest result measured.
- **It keeps getting faster:** pack mode is being written now, compression and a commit-chain object are designed, and none of it needs a server change.

## The question {#question}

I posted on LinkedIn about [sgit in a CI pipeline](https://newsroom.sgit.ai/articles/sgit-in-a-ci-pipeline.html), the newsroom's article on running a vault as a job's encrypted state. One reply asked the question every engineer should ask of a design like that:

> It'd be nice to know the performance stats for this setup. Is there any overhead?

It deserves a measured answer rather than a reassuring one, so this is it: where the overhead is, how big it is, what sgit does about it, and where git is still faster. Every number below was measured, and the source of each is at the end.

## The short answer {#short-answer}

There is a fixed cost per command, a fraction of a second. Everything after that depends on what the job asks for, and a job can ask for very little. The overhead people worry about, encryption, is the smallest part of it. The part that matters is the number of requests, because from a cloud runner a 28-byte object costs half a second, the same as a much larger one. So sgit's performance work has been, and is, about making fewer requests: fetch one folder and not the vault, one commit and not the history, a pack and not a thousand objects.

## One command {#per-command}

Measured in a cloud sandbox with sgit-ai 0.23.0, on the commands a job runs most:

| Where the time goes | Time |
|---|---|
| Starting Python and loading sgit | 0.22 s |
| Deriving the key from the vault key, PBKDF2 at 600,000 rounds, once per process | 0.18 s |
| Encrypting or decrypting 100 MB, AES-GCM | 0.4 s |
| A local command end to end (`status`, `commit` of a small change, `history log`) | 0.25 to 0.4 s |

So a command costs about four tenths of a second before it sends anything. That is the honest overhead against git, which starts in milliseconds. It matters for a loop of hundreds of commands and not for a job that runs a clone, some work and a push. The key derivation is deliberately slow, because it is what protects a vault key that is guessed rather than stolen.

## In a CI job {#ci-job}

The newsroom measured this in [sgit in GitHub Actions, side by side](https://newsroom.sgit.ai/articles/sgit-actions-side-by-side.html), with a vault server as the job's sidecar and the vault growing from 100 to 2,000 files:

![As the vault grows, a one-folder clone stays flat. Clone time against the number of files in the vault, median of three runs, against a local vault server. The full clone goes from 0.95 to 1.98 to 5.55 seconds and holds 82.7 MB on disk at 2,000 files. The clone of one folder with --path goes from 0.59 to 0.64 to 0.77 seconds and holds 4.1 MB. Ten one-folder clones together take 1.9 seconds; ten full clones, 21.1.](../articles/images/pf-scaling.webp)

*As the vault grows, a one-folder clone stays flat. Clone time against the number of files in the vault, median of three runs, against a local vault server. The full clone goes from 0.95 to 1.98 to 5.55 seconds and holds 82.7 MB on disk at 2,000 files. The clone of one folder with --path goes from 0.59 to 0.64 to 0.77 seconds and holds 4.1 MB. Ten one-folder clones together take 1.9 seconds; ten full clones, 21.1.*


This is the result I care most about. A job that clones the folder it works on pays for that folder, not for the vault it lives in, and the vault can keep growing without the job getting slower. Ten jobs at once barely load the server, because a scoped clone is a few requests and the work, decrypting and checking, happens on the runners. The usual pattern is one folder per job, `--depth 1`, and a push of what the job produced:

```text
$ sgit clone --path runs/2026-10-21 --depth 1 <vault-key> work
$ cd work && ./the-job.sh && sgit commit -m "run 2026-10-21" && sgit push
```

The rest of the vault is carried by id. Nothing the job does not track is fetched, and nothing another job does in another folder can conflict with it. Because every object is named by the hash of its ciphertext, a CI cache can keep the objects between runs without being told what they are; the [agent workflows on ephemeral vaults](https://newsroom.sgit.ai/articles/agent-workflows-on-ephemeral-vaults.html) article does exactly that, a vault per job that lives for the job and leaves only ciphertext behind.

## In a big vault {#big-vault}

The comms vault is the biggest we have: ten agents and I keep mail, briefs, runs and analysis in it, 1,295 commits and about 35,000 encrypted objects, 527 MB. From a cloud sandbox to the hosted service, [measured on 16 October](../articles/one-vault-ten-agents-measured.md):

| How the agent clones | Time | Data |
|---|---|---|
| The whole vault, every commit | 3½ min | 527 MB |
| The whole tree at one commit, `--depth 1` | 57 s | |
| One folder at one commit, `--path <folder> --depth 1` | 13 s | 3 MB |
| A pull when nothing changed | 2.5 s | nothing |

The same objects moved to local disk turn 13 seconds into 0.8: sgit is not the bottleneck, the distance to the storage is. On a 600-commit vault, one folder of 365 files took 14 seconds against 80 for the whole vault, as [the partial clones guide](../docs/partial-clones.md) records. Once a clone exists, everything is a few requests: one file on demand is under 3 seconds including the process start, and that number does not depend on the size of the vault.

```mermaid
%% Choosing the clone for the job. Most jobs need one folder and one commit; the full clone is for the jobs that need the whole history, and a clone from a folder or a zip needs no server at all.
flowchart TD
    A[A job needs a vault] --> B{{Does it write?}}
    B -- no, it only reads --> C{{From a server or from files?}}
    C -- files on disk, a bucket, a zip --> D[clone --transport local, 0.48 s]
    C -- a server --> E{{One folder or all of it?}}
    B -- yes --> E
    E -- one folder --> F[clone --path folder --depth 1, 13 s and 3 MB on 35k objects]
    E -- the whole tree --> G{{Does it need the history?}}
    G -- no --> H[clone --depth 1, 57 s]
    G -- yes --> I[full clone, 3.5 min, then pull in 2.5 s]
```

## Against git {#against-git}

This is not a race between equals. git reads plaintext and trusts its server; sgit decrypts everything it touches, checks every object against its name, and its server can read nothing. Even so, there are jobs where sgit does less work than git, and jobs where git is simply faster:

![Where sgit does less work than git, and where git is faster. sgit does less for large binary files (a full clone of 40 files of 3 MB in 4.4 seconds against git's 16.1), for one folder of a big vault (3 MB of 527), for caching (every object named by its hash, cacheable for ever), for readers on any static host, and for many agents at once. git is faster with its own partial clone and sparse checkout from local disk (0.4 seconds), for many tiny commands, for a high rate of single writes, and for tools sgit does not have yet such as blame and bisect.](../articles/images/pf-vs-git.webp)

*Where sgit does less work than git, and where git is faster. sgit does less for large binary files (a full clone of 40 files of 3 MB in 4.4 seconds against git's 16.1), for one folder of a big vault (3 MB of 527), for caching (every object named by its hash, cacheable for ever), for readers on any static host, and for many agents at once. git is faster with its own partial clone and sparse checkout from local disk (0.4 seconds), for many tiny commands, for a high rate of single writes, and for tools sgit does not have yet such as blame and bisect.*


Why I argue sgit performs better than git and its alternatives in many of the cases we use it for:

- **It is selective by design.** A scoped clone takes the spine of trees down to one folder and the files in it, and carries the rest by id. git can do this too, with a partial clone, a filter and a sparse checkout, but it needs a server that supports filters; sgit needs only a store that serves objects by name.
- **Large files cost what they weigh.** On 40 files of 3 MB, a full sgit clone took 4.4 seconds and a full git clone of the same files from local disk 16.1, most likely because git tries to compress data that cannot be compressed; sgit encrypts and stores.
- **Everything but the ref is immutable and named by its hash.** A browser, a CDN or a CI cache can keep an object for ever without being told; a reload inside two minutes fetches nothing. git's smart protocol computes a pack per fetch, which a cache in the path cannot reuse.
- **There is no server to run for readers.** A vault on S3, GitHub Pages, a folder or [one zip](../articles/a-vault-you-can-carry.md) is cloned with the same command; from a local folder, 0.48 seconds.
- **The alternatives that encrypt give up the selectivity.** A filter that encrypts git's blobs loses git's deltas, an encrypting remote helper pushes packs no cache can share, and a sync service that encrypts whole folders has no notion of one folder at one commit. That is an argument from how they work, not a measurement.

And where git wins: its own partial clone with a sparse checkout from local disk, 0.4 seconds, was the fastest result in the same measurement, and it starts in milliseconds where sgit starts in 0.4 seconds. A loop of hundreds of tiny commits is the wrong shape for sgit today; it is the right shape for an append lane, or for pack mode.

## Many writers, and hives {#hives}

The other half of the CI question is what happens when many writers share a vault. Two numbers, both measured:

- **An append lane** took a thousand entries from a hundred concurrent writers in 4.9 seconds, 205 a second, none lost, on the in-memory server. A lane is a write-only channel with no tree and no read-back, for streams; the fold that turns a lane into commits is [designed](../articles/streaming-changes-into-a-vault.md). On the disk-backed server lanes are much slower, about three a second, until a listing defect reported on 14 October is fixed.
- **A hive.** [ruv.sgit.ai](https://ruv.sgit.ai/ruv-sgit/ledger/index.html) runs Ruflo's hives against a vault: up to six workers, each on its own branch, the host merging them, every command logged. Its ledger is the best real-world record we have:

![A hive's 603 sgit operations, from the ruv.sgit ledger, 15 to 21 October 2026: 27 runs, up to six workers each, against a local vault server on disk. Median times, every one including the process start and the key derivation: push 1.01 seconds over 177 pushes, commit 0.83 over 102, branch new 0.86, branch switch 0.91, merge 0.88, clone 0.92, init 0.86. The runs held 478 files and 20 MB of delivered work in 129 commits; all 27 clone checks were identical to what was delivered, and no plaintext was found in the server's storage. 7 of the 603 commands exited with an error, each one recorded.](../articles/images/pf-hive.webp)

*A hive's 603 sgit operations, from the ruv.sgit ledger, 15 to 21 October 2026: 27 runs, up to six workers each, against a local vault server on disk. Median times, every one including the process start and the key derivation: push 1.01 seconds over 177 pushes, commit 0.83 over 102, branch new 0.86, branch switch 0.91, merge 0.88, clone 0.92, init 0.86. The runs held 478 files and 20 MB of delivered work in 129 commits; all 27 clone checks were identical to what was delivered, and no plaintext was found in the server's storage. 7 of the 603 commands exited with an error, each one recorded.*


About a second per operation, whatever the run's size: the cost is per command, not per byte. The largest run, 142 files and 6.9 MB, cloned back in 0.74 seconds. For a hive whose workers think for minutes between commands, a second of version control per step is noise, and what it buys is a history that every worker signed and the server cannot read.

## What is being added {#coming}

The work on performance is not finished, and the next steps are concrete:

- **Pack mode, a zip per push,** [specified](../research/pack-mode-spec.md) and being written by the CLI team now. A push becomes one upload and one compare-and-swap, whatever its size; a cold clone of the 35,000-object vault becomes one snapshot and a few packs, about 40 seconds from the sandbox where it is three and a half minutes today. Those are arithmetic from measured request costs; the spec's five performance runs will replace them with measurements, and this article will be updated with them.
- **Blob compression before encryption,** measured on the comms vault's files: deflate at level 6 makes them 1.58 times smaller in 2.9 seconds of CPU for 120 MB, so a 527 MB store would be about 330 MB.
- **A commit-chain object,** so a scoped clone that wants a folder's whole history fetches the chain in 26 batched requests instead of walking 1,295 commits one at a time (181 seconds today). Until then, `--depth` is the answer.
- **A vault in one file,** already [measured](../articles/a-vault-you-can-carry.md): zipped, sealed to a public key, and cloned from a folder in 0.48 seconds. A command for it is proposed.

## Why it keeps getting faster {#why}

None of the changes above needs a new server. The vault convention is open: immutable objects named by their hash, a few small refs moved by compare-and-swap, and a store that only needs to read and write bytes. So a new way of moving those objects, a pack, a zip, a cache, a lane, is a client-side decision, and anyone can build a workflow on top of it without asking the server for anything. That is why I am comfortable saying sgit now scales quite nicely: the design puts the cost where the job can control it, and every improvement since October has been one more way of asking for less.

## What this does not claim {#limits}

- **Most numbers are from one cloud sandbox**, behind a proxy, so hosted times are worse than a plain connection; the CI and hive numbers are against a local server. None were run at the scale of a large company's monorepo.
- **The comparison with git is from one measurement each way**, on the files named; git with a filter-capable server and a warm cache will beat several of sgit's numbers.
- **The append lane's 205 a second is in memory**; on disk it is about three a second until the defect is fixed.
- **Pack mode's numbers are expected, not measured.** The code is not pushed yet.
- **Compression is an option in the spec**, not a decision, and it lets the host see how compressible a file is.
- **The same CI measurement found three faults,** which the newsroom reported: a push of a file over 4 MB failed against a server on local disk, a headless clone could not fetch a single file in that version, and full clones queue on one server process.

If you run sgit in a pipeline, a hive or a vault of your own and have numbers, or want them taken, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.

## Where this comes from {#sources}

A reply to my LinkedIn post about the newsroom's CI article, on 18 October 2026; the question is quoted and its author is not named. Written up by cli.sgit.ai's build agent, cli.build, on 21 October; the editorial responsibility is mine. The per-command times were measured by the agent in a cloud sandbox with sgit-ai 0.23.0 on 21 October. The CI numbers are from the newsroom's [sgit in a CI pipeline](https://newsroom.sgit.ai/articles/sgit-in-a-ci-pipeline.html) and [sgit in GitHub Actions, side by side](https://newsroom.sgit.ai/articles/sgit-actions-side-by-side.html) (sgit 0.21.0, local server, median of three); the ephemeral-vault pattern from [agent workflows on ephemeral vaults](https://newsroom.sgit.ai/articles/agent-workflows-on-ephemeral-vaults.html); the big-vault numbers from [one vault, ten agents, measured](../articles/one-vault-ten-agents-measured.md) and its source note, [Response to "Scion and sgit"](../research/response-to-scion-and-sgit.md), which also designs the commit-chain object; the 600-commit numbers from [Partial clones](../docs/partial-clones.md); the git comparison from the newsroom's measured articles; the append lane from [Streaming changes into a vault](../articles/streaming-changes-into-a-vault.md); the hive numbers computed from [ruv.sgit.ai's ledger](https://ruv.sgit.ai/ruv-sgit/ledger/index.html), `data/vaults.json` as updated at 13:42 UTC on 21 October; pack mode and compression from [the pack-mode spec](../research/pack-mode-spec.md) at `477d328`. The research topics: [Big vaults and many agents](../research/topics/scale.md) and [How a vault takes writes](../research/topics/write-path.md).
