A vault is a set of files laid out by a convention: blobs, trees, commits and one mutable ref per branch, all ciphertext, and every object except the ref and the branch index named by the SHA-256 of its own bytes. The name says which is which, `-imm-` or `-muw-`, so a browser, a proxy, a CDN or a CI cache can keep an object for ever by reading its name and never its content. Nothing in a vault has to be discovered: the read key gives the ref's name, the ref gives the commit, the commit the tree, and a file is four plain GETs of fixed paths, so any storage that answers a GET implements the read half, from S3 to GitHub Pages to a folder. Writing needs one thing storage does not give, a compare-and-swap on the ref, and that is what the API is for. A shipped cache layer lets a reader compute where a hot file's encrypted copy lives and fetch it in one batch. When you look at sgit's timings you are looking at the storage: 317 ms a request through the hosted API, 44 ms from GitHub Pages, 0.8 s for a scoped clone against a local server that takes 13 s hosted. The work stays on the client, as it did in git, because a merge needs the context of the change. The server cannot read a byte, so every feature had to be objects a writer produces and a reader derives, and that constraint is why the design is small enough to be a standard.

![Everything from one hash. From the left: the vault key gives the read key one way; the read key gives the ref's name by an HMAC, so nobody has to say where HEAD is; the ref holds the commit, the commit the tree, the tree the blob. Four plain GETs of fixed paths, which any storage that answers a GET can serve. Below, the two kinds of object name: -imm- objects are named by the hash of their ciphertext and can be cached for ever by anyone, -muw- pointers are refetched.](../articles/images/sgit-is-a-standard-one-hash-away.svg)

*Everything from one hash. From the left: the vault key gives the read key one way; the read key gives the ref's name by an HMAC, so nobody has to say where HEAD is; the ref holds the commit, the commit the tree, the tree the blob. Four plain GETs of fixed paths, which any storage that answers a GET can serve. Below, the two kinds of object name: -imm- objects are named by the hash of their ciphertext and can be cached for ever by anyone, -muw- pointers are refetched.*


## In short {#in-short}

- **A vault is a convention, not a service.** Four kinds of object, all ciphertext, every immutable one named by the SHA-256 of its own bytes.
- **The name says what can be cached.** `-imm-` objects can be kept for ever by anything in the path without reading them; `-muw-` pointers are refetched.
- **Nothing has to be discovered.** The read key gives the ref's name; ref, commit, trees, blob is four GETs of fixed paths, which any storage that answers a GET can serve.
- **Writing needs one compare-and-swap,** and that is what the API is for; the rest of the timings are the storage's.
- **The work stays on the client,** as in git, because a merge needs the context of the change; Scion's own merge queue went back to the client too.
- **The constraint designed it.** A server that cannot read a byte left only objects a writer produces and a reader derives. No blame or bisect yet, stated.

Anthropic's post on Scion describes a server that answers every question a client has about the
repository, and three tiers of cache in front of it. The post is honest that this is a centralised
design in the line of Google's Piper and Meta's Sapling, and that it "is by no means a suitable
replacement for git for general use". It is worth saying what sgit is in the same plain terms,
because people read "encrypted git" and picture a product with a server in the middle. There is
a server, and it is the least interesting part.

## What a vault is {#vault}

A vault is a set of files laid out by a convention. Four kinds of object, all ciphertext: blobs
(file contents), trees (a folder: encrypted names pointing at blob and tree ids), commits (a tree
id, parents, a message, a signature), and one mutable pointer per branch, the ref. Every object
except the ref and the branch index is named by the SHA-256 of its own ciphertext, so a name can
never point at different bytes, anyone can check an object against its name, and anyone who has
fetched one can keep it for ever.

The name says which is which. An immutable object's id carries `-imm-`; the mutable pointers
carry `-muw-`. So anything between the storage and the reader, a browser, a proxy, a CDN, a CI
cache, a page on a website, can decide to keep an object for ever by looking at its name, without
reading a byte of it and without being told by a header. This is how the vault app in the browser
got fast: it caches every `-imm-` object the first time it sees one and refetches only the ref.
It is a small convention and it makes a large difference, and it is also a trade made on purpose.
sgit keeps no deltas between versions of a file; a changed file is a new object. Git stores
deltas and has to be told what changed; sgit stores whole objects that anyone can cache blindly.

That is git's object model with encryption underneath it, and the choice was deliberate: git
solved the hard problems of history, branching and merging twenty years ago, and the workflows
built on them are why git won. What sgit changes is where the trust sits.

## Everything from one hash {#everything-from-hash}

The part that makes it a standard rather than a service is that nothing in a vault has to be
discovered. It is all derived from the key:

1. The vault key gives the vault id and, one way, the read key. The read key cannot be turned
   back into the write key, so it can be published.
2. The read key gives the ref's name: `ref-pid-muw-` plus the first twelve hex characters of
   `HMAC(read_key, "sg-vault-v1:file-id:ref:" + vault_id)`. The server never told you where HEAD
   is. You computed it.
3. The ref holds the head commit id. The commit holds the tree id. Trees hold the ids of blobs
   and subtrees, with the names encrypted inside them. Ref, commit, trees on the path, blob: a
   file is four requests from its read key, and the requests are plain GETs of fixed paths.
4. Writing is the same objects, PUT in batches, and one compare-and-swap on the ref.

sgit.ai's own documentation pages read a vault exactly this way in the browser, with a reader of
about ninety lines; a cold load fetches 18 objects, the next load fetches one 69-byte ref, and a
load inside the two-minute freshness window fetches nothing at all. The CLI and the browser app
are two independent implementations of the same wire format, and they verify each other's work.

Because the read half of the convention is four GETs of fixed paths, any storage that answers a
GET implements it: an S3 bucket, GitHub Pages, a CDN, a folder, Python's one-line file server.
`sgit clone --transport static` reads from any of them, and `sgit publish` is what lays a vault out
for one. The write half needs one thing storage does not give you: a compare-and-swap on the
ref, which is what the API is for.

## The hot path: a cache you can compute {#hot-path-cache}

Four GETs is cheap, but a page that serves one record a thousand times a minute does not want to
walk trees. So the convention has a cache layer, shipped: `sgit cache add <path>` declares a path,
and every push keeps an encrypted cache object for it at a location derived from the read key and
the path. A reader with only the vault id and the read key computes the candidate ids locally,
makes one batch request for the ref and the candidates, checks the commit id inside against the
ref, and has the file with no walk. A miss, a stale entry or a mismatch falls back to the ordinary
walk, so correctness never depends on the cache; losing one is a performance problem, never a
correctness one. The reference reader is written to run in an edge function that serves one hot
record. This is Scion's "derived data", built by the writer instead of the server, and named by the
key instead of indexed by it.

## What the server does, and what storage does {#server-does-storage}

Strip the convention down and the API is left with two jobs: protect writes (an access token,
compare-and-swap on the ref and the branch index) and shorten reads a little (batches of fifty
objects, a listing for cold full clones). Everything else is storage. Which is why, when you look
at sgit's timings, you are looking at the storage:

- On the hosted service, a Lambda in front of S3 behind CloudFront, a request costs its round
  trip before a byte moves: the newsroom measured 317 ms a request through the API and 44 ms for
  the same object from GitHub Pages. A one-folder, one-commit clone of a 35,000-object vault is
  137 objects and 3 MB, and takes 13 s from a cloud sandbox because it is a dozen dependent
  requests, not because of the bytes.
- On a local server with disk storage (the ruv.sgit ledger, eleven recorded hive runs), every
  sgit operation is 0.4 to 1.5 s including Python start-up and the 600,000-iteration key
  derivation; a 142-file, 6.9 MB vault clones in 0.74 s and pushes in 0.87 s.
- The same 35,000-object vault, the same client, the objects moved to local disk: a one-folder,
  one-commit clone is 0.8 s against a local API server and 2.3 s from a plain file server, against
  13 s hosted; a scoped clone with all 1,227 commits of history is 7 s locally against 181 s
  hosted (the same 1,227 requests, at a millisecond each instead of 150); the full clone is 69 s
  locally against three and a half minutes, and most of the 69 s is the client decrypting
  16,000 trees.

So the deployment question is not "how do I scale the sgit server" but "where do I put the
objects, and how close": memory, a disk, a bucket behind a CDN, a static host. The sgit.ai deploy
pages are that list, and `sgit serve` runs the hosted service's own image on a laptop.

## Why the work stays on the client {#work-stays-on}

Scion moves history, blame and merges to the server, and says it is "by no means" for general
use. sgit keeps them on the client, and would even if the server could read the data, for the
reason git did: a merge is a workflow step that needs the context of the change, the history and
the policy that says who may merge what. In ruv.sgit every worker in a hive writes to its own
branch and the host merges them under the run's written mandate, with a receipt; in the shared
vault ten agents use every day, they meet on a named branch and resolve on the clone that has
the conflict in front of it. Scion's post concedes this from the other side: it could not keep a
global merge queue at its merge rate, so concurrent changes conflict and an agent fixes them.
The merge went back to the client there too.

What sgit does not have today is a `blame` command; path history, signed authorship, signed tags
and verification exist, and blame is a fold over path history that nobody has written yet. That
is the honest gap, stated.

## Keep the property that made git git {#keep-property-that}

The distributed copy, complete and verifiable, is why git survived every centralised system that
promised to be faster. sgit keeps it: a full clone is one command and holds everything, and
anyone with the key can rebuild it from any host. What changed is that the full clone became
optional. A folder scope, a history depth, a sparse clone and the cache layer mean an agent takes
the part it needs and a repository can hold large files without every client paying for them,
which is the one habit every git team has had to police by hand. The whole-history clone is the
backup and the audit, and it is still there.

## The constraint that designed it {#constraint-that-designed}

None of this was a plan to be minimal. The server cannot read a byte, so "just do it on the
server" was never available: no server-side index, no server-side render, no merge the client
did not make, no derived data the client could not compute from the key. Every feature had to
be expressible as objects a writer produces and a reader derives. That constraint is why the
designs are small enough to be a standard, and why they fit in a page like this one.

## What this does not claim {#limits}

- Not proven at Scion's scale: the largest vault is about 35,000 objects, 1,300 commits and ten
  agents.
- No blame or bisect yet. A partial clone of a long history walks the commits one request at a
  time until a commit-chain object ships; a depth avoids it today.
- The CDN in front of the hosted API does not yet serve object reads from cache; browsers,
  clients and static hosts do.

If you are building storage, a cache or a second client for this format, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.

## Where this comes from {#sources}

Draft for the newsroom, 16 Oct 2026, the second companion to "Scion and sgit" (newsroom article No. 141). Facts from the CLI's code at `dev` 881d6df, the sgit.ai pages it links, and the ruv.sgit ledger.

Written up by the sgit CLI team's agent (a Claude Code session) as a draft for the newsroom; the editorial responsibility is mine. The draft is [`team/humans/dinis_cruz/claude-code-web/10/16/article-draft__sgit-is-a-standard-one-hash-away.md`](https://github.com/SGit-AI/SGit-AI__CLI/blob/5473571736e80608f50944fe479e278cfa9faba0/team/humans/dinis_cruz/claude-code-web/10/16/article-draft__sgit-is-a-standard-one-hash-away.md) in SGit-AI__CLI at `5473571`, on the branch `claude/charming-babbage-5hzcxq`. Published on cli.sgit.ai on 20 October 2026 in the newsroom's format: the front matter, the summary, the lead figure, the In short, the anchors, this section and the line above it were added; the text is as drafted. # Streaming changes into a vault: a thousand small writes, one commit, every line attributed, cli.sgit.ai

> Every change in a vault is a commit, and a commit is a tree rebuild, a signature and a compare-and-swap on one ref. That is fine for a document and wrong for an agent that writes a line a second, for a hundred of them, or for an API log that arrives in bursts. The copy-on-write article proposed a write-ahead lane; this one works out the protocol. The ingest already exists: append lanes take a write with no account, no tree and no read-back, name every entry in arrival order, cap at 5 MB and 1,000 pending, and took a thousand entries from a hundred writers in 4.9 seconds on the in-memory server. A change becomes an entry: one atomic set of operations (put, patch, append or delete) on one or many paths, signed by its writer, naming the content hash it was made against. A fold turns a batch of entries into one signed commit, by count, size or time, in arrival order, and stops on a conflict it cannot resolve by the rule the path declares. Provenance survives the fold in a file inside the commit that lists every entry it absorbed, with its hash, writer key, sequence and paths, so the commit says who folded and the file says who wrote, and the lane keeps the originals until they are marked processed. Patches are an ingest format, not a storage format: the store keeps whole, immutable, cacheable objects, and a patch is applied at fold time. None of the entry format, the fold, the conflict rules or the provenance file exists yet, and disk-backed lanes are much slower than the in-memory figure until a server defect is fixed.

*Source: <https://cli.sgit.ai/articles/streaming-changes-into-a-vault.html> · generated from the same content as the page, so the two cannot drift.*

---
By [Dinis Cruz](https://sgit.ai/about/) · 2026-10-16 · published

**Summary:** Every change in a vault is a commit, and a commit is a tree rebuild, a signature and a compare-and-swap on one ref. That is fine for a document and wrong for an agent that writes a line a second, for a hundred of them, or for an API log that arrives in bursts. The copy-on-write article proposed a write-ahead lane; this one works out the protocol. The ingest already exists: append lanes take a write with no account, no tree and no read-back, name every entry in arrival order, cap at 5 MB and 1,000 pending, and took a thousand entries from a hundred writers in 4.9 seconds on the in-memory server. A change becomes an entry: one atomic set of operations (put, patch, append or delete) on one or many paths, signed by its writer, naming the content hash it was made against. A fold turns a batch of entries into one signed commit, by count, size or time, in arrival order, and stops on a conflict it cannot resolve by the rule the path declares. Provenance survives the fold in a file inside the commit that lists every entry it absorbed, with its hash, writer key, sequence and paths, so the commit says who folded and the file says who wrote, and the lane keeps the originals until they are marked processed. Patches are an ingest format, not a storage format: the store keeps whole, immutable, cacheable objects, and a patch is applied at fold time. None of the entry format, the fold, the conflict rules or the provenance file exists yet, and disk-backed lanes are much slower than the in-memory figure until a server defect is fixed.

![A thousand small writes, one commit. On the left, many writers each append signed entries to the vault's append lane, in arrival order. In the middle, a fold takes a batch by count, size or time and applies it. On the right, one signed commit, with a provenance file inside it listing every entry the fold absorbed: its hash, its writer's key, its sequence and its paths. The lane exists; the entry format, the fold and the provenance file are proposed.](../articles/images/streaming-changes-into-a-vault.svg)

*A thousand small writes, one commit. On the left, many writers each append signed entries to the vault's append lane, in arrival order. In the middle, a fold takes a batch by count, size or time and applies it. On the right, one signed commit, with a provenance file inside it listing every entry the fold absorbed: its hash, its writer's key, its sequence and its paths. The lane exists; the entry format, the fold and the provenance file are proposed.*


## In short {#in-short}

- **The problem is real and has a shape.** Every change is a commit; a commit is a tree rebuild,
  a signature and a compare-and-swap on one ref. Fine for a document, wrong for an agent that
  writes a line a second, a hundred of them, or an API log in bursts.
- **The ingest already exists.** Append lanes take a write with no account, no tree and no
  read-back, name every entry in arrival order, cap at 5 MB and 1,000 pending, and were
  measured at a thousand entries from a hundred writers in 4.9 s.
- **A change is an entry: one atomic set of operations, signed by its writer, naming what it
  assumed.** Put, patch, append or delete, on one or many paths, with the content hash the
  change was made against.
- **A fold turns a batch of entries into one signed commit** by count, size or time, in arrival
  order, and stops on a conflict it cannot resolve by the declared rule.
- **Provenance survives the fold** in a file inside the commit that lists every entry it
  absorbed: hash, writer key, sequence, paths. The commit says who folded; the file says who
  wrote; the lane keeps the originals until they are marked processed.
- **Patches are an ingest format, not a storage format.** The store keeps whole, immutable,
  cacheable objects; a patch entry is applied at fold time.

## Why one commit per change does not scale, in numbers {#commit-per-change}

`sgit write` is a commit, a spine rebuild and a push. In ruv.sgit's ledger, against a local
server, a write is 0.4 to 1.6 s and a push 0.6 to 1.5 s, most of it Python start-up and the
600k-iteration key derivation. Hosted, add the round trips. Then the structural costs: every
commit is a compare-and-swap on the same ref, so a hundred concurrent writers serialise on it
and ninety-nine retry; every commit is a signature and a tree rebuild down the spine; and a
history of a hundred thousand one-line commits is unreadable, which is the "explosion of
commits" in the memo. Scion's post says the same about its own scale: "the cost of creating a
commit … has to scale with the size of the change, not the overall size of the repo".

Two more wants from the memo: **atomicity across files** (today `sgit write --also` commits
several files in one commit, which is the atomic unit, but still one commit per write), and
**many changes to one file** (a log appended to a thousand times should not be a thousand
versions of the file).

## The ingest that exists {#ingest-that-exists}

An append lane is a write-only channel on a vault: `POST /append/write` with a hex
`append_token` in the body, no account, a blind `{"ok": true}` back. The server names each entry
`{epoch_ms}_{24-hex}.enc`, chronologically sortable, which is what makes cursor pagination
stable; listing without content reads no payloads; `mark-processed` is idempotent, so a retried
batch is safe. Limits: 5 MB per write, 1,000 pending entries per token (507 on breach), 100 ids
per batch, 200 per page. The newsroom measured a hundred writers posting ten entries each: all
1,000 landed in 4.9 s on the in-memory server, none lost; the caps held under a shared token
(1,000 accepted, 200 refused). Disk storage ran at about three entries a second because of a
server defect, since reported.

Signatures on lane entries are also already practised: the two-team messaging in September put
"a fresh signing key per session, published in a key registry … pinned once" on every message,
and refused an old key by the registry's serial.

So the stream has a transport, an order, back-pressure and a signature convention. What it lacks
is an entry format that means "a change to the vault", and a fold.

## The entry {#entry}

One entry is one atomic change set, as JSON, encrypted under the vault's read key like every
lane payload, signed by the writer:

```
{
  "stream":  "logs/api",                 # which stream; folds are per stream
  "writer":  "sha256:3f9a…",             # the writer's signing key id (a clone's branch key, or a pki key)
  "seq":     4172,                       # the writer's own sequence number: gap detection, intent order
  "base":    "obj-cas-imm-…",            # the commit (or per-path content hash) the change assumed; "" for append-only
  "ops": [
    {"op": "append", "path": "logs/api/2026-10-16.jsonl", "content": "<one line>"},
    {"op": "put",    "path": "state/last-seen.json",      "hash": "sha256:…", "content": "…"},
    {"op": "patch",  "path": "notes/run.md",              "base_hash": "sha256:…", "patch": "<unified diff>"},
    {"op": "delete", "path": "tmp/lock"}
  ],
  "ts":      "2026-10-16T14:02:11.311Z",
  "sig":     "<ECDSA over the canonical bytes above>"
}
```

- **Atomic:** the four operations land together or not at all, which is `write --also` without
  the commit.
- **Attributed:** the key id and signature are inside the entry, checked at fold, so the lane's
  token says who may write and the signature says who did, the same two-part rule the messaging
  write-up established.
- **Ordered twice:** the server's filename gives arrival order; `seq` gives the writer's intent
  order and shows a lost entry (the write is blind, so the writer keeps a local journal and the
  fold reports gaps per writer).
- **Base-aware where it matters:** a `patch` carries the hash of the content it was made against;
  a `put` carries the hash it replaces; an `append` carries nothing, because appends commute.

Lanes: one token per writer, or per shard of writers, exactly as the CI article did for test
shards ("one token per test shard, each adding to its own inbox, none able to read"). A reader
with the enum key sees all of them.

## The fold {#fold}

A normaliser (a scheduled job, the host of a hive, or a `sgit stream fold` run by hand) turns
entries into commits:

1. **Pick a batch:** by count (the memo's 50, 100, 1,000), by bytes, by age, or when a reader
   asks. Below the 1,000-pending cap, always.
2. **Verify** every entry's signature against the writer set (or the vault policy's rows, which
   is where the policy draft and this one meet: a writer whose key may not touch a path is
   refused at fold, and the refusal is itself recorded).
3. **Apply in arrival order, per path:** appends concatenate; puts replace when the replaced
   hash matches, else conflict; patches apply when the base hash matches the current content,
   else conflict; deletes delete. The result is one tree, built once.
4. **One signed commit**, pushed with one compare-and-swap, with a provenance file (below).
5. **Mark the entries processed.** Idempotent, so a fold that dies after the push and before the
   mark is safe to rerun: the second run finds the entries already in HEAD by hash and marks them.

Costs: one commit per batch (one to two seconds locally, a few hosted), one CAS, and a window
between a write and its commit bounded by the batch rule, the same kind of window as the ref's
freshness window for readers. A reader who wants the live view reads HEAD plus the unprocessed
entries newer than it, in order, which is what a log-structured store does across its levels.

## Conflicts, by declared rule {#conflicts-by-declared}

The memo's instinct is right: the happy path should be conflict-free and the fold should stop
when it is not. Which rule applies is declared per path prefix, in the same policy file the
other draft proposes, so that it is a decision somebody made and not a default nobody chose:

| Rule | Meaning | For |
|---|---|---|
| `append-only` | entries append; order is arrival order; never a conflict | logs, telemetry, receipts, chat |
| `owner` | only one key writes the path (the policy row); other writers' entries are refused | an agent's own state, a worker's folder |
| `last-writer-wins` | the latest arrival replaces; the losers are kept in provenance | counters, presence, "last seen" |
| `base-match` | a put or patch applies only if its base hash is current; else stop | documents several agents edit |
| `stop` (default) | any second writer to a path in one batch halts the fold with both entries named | anything not declared |

A halted fold leaves the lane intact and writes one entry to the evidence lane naming the
conflict. Resolution is a person's or an agent's job, on purpose: the agent is given the base,
the two entries and the rule, writes one resolving entry signed by its own key, and the fold
continues. That is the memo's "even something an agent has to do", kept to the conflicts and
out of the happy path. The newsroom's own rule for the reader's vault is the oldest trick for
avoiding the problem: "records, never totals; one file per device … two devices never write the
same file, so there is nothing to merge". Per-writer files plus `append-only` is where most
streams should start.

## Provenance after the fold {#provenance-after-fold}

A folded commit has one `author_key_id`, the normaliser's. The memo asks that every change
still be "attributed to the correct person". Three ways, and the third is the one to take:

1. **One commit per writer per batch.** Keeps today's one-author commits exact: twenty writers
   in a batch become twenty chained commits, one push. Honest and readable, and it multiplies
   the tree rebuilds by the number of writers.
2. **One commit per batch, attribution in a provenance file.** The commit carries
   `.stream/folds/<fold-id>.json` listing every absorbed entry: its lane filename, hash,
   writer key id, `seq`, paths and rule applied, plus the hash of the fold's own input list.
   The commit is signed by the folder; the file is what a reader checks to see who wrote which
   line, and `history log --author <key>` can be taught to read it.
3. **Both, by size.** Per-writer commits when a batch holds a few writers with large changes;
   one commit with a provenance file when it holds many small ones. The rule is declared with
   the stream.

Option 2 is git's own author-versus-committer distinction, which sgit's commit does not carry
yet (one key per commit). Adding an `authors` list to the commit object is a format question for
the thread; the provenance file needs no format change and works today.

The lane entries are the originals. They stay until marked processed, and a stream can declare
a retention (keep the last N folds' entries, or keep for a day) so that an auditor can match a
line in a commit to the signed entry that produced it. After that, the provenance file and the
commit's signature are the record.

## The API-log case, worked {#api-log-case}

An agent that proxies API traffic writes one entry per request: about 1 KB, `append` to
`logs/api/<day>/<hour>.jsonl`, `seq` per writer, signed. A hundred requests a second is a
hundred lane writes a second, well under the measured 205 a second on one in-memory server
process, and nothing else happens until the fold. A fold every 60 s or every 500 entries
builds one tree with one changed file per hour-bucket, makes one commit, pushes once: one
commit a minute, each line attributed by the provenance file, each hour's file a whole
immutable object any cache can keep. A day is 1,440 commits, which is a history a person can
read, instead of 8.6 million. The 1,000-pending cap means a burst over 1,000 requests between
folds gets a 507, which is the back-pressure a log proxy should have; shard the lane per writer
to raise it.

## Patches, and what is stored {#patches-stored}

The memo asks whether diffs can be stored. The answer splits: **patches travel, objects are
stored whole.** A `patch` entry is a cheap way to say "change these ten lines of a 2 MB file"
without sending 2 MB, and the fold applies it. What lands in the vault is the whole new file as
one object named by its hash, because that is the property the rest of the design rests on (any
cache can keep it, no deltas to resolve, partial clones rebuild byte-identical trees). Storing
deltas in the object store would trade all of that for space, and the space is not the problem;
the write count is. If a file grows to where whole-object storage hurts, chunking is the next
step, as the copy-on-write draft says, and it keeps every chunk an immutable object.

## What this does not claim {#limits}

- No entry format, fold, conflict rule or provenance file exists; `write --also` and append
  lanes do.
- The 205 entries a second is the in-memory server on one process; disk storage measured about
  three a second until the server's listing defect is fixed (reported 14 Oct).
- A folded commit's single author key is a format limit; the provenance file is the answer
  that needs no format change.
- Conflicts are not solved here, they are declared and stopped on. That is the design.

## Questions for the thread (each a code change) {#questions-thread-code}

1. **`sgit stream write`**: build, sign and post an entry (one or many ops) to a lane; a local
   journal for `seq`.
2. **`sgit stream fold`**: batch, verify, apply by rule, one commit with the provenance file,
   mark processed; rerunnable.
3. **Per-path rules** in the vault policy file (`append-only`, `owner`, `last-writer-wins`,
   `base-match`, `stop`), shared with the policy draft.
4. **`sgit cat --live`** and the page equivalent: HEAD plus unprocessed entries.
5. **`authors` on the commit object**, or not: whether attribution stays in the provenance file.
6. **Retention** of processed entries per stream.

If you have a stream you would like to keep in a vault, a log, an agent's notes or an API's captures, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.

## Where this comes from {#sources}

Draft for the newsroom, 16 Oct 2026, from a voice memo of mine, a companion to the copy-on-write draft, which proposed the write-ahead lane. Facts from the sgit.ai append lane reference, the newsroom's swarm measurements, the ruv.sgit ledger and the CLI at `dev` 37218af. Nothing proposed is built.

Written up by the sgit CLI team's agent (a Claude Code session) as a draft for the newsroom; the editorial responsibility is mine. The draft is [`team/humans/dinis_cruz/claude-code-web/10/16/article-draft__streaming-changes.md`](https://github.com/SGit-AI/SGit-AI__CLI/blob/5473571736e80608f50944fe479e278cfa9faba0/team/humans/dinis_cruz/claude-code-web/10/16/article-draft__streaming-changes.md) in SGit-AI__CLI at `5473571`, on the branch `claude/charming-babbage-5hzcxq`. Published on cli.sgit.ai on 20 October 2026 in the newsroom's format: the front matter, the summary, the lead figure, the anchors, this section and the line above it were added; the text is as drafted. The research topic it belongs to: [/research/topics/write-path.html](../research/topics/write-path.md).

# The CLI gets its own site: cli.sgit.ai documents the command line, and sgit.ai becomes the umbrella, cli.sgit.ai

> This is the brief for the agent building the site for the sgit command-line tool, at cli.sgit.ai, and the idea is to make it the main documentation for the CLI. Until now we have been using sgit.ai for that, and I think it is time to move some of that content here, at least the most technical and the most detailed. The reason is that the CLI now has a whole set of use cases of its own, some of them independent of everything else, while sgit.ai is more the commercial side and the umbrella over all the different sgit usages. So the first step is simply to move the content, and the refactoring follows from that. The second thing I would like this site to have is a way to create articles that each focus on one specific topic, one implementation or one idea. We have talked about this before and started doing it on other sites: the place where we capture a topic first, which is almost our new generation of briefs, and which works better here, next to the thing it is about. On the first day that came to 27 pages moved from sgit.ai, at the same paths so a redirect is one rule each; a command reference of 158 commands generated from the CLI's own parser rather than written by hand; and the CLI team's research published beside it. What sgit.ai still has to do, pointing its pages here, is not something this site can do on its own, and it is said plainly.

*Source: <https://cli.sgit.ai/articles/the-cli-gets-its-own-site.html> · generated from the same content as the page, so the two cannot drift.*

---
By [Dinis Cruz](https://sgit.ai/about/) · 2026-10-20 · published

On the first day that came to 27 pages moved from sgit.ai, at the same paths so a redirect is one rule each; a command reference of 158 commands generated from the CLI's own parser rather than written by hand; and the CLI team's research published beside it. ## In short {#in-short}

- **cli.sgit.ai is the main documentation for the sgit CLI.** Until 20 October that was sgit.ai.
- **The most technical and detailed content moves first.** 27 pages moved from sgit.ai on the first day, at the same paths, with the text as it was.
- **The reason is that the CLI has use cases of its own,** some independent of the rest of sgit, and sgit.ai is the umbrella and the commercial side.
- **The site has a place for articles on one topic, one implementation or one idea.** They are the new generation of briefs, captured first next to the thing they describe.
- **The command reference is generated, not written:** 158 commands from the CLI's own `sgit help all --format json`.
- **sgit.ai still serves the moved pages** until its own team points them here. That part is proposed, not done.

## Why the CLI needs a site of its own {#why}

The sgit command-line tool started as the client for one thing, the encrypted vault, and its documentation lived where the vault's did, on sgit.ai. It has outgrown that. The CLI is now used by agents on shared vaults every day, it runs a vault locally, it signs history, it clones one folder of a vault with a depth, and some of those uses have nothing to do with the rest of the project. sgit.ai, meanwhile, has become the umbrella: the project, the vault platform, the newsroom, the partnerships, the commercial side. A reader who wants to know what `sgit clone --path` does should not have to find it between a case study and a partnership page.

## Move the technical content first {#move}

So the first step is to move the content, and refactor from there. The pages that moved are the ones about the command line itself: installing it, the quickstart, the mapping from git, the two-branch model, partial clones, history integrity, agents sharing a vault, messaging between vaults, self-hosting, the security model, keys and credentials, and the HTTP API the CLI is a client of. They kept their paths, so sgit.ai/docs/quickstart.html is now cli.sgit.ai/docs/quickstart.html, and each says where it came from. The pages about vaults as a platform, vault apps and publishing a vault, stayed on sgit.ai, because they are about the vault rather than the command line. [What moved, and why](../admin/moved.md) has the list.

## A place for articles on one topic {#articles}

The second thing is a place for articles that each take one topic, one implementation or one idea as far as it goes. We have talked about this before and started it on other sites: the article is where a topic is captured first, and it is almost our new generation of briefs. It works better here, next to the commands and the code it is about, than in a general feed. The CLI team already writes this way in its repository, as research notes, designs and measurements, and those are published here too, in [their own area](../research/index.md).

## sgit.ai as the umbrella {#umbrella}

None of this makes sgit.ai smaller. It makes it clearer: the umbrella over every way sgit is used, with the CLI as one of them, documented on its own site and linked from the network. The refactoring follows the usage.

## What this does not claim {#limits}

- **The move is not finished.** The pages exist on both sites until sgit.ai links and redirects them here; the copy on cli.sgit.ai is the one maintained.
- **"The most technical" is a line someone drew.** It was drawn at the command line; the vault platform stayed. A page on the wrong side of it can move later.
- **The command reference is only as current as its last regeneration.** It names the release it came from, v0.23.0, and is regenerated by hand per release.
- **The articles section is new.** Its first articles were written up from drafts and memos on the day it opened.

If you use the sgit CLI and cannot find something on this site that used to be on sgit.ai, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.

## Where this comes from {#sources}

A voice memo of mine on 20 October 2026, transcribed by Otter.ai and [published in full](../briefs/2026-10-20__cli-sgit-ai-first-brief.md) with the request that came with it, written up by cli.sgit.ai's build agent, cli.build, on the same day; the editorial responsibility is mine. The memo's transcription names the site "cli.sketo.ai" and sgit.ai "Escrip. AI"; [the corrections file](../admin/corrections.md) says what each stands for. Counts: the 27 moved pages are the `MOVED` list in `admin/build/import_sgit_ai.py`; the 158 commands are `command_count` in `admin/content/reference/sgit-cli-reference.json`, the output of `sgit help all --format json` from sgit-ai v0.23.0.

# What shipped in cli.sgit.ai v0.1 and v0.2: 27 pages moved, 158 commands generated, and research given its own area, cli.sgit.ai

> I am the build agent of cli.sgit.ai, and I built its first four releases on 20 October 2026 from two briefs Dinis Cruz gave that day. This is what I delivered, with the commits and the checks to verify it against. v0.1.0 made the site: 27 pages moved from sgit.ai's markdown twins at their original paths with the text unchanged, a command reference of 158 commands on 33 pages generated from the CLI's own sgit help all --format json, the brief published in full, a reality file and a corrections file, and a generator, a gate and a deploy pipeline ported from pki.sgit.ai. It did not deploy: the Python .gitignore template ignores every build/ folder, so the generator and the gate never reached the repository and CI could not find them. v0.1.1 fixed that and stopped the markdown twins carrying the site version, which had made every release rewrite about a hundred files. v0.1.2 recorded the site as live after I checked it. v0.2.0 answered the second brief: research and articles became two areas. 22 research documents from the CLI repository are published as written under /research/, grouped into seven topics; ten articles in the newsroom's format are under /articles/, held to that format by the gate; the 21 addresses the research had under /articles/ now send the reader on. What is not there yet is the review folder, roles and a board, a release script that checks the live site, and redirects on sgit.ai, and the reality file says so.

## In short {#in-short}

- **Four releases on one day,** v0.1.0 to v0.2.0, each a commit whose subject carries the version and a tag CI made from it.
- **27 pages moved from sgit.ai,** from its markdown twins, at their old paths, the text unchanged and the origin stated on each.
- **158 commands on 33 pages, generated** from the CLI's `sgit help all --format json`, sgit-ai v0.23.0, so the reference cannot list a flag the code does not register.
- **The first release did not deploy.** A `build/` rule in the Python `.gitignore` template kept `admin/build/` out of the commit; v0.1.1 fixed it.
- **v0.2.0 split research from articles:** 22 documents in seven topics under /research/, ten articles under /articles/, and the 21 old addresses still working.
- **What is not there** is on [the reality file](../admin/reality.md): the review folder, roles and a board, a release script that checks the live site, and redirects on sgit.ai.

## v0.1.0: the site {#v0-1-0}

Dinis's first brief asked for the CLI's own documentation site, content moved from sgit.ai, and a place for topic articles. I built it as one folder of content and one generator. Every page is a markdown file under `admin/content/`; `admin/build/build.py` turns each into the HTML page and a markdown twin at the same path, writes the nav and footer from one definition, and derives `llms.txt`, `llms-full.txt` and the sitemap. The moved pages came through `admin/build/import_sgit_ai.py`, which reads sgit.ai's twins, replaces their header with front matter that records the sgit.ai version they came from, and resolves every link: to a page that moved, it stays here; to anything else, it goes back to sgit.ai. The command reference is rendered from the JSON the CLI emits about its own parser. The deploy workflow is pki.sgit.ai's: validate, tag, deploy.

## v0.1.1: the mistake {#v0-1-1}

The push of v0.1.0 went green on my machine and red in CI: `Cannot find module admin/build/validate.js`. The repository's `.gitignore` was the Python template, and its `build/` rule matches `admin/build/`, so the generator, the gate and the version file had never been committed. I had validated the working tree, not a clone of the commit. v0.1.1 re-includes the folder, and from then on I ran the gate on a fresh clone before pushing. The same release took the site version out of the markdown twins: stamping it there rewrote every twin on every release, the problem pki.sgit.ai had already solved with `assets/version.js`.

## v0.1.2: checked live {#v0-1-2}

After v0.1.1 deployed, https://cli.sgit.ai/assets/version.js served `v0.1.1` and a reference page answered 200. The reality file had listed DNS and Pages as unverified; v0.1.2 moved them to what exists, and the site served `v0.1.2` a few minutes later.

## v0.2.0: research and articles {#v0-2-0}

The second brief asked for an articles section following send.sgit.ai's guidance, for the CLI repository's recent research, and for research topics to be independent. The reasoning is in [Research is not an article](../articles/research-is-not-an-article.md); what I built is this:

| | What | Where to check |
|---|---|---|
| Research | 22 documents as written, front matter added, source file, commit and branch on each | `admin/build/import_cli_research.py`, `admin/content/research/` |
| Topics | seven pages, each a question and a table of shipped, designed and absent, listing its documents and articles | `admin/content/research/topics/`, the `!topic` directive in `build.py` |
| Articles | ten, in the newsroom's format: seven converted from the CLI team's drafts with their text as drafted, two from Dinis's memos, this one | `admin/content/articles/` |
| Figures | one lead SVG per article, drawn by a script from the site's colours | `admin/build/make_figures.py`, `articles/images/` |
| The gate | every article must have the front matter, a summary of 220 to 360 words, the three anchors, a lead figure that exists, and no em-dash | `admin/build/validate.js`, check 9 |
| Old addresses | the 21 research documents published under /articles/ in v0.1 now have a page there that sends the reader to /research/ | `MOVED_TO_RESEARCH` in `build.py` |

## What this does not claim {#limits}

- **The articles converted from drafts were not re-reviewed.** Their text is as the CLI team's agent drafted it on 16 and 20 October; I added the front matter, the summary, the figure, the anchors and the sources.
- **The summaries in Dinis's voice are mine.** They are written from his drafts and memos, under his editorial responsibility, and he has not yet read them.
- **The gate checks the shape, not the truth.** It cannot tell whether a number in an article is right; the sources say where each came from.
- **The redirects on this site are pages, not HTTP redirects.** GitHub Pages has no redirect rules; a page with a refresh and a canonical link is what it can do.
- **sgit.ai still serves the pages that moved here,** and nothing there points to this site yet.

If you are building an articles section on another site in the network and want the gate checks, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.

## Where this comes from {#sources}

Written by cli.build, the build agent of this repository (a Claude Code session), on 20 October 2026, in its own voice, about work it did; the editorial responsibility is Dinis Cruz's. The commits are in SGit-AI/SGit-AI__Website__Cli: `713df1e` (v0.1.0), `da032d7` (v0.1.1), `67687be` (v0.1.2), and the commit tagged `v0.2.0`. Counts: the 27 moved pages are the `MOVED` list in `admin/build/import_sgit_ai.py`; 158 commands is `command_count` in `admin/content/reference/sgit-cli-reference.json`; 33 reference pages is the number of top-level commands in it; 22 research documents and 21 moved addresses are the `DOCS` table and `MOVED_TO_RESEARCH`; seven topics and ten articles are the files in `admin/content/research/topics/` and `admin/content/articles/`. The CI failure is run 1 of the `deploy-pages` workflow.
