# Research, cli.sgit.ai

> The sgit CLI team's research, kept as written and grouped into topics: measurements on real vaults, designs and the reviews that corrected them, security reviews, and the bugs found in daily use, each with its source in the CLI repository.

*Source: <https://cli.sgit.ai/research/index.html> · generated from the same content as the page, so the two cannot drift.*

---
# Research

The CLI team's working documents, **published as written**: measurements on real vaults, designs and the reviews that corrected them, decisions, security reviews and the bugs found in daily use. Each one takes one question as far as the evidence went on the day it was written. They are the record, so they are not edited here; where one was wrong, a later document says so, usually above the mistake.

**Research is not the same as an article.** An [article](../articles/index.md) makes one argument for a reader, in the newsroom's format, and is written to be read start to finish. A research document is the work itself: tables, open questions, the plan that was later superseded. When a research thread produces an argument, it becomes an article, and the topic page links both.

## Topics

Each topic is one open question, with where it stands today: what is shipped, what is designed, what is absent.

- [Keys, members and who may write](../research/topics/keys.md): Should the read key and the write key become key pairs, can a vault have members who join and leave by a file each, and can a vault enforce who writes where? What is built, what is designed, and what is still a question.
- [History integrity and signatures](../research/topics/integrity.md): How sgit made a vault's history verifiable without a vault move: signed commits, a format gate, rewind detection, and the compatibility rule that a newer client must never break an older one still writing.
- [Big vaults and many agents](../research/topics/scale.md): What happens when a vault reaches 35,000 objects and ten agents use it every day: what a clone fetches, what each session costs, which fixes came from measuring it, and why the server can stay simple.
- [How a vault takes writes](../research/topics/write-path.md): One commit per change is right for documents and wrong for a stream, and many small objects cost a request each. Copy-on-write, a write-ahead append lane, a vault in one zip, and pack mode, a zip per push: what sgit already does, and what is proposed.
- [Running a vault locally](../research/topics/serve.md): How to run a working vault, UI and API, on your own machine: the research into the server's API, the decision to run the SG/Send container rather than re-implement it, and the runtimes sgit supports.
- [Reviewing sgit's security with tools and agents](../research/topics/security-review.md): A tool-assisted security review of the code the zero-knowledge guarantee lives in: which agent skills and threat-modelling tools were worth running, what each found, and a CI pipeline where an AI review can break the build.
- [Found in daily use](../research/topics/correctness.md): The bugs that agents and people hit while using sgit every day, each traced to its cause in the code, with what was fixed and what is still open.

## Every document, newest first

- [Spec: pack mode for sgit (CLI-only, packs-only vaults, no server change)](../research/pack-mode-spec.md): The specification for pack mode: every push writes one zip pack, a snapshot pack compacts them, nothing is deleted, large packs go straight to S3 by presigned URL, and a gated packs-only vault needs no server change. Commands, layout, failure handling, tests and the four performance runs.
- [Brief to the SG/Send team: append to a vault object on S3 without re-uploading it, and conditional completes](../research/zip-append-via-s3-brief.md): A brief to the SG/Send team: a presigned append route that grows a zip on S3 by UploadPartCopy, conditional completes with If-Match and If-None-Match, and size and ETag with the read URL. Written for a single appended zip; the pack-mode spec of the next day needs none of it for its first version.
- [Keys the way git does them, PKI access to a vault, and copy-on-write: what is already published, and what is not](../research/keys-pki-copy-on-write-coverage-map.md): Before writing two articles, a map of what is already published on keys the way git does them, PKI access to a vault and copy-on-write: seven questions from the memo, where each stands, the facts the articles must not get wrong, and seven code questions for the thread.
- [Response to "Scion and sgit" (newsroom.sgit.ai, article No. 141, v1.0.0)](../research/response-to-scion-and-sgit.md): The CLI team's response to the newsroom's "Scion and sgit" article: what it gets right, the three factual errors, and the measurements from a 35k-object vault the article should have carried.
- [Response to "sgit issues found on 14 October 2026", and the comms-vault performance report](../research/sgit-issues-2026-10-14.md): The issues reported on 14 October, each traced to its cause in the code, with what was fixed in the same push and what was left open.
- [Security CI: a dedicated pipeline, and an AI review that can break the build](../research/security-ci-and-ai-review.md): A dedicated security pipeline on every pull request, and a keyless AI security review that can break the build on anything new: why, how it is wired, and what it costs per reviewed change.
- [AC-L-001 / TM-R36 — characters outside `[a-zA-Z0-9/\_.- ]` in paths: what really happens](../research/non-ascii-paths-refuse-dont-rewrite.md): Characters outside a narrow set in a path are silently rewritten, so one vault gets two roots and a false push conflict. What really happens, reproduced, and a fix that raises an alarm instead of rewriting.
- [`sgit serve`: container first. Options map and spike results](../research/sgit-serve-container-first.md): The decision to run the SG/Send container image rather than re-implement the server: the runtimes supported (including Apple's container and Podman), the spike results, and phase 1 as built.
- [`sgit serve`: running a vault locally — research and plan](../research/sgit-serve-running-a-vault-locally.md): How to run a vault locally: the vault server's API inventory, the browser modes, when TLS is and is not needed, and how much plumbing sgit would need.
- [Case study — a tool-assisted security review of sgit-ai 0.21.0 (round 1)](../research/security-review-case-study.md): What each tool found in the round-1 security review of sgit-ai 0.21.0, with counts and cost: the skill vetting, the derived graph, 270 function records, 68 STRIDE threats and the insider overlay.
- [Threat-modeling tools for an agent-driven review — Matt Adams' stack, the classics, and the house method](../research/threat-modeling-tools.md): Threat-modeling tools for an agent-driven review: Matt Adams' stack (STRIDE GPT, the insider-threat model), the classics, and the house method, with the agent itself named as an actor.
- [Agent skills for security review — what exists, what it would do here](../research/security-review-skills.md): Agent skills for security review, each checked at its source, ranked by whether it brings a method, a tool with deterministic output, or vets the other skills, against this code base.
- [Plan — the next security review of sgit-ai, with skills, and the review graphs it produces](../research/security-review-plan.md): The plan for a tool-assisted, data-producing security review of one slice of sgit-ai: the code the zero-knowledge guarantee and the trust boundaries live in.
- [Sealed files — a second encryption layer on top of a vault](../research/sealed-files-layer.md): A second encryption layer on top of either vault mode: files sealed to named recipients with ECDH P-256, HKDF and AES-256-GCM, with the corrections from the sgit.ai agent's review.
- [Native PKI vault mode — architecture map](../research/native-pki-vault-mode.md): An architecture map for a second vault mode built on key pairs from the start, revised twice after review: sequence-number pinning, frozen hosts, concurrent writers.
- [Read and write keys as PKI — design analysis](../research/read-write-keys-as-pki.md): Are the read key and the write key really a public and a private key? Half right: the write key should become a signing key, and the read key cannot become a public key. What that would take.
- [Branches check, test performance, test quality — 8 Oct 2026](../research/branches-and-test-suite-review.md): An end-to-end check found that branches did not work. What was fixed behind it, the tests that now cover it, and a review of the test suite's speed and quality.
- [Possible future features, after 0.21.0](../research/future-features-after-0-21.md): The git-parity and security ideas that are not in 0.21.0, what each would take and what it could break, starting from the constraint that a new commit field breaks older clients' signature checks.
- [Review: "Git security features → sgit: a one-way mapping](../research/git-to-sgit-security-mapping.md): A review of the one-way map from git's security features to sgit, checked against the code: three corrections, one missing gap, and the four easy gaps closed for 0.21.0.
- [Compatibility matrix: sgit CLI × vault web UI × SG/Send API, across the integrity roll-out](../research/compatibility-matrix-cli-web-ui-api.md): The CLI, the vault web UI and the SG/Send API across the integrity roll-out, step by step: what each version reads, writes and loses, under the rule that no client may break another still writing.
- [History integrity: what the three fixes would cost, and how to ship them without a `vault move`](../research/history-integrity-cost-and-compatibility.md): What signature verification, ref monotonicity and 128-bit ids would cost, measured on a real vault, and how to ship all three without a vault move.
- [Partial clones — a folder scope and a history depth (6 Oct 2026)](../research/partial-clones-scope-and-depth.md): Cloning just the folders an agent reads and writes, read and write, plus a shallow mode, without changing the full clone: the Merkle-spine idea and the measurements.
- [Fix — `sgit pull` silently discarded uncommitted edits to tracked files](../research/pull-discarded-uncommitted-edits.md): sgit pull silently discarded uncommitted edits to tracked files. The root cause, and the fix: git's rules for the working tree, applied before any write.
- [Clone performance — the tree walk re-fetched shared sub-trees once per parent](../research/clone-refetched-shared-subtrees.md): A clone stuck walking trees: the walk re-fetched shared sub-trees once per parent, 10,098 requests for 2,236 unique trees. The instrumented run and the fix.

# Keys the way git does them, PKI access to a vault, and copy-on-write: what is already published, and what is not, cli.sgit.ai

> Before writing two articles, a map of what is already published on keys the way git does them, PKI access to a vault and copy-on-write: seven questions from the memo, where each stands, the facts the articles must not get wrong, and seven code questions for the thread.

*Source: <https://cli.sgit.ai/research/keys-pki-copy-on-write-coverage-map.html> · generated from the same content as the page, so the two cannot drift. Published from <https://github.com/SGit-AI/SGit-AI__CLI/blob/477d328536b04147e78281fb1f13550df1abf140/team/humans/dinis_cruz/claude-code-web/10/16/research__keys-pki-cow__coverage-map.md>.*

# Keys the way git does them, PKI access to a vault, and copy-on-write: what is already published, and what is not

**Date:** 16 Oct 2026. **For:** the agent that manages sgit; input to one or two newsroom articles.
**No code changes:** this is research and mapping. Anything that would need code is listed in §5 as a
question for the thread. **Sources read:** every newsroom article on keys and identity (11), the
sgit.ai pages on PKI, credentials, key management, messaging, authentication and history purging
(14), the threat model and the CLI at `dev` 37218af, RuVector's and RVF's READMEs, ruv.sgit.ai.

## 1. The questions in the memo, and where each stands

| # | Question (from the memo) | Already published? | Where | Gap |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Native public/private keys for a vault (read key pair, write key pair) | **Yes, as a design (RFC)** | newsroom *RFC 0001: two ways to add public-key cryptography to sgit* (9 Oct): Design 1, native PKI vault mode, two key pairs neither derivable from the other, data key sealed to the read public key, heads signed by the write private key, a write-only depositor; Design 2, sealed files; a shared first step, a vault signing key on today's vaults. Effort estimates and 11 reviewer questions. | Not built. The memo's "public key as read key, private key as write key" is the exact construction the RFC corrects ("whatever decrypts must be secret"): two pairs, not one. |
| 2 | The git + SSH + GitHub model: authenticate once, then anything goes; no per-commit check unless signed; local copies are unrestricted | **Partly.** The server-side half is documented (`api/authentication`: six capability headers, SHA-256 hash comparison, reads open by default; `docs/credentials`: what a read key can and cannot do). The git comparison is not written anywhere. | sgit.ai `api/authentication`, `docs/credentials`, `docs/sgit-for-git-users` (no auth row) | **No article maps git's SSH/HTTPS authorisation onto sgit's write key, read key, access token and signatures.** That is the article to write (§2 of the draft). |
| 3 | "The read key locally does not prevent changes", like a git clone | **Yes, as a threat-model fact, not as prose.** A read-only clone holds the read key on disk (TM-R15, KI-SEC-03); it cannot push (the server wants the write key hash); the host cannot tell a reader from a writer by the bytes (RFC 0001 "The honest problem"). | threat model TM-R15, TM-R12; RFC 0001 | Same as 2: the comparison is the missing piece, and it is a good one, because the answer is "exactly like git, and here is what git adds on the server that sgit adds with signatures". |
| 4 | A vault's members get in with their own key pair: a file per member, sealed to their public key, holding the read (or write) key | **Yes, three times, in three shapes.** (a) RFC 0001 Design 1 "Rotation": an owner key signs a **writer set**; removing a reader is a new read pair and data key "sealed to the remaining members". (b) *The passkey opens the vault* (11 Oct): a **door per path**, one file holding the master's key encrypted under the door's read key, "retired by deleting its one file"; built and tested against a real vault server. (c) *secrets.sgit.ai on public keys* (14 Oct), way 8: "A team. One inbox per member… with revocation by rotating and re-sharing"; and "The private key lives in a vault". Also `docs/pki` "Where public keys live in a vault": `bare/keys/key-rnd-imm-*`. | RFC 0001; passkey article §"A lost device", "Moving keys between masters"; secrets article; `docs/pki` | The pieces are published separately. **Nobody has written the membership pattern as one thing**: a members folder (or branch), join by adding a file, leave by deleting it, and the honest limit. |
| 5 | Revocation: delete the member's file; but history keeps it | **Yes, the problem is stated, and the current rule is "rotate".** Passkey article: "The catch is history. Vaults keep their versions, so an entry deleted from A is still in A's past for anyone who can open A. The rule: keys that move for security reasons get rotated." `docs/key-management`: "Rotation is not retroactive." TM-R12: "Read access cannot be revoked: a read key reads all history forever." `case-studies/purging-history`: how a git history rewrite works and why "rotate the secret, then rewrite". | passkey article; key-management; credentials; TM-R12; purging-history | **The feature the memo asks for, files that exist only at the current version, is not designed anywhere.** §3 of the draft lays out the three ways to get it and which one is already a primitive in the code. |
| 6 | The key never stored locally, only in memory for the run | **Partly.** `sgit clone -` reads the key from stdin "keeps it out of argv and history" (0.21.0); the passkey design computes the door key from PRF bytes and stores nothing; *Handing secrets to agents*: the session makes its key pair, the secret is piped "into the tool, not the chat". But every clone still writes `.sg_vault/local/vault_key` (0600) and a read-only clone writes the read key to `clone_mode.json` (TM-R15). | CHANGELOG 0.21.0; passkey article; handing-secrets; TM-R15 | **A "no key on disk" clone mode** (derive at start, hold in memory, re-derive from the member's private key next time) is not designed. It falls out of §3's pattern. |
| 7 | Copy-on-write, as asked for by rUv's team | **No.** The only mention anywhere is a secure-unlink debrief noting that on btrfs/APFS/ZFS an overwrite does not erase. ruv.sgit.ai records that RuVector "already has snapshots and copy-on-write branching (rvf derive)" and that POC2 "adds an sgit vault around the memory files", without saying what copy-on-write would mean for the vault itself. | ruv.sgit.ai `ruv-stack`; RuVector README ("Copy on write branches: isolated memory experiments without full copies"); RVF README (COW_MAP, lineage) | **A whole article**: what copy-on-write is, how sgit's object model already is one, what RVF's version adds, and where sgit would need a write-ahead lane and compaction to keep up. §4 and the second draft. |

## 2. What the code does today (the facts the articles must not get wrong)

- **Three credentials, one derivation.** `passphrase:vault_id` → PBKDF2 (600k) → read key (encrypts everything, AES-256-GCM) and write key (a bearer the server compares as a SHA-256 hash in `x-sgraph-vault-write-key`); a separate account token `x-sgraph-access-token`. Reads on the shared host need no credential; the ciphertext is the protection (`api/authentication`).
- **The server authorises a write by a shared secret, not by who you are.** Every writer presents the same write-key hash. The server cannot tell writers apart; nor can a reader tell whether a head was written by a writer or by the host (RFC 0001).
- **Commits are signed already.** Each clone has an ECDSA P-256 branch key pair (`Vault__Key_Manager`, raw r||s for Web Crypto); the public half is stored as `bare/keys/key-rnd-imm-*`; commits carry `author_key_id`; `sgit check verify` classifies every commit (verified / bad / unsigned / unknown key); the vault feature `signatures-required` makes `pull` refuse the first unsigned incoming commit, and `signed-since-<hex>` records where the policy began (0.19.0). `sgit pki` separately makes RSA-4096 encryption pairs and ECDSA signing pairs, encrypts to a recipient (RSA-OAEP wrapping AES-256-GCM), signs and verifies files; no revocation, no expiry, no directory (`docs/pki`).
- **The named branch only moves forward** (`last_remote_head`, rewind detection, `--accept-rewind`), and the branch index is a shared document merged by every client under compare-and-swap (0.19.0).
- **Mutable objects exist and are a first-class pattern.** Refs (`ref-pid-muw-*`), the branch index, the cache layer's value and pointer objects (`bare/cache/`, written directly to a path-derived id, random IV, "derived, never authoritative", D10), and the door file in the passkey design. These are the objects that have no history by construction.
- **Deletion exists.** `DELETE` of one object with the write key; `destroy` of a vault with a tombstone (`api/vault-objects`); `sgit vault delete-on-remote`; `sgit vault rekey` (wipe, init, commit under a new key: a new vault); `sgit vault move`.
- **History cannot be rewritten in place.** `history reset` + `push --force` rewinds a branch, but the old objects stay on the host until deleted, and every reader keeps what it fetched (TM-R12). The purge case study is about git, and its rule applies here: rotate first.

## 3. The membership pattern, assembled from what exists (for the first article)

What the memo describes is RFC 0001's writer set plus the passkey article's door, applied to a vault's members. In one place:

- A member is a public key (the `sgit pki` export, or an SSH key: Ed25519 SSH keys sign and X25519-convert for sealing; RSA SSH keys seal with RSA-OAEP as `pki encrypt` does today).
- The vault keeps, per member, one small object holding the data key (today's read key; under Design 1 the sealed data key) **encrypted to that member's public key**, at a location derived from the member's fingerprint. Opening the vault = fetch that one object, unwrap it with the private key, hold the data key in memory, never write it to disk.
- Join = a writer adds the member's object (it needs only the public key). Leave = delete it. Nothing else changes for the other members.
- The honest limit, stated by every existing page: deletion stops the next open, it does not undo a copy already made (TM-R12, `docs/credentials`). A member removed for cause means a rotation of the data key and re-sealing to the rest, which is RFC 0001's "removing a reader" step, and which `rekey` approximates today at the cost of a new vault.
- For writing, Design 1's write key pair: the server verifies a signature from a key in the writer set instead of comparing a shared hash. That is the "GitHub-equivalent": the SSH key authorises the push, and the commit signature says who wrote it.

The piece that is genuinely new is **where the member objects live**: in the Merkle tree they would be in history forever (the passkey article's catch), so they must be mutable objects outside it, like refs and the cache layer, which already exist, or a branch with a feature flag that says "no history here". §3 of the draft compares the three options and why the first is the primitive the code already has.

## 4. Copy-on-write, in one paragraph each (for the second article)

- **What it is.** Share until you write; copy only the part you change. Filesystems (ZFS, btrfs, APFS) use it for snapshots; virtual machines for disk images; the kernel for `fork()`; git for its object store (a commit is a new tree that shares every unchanged subtree by hash). The cost moves from the copy to the first write, and the gain is that a snapshot or a branch is free.
- **What RVF does.** A `.rvf` child file "shares all parent data; only changed vectors are copied: a 1M-vector parent with 100 edits produces a ~2.5 MB child instead of a 512 MB copy" (`COW_MAP` segment, cluster granularity, lineage recorded parent to child with hashes, a hash-linked witness chain, append-only so a crash never corrupts). That is a file format doing what a filesystem does, for one memory artefact. `rvf derive` is the verb.
- **What sgit already is.** A branch is a ref to a commit: creating one copies nothing. A commit stores only the new blobs and the rebuilt spine; every unchanged folder keeps its tree id. A scoped clone takes the spine and its folder. So sgit is copy-on-write at the object level with Merkle sharing, which is git's design, and the newsroom's *Agent workflows on ephemeral vaults* measured the consequence ("scoped clones that barely grow with the vault").
- **What it is not.** Two things RVF and the filesystems have that sgit does not: copy-on-write **inside a file** (a changed byte in a 100 MB file is a new 100 MB object in sgit; RVF copies the changed cluster), and a **cheap derived vault** (a vault cannot share objects with another vault, because they are encrypted under different keys; a fork is a branch, or a re-encryption). And a write path that is one commit per write (`sgit write`: a commit, a spine rebuild, a push, 0.5 to 1.5 s against a local server in the ruv.sgit ledger), which is fine for a hundred writes an hour and not for a hundred a second.
- **The memo's proposal, and why it is the right one.** Writes go to an append lane first (the newsroom measured 205 entries a second with none lost; caps of 1,000 waiting entries and 5 MB each), and a normaliser folds them into commits later. That is a write-ahead log with compaction, the shape of every LSM store, of RuVector's own `ruvector-lsm-ann` ("mutable L0 memory plus background L1 and L2 compaction") and of Scion's changeset log. The second draft sets out the semantics (what a reader sees between compactions, who signs the folded commit, de-duplication by hash) and the numbers.

## 5. Questions for the thread (each would be a code change; none is made here)

1. **Member objects outside the tree.** Add a `bare/members/` class of mutable objects (the cache layer's D10 pattern: path-derived id from the member's fingerprint, random IV, deletable), holding the data key sealed to the member's public key. Is a mutable object outside history acceptable for a credential, given the cache layer already is one for content?
2. **Or a `no-history` branch feature.** A branch whose ref moves without keeping parents and whose superseded objects the client deletes on push. Simpler to explain, harder to make safe (every client must honour it; a stale client would keep the parents).
3. **A no-key-on-disk open.** `sgit open --member <fingerprint>`: unwrap the data key with the local private key (or an SSH agent), hold it in memory, write nothing under `.sg_vault/local/`. The read-only clone's `clone_mode.json` (TM-R15) is the thing this replaces.
4. **Signed writes (RFC 0001 Design 1, first three phases).** Server verifies an Ed25519 (or the existing ECDSA P-256) signature from the writer set on each batch and CAS, instead of the shared write-key hash. Server work with the SG/Send team.
5. **SSH keys as sgit keys.** Accept an `~/.ssh/id_ed25519` (sign; X25519-convert to seal) or `id_rsa` (RSA-OAEP, as `pki encrypt` already does) as a member identity, and an SSH agent for signing. Pure client work; the RFC's "an ssh key" box in Design 2's provider list.
6. **Copy-on-write write path.** `sgit write --lane`: append-lane first, `sgit lane compact` (or a scheduled normaliser) folds entries into one signed commit. Needs a lane-entry envelope that names path, content hash and the writer's key, and a reader rule for "lane entries newer than HEAD".
7. **In-file copy-on-write for large files.** Content-defined chunking of blobs over a threshold, so a changed region is a new chunk, not a new file; keeps every chunk a `-imm-` object. The trade is against the whole-object simplicity the Scion response praised; probably a later step, and only for the large-file case.

---

*[Site index for agents](../llms.txt) · [HTML version](https://cli.sgit.ai/research/keys-pki-copy-on-write-coverage-map.html)*


# Native PKI vault mode — architecture map, cli.sgit.ai

> An architecture map for a second vault mode built on key pairs from the start, revised twice after review: sequence-number pinning, frozen hosts, concurrent writers.

*Source: <https://cli.sgit.ai/research/native-pki-vault-mode.html> · generated from the same content as the page, so the two cannot drift. Published from <https://github.com/SGit-AI/SGit-AI__CLI/blob/477d328536b04147e78281fb1f13550df1abf140/team/humans/dinis_cruz/claude-code-web/10/09/design__native-pki-vault-mode.md>.*

---
# Native PKI vault mode — architecture map

**Date:** 2026-10-09 · **Status:** design for review, no code · **Follows:**
[`design-analysis__read-write-keys-as-pki.md`](../research/read-write-keys-as-pki.md) (same folder), which covered adding a writer
signature to today's symmetric vaults. This document maps a second **vault mode** built on
key pairs from the start. Companion: [`design__sealed-files-layer.md`](../research/sealed-files-layer.md) (encryption on top of
either mode).

> **Revised 2026-10-10 after the sgit.ai agent's review (dev at 0a0707d).** **Sequence-number
> pinning is a requirement, not an option.** Every signed ref and the signed index carry a
> monotonic `seq`. Each clone pins the highest `seq` it has accepted per ref and for the
> index, and refuses (fails closed) anything lower, or equal with different content. Without
> it, a host replaying an old signed ref or index (TM-R29) survives the signatures. A fresh
> clone still has nothing to compare against: it is told the `seq` it got, and a witness or
> transparency log stays optional (RFC question 5).

> **Revised again 2026-10-10 after the release-gate review (dev at eed8084).** `seq` pinning
> closes replay for clones that have seen a state. Four things it leaves open are now
> specified in §3.1:
> - **a host that freezes** (stops serving new states): writers sign a periodic checkpoint,
>   and the vault sets how stale one may be;
> - **two writers producing the same next `seq`**: each signed state names its predecessor's
>   hash, the server's compare-and-swap picks one, and two valid states with one `seq` are
>   equivocation, refused and reported;
> - **the pin store**: written by the secret writer, never lowered, fail-closed when it is
>   missing once recorded, merged by maximum on restore;
> - **fresh clones**: still trust on first use, as before, but a share link can carry a floor.

## 1. Your question, checked

> A vault where one key lets you read and a different key lets you write, and neither
> key can be computed from the other. Can one public/private pair do that, used either
> way round?

**One key pair cannot. Two key pairs can, and they give exactly what you describe.**

A key pair supports two operations, and in each the direction is fixed:

| Operation | Done with | Undone / checked with | What it gives |
|---|---|---|---|
| encrypt → decrypt | **public** key | **private** key | confidentiality *to the private-key holder* |
| sign → verify | **private** key | **public** key | proof that the private-key holder wrote it |

Two facts settle it:
- **The private half always yields the public half** (for Ed25519 / X25519 trivially, and
  for RSA the public key sits inside the private key). Only the reverse is infeasible.
  So whichever key goes to the *less trusted* party must be the public one.
- **"Decrypt with the public key" is not confidentiality.** With RSA you can run the math
  the other way, but that is signing: anyone with the public key can undo it. Keeping a
  "public" key secret to use it as a read key is not sound either. RSA public exponents
  are conventionally 65537, and EC public keys are derived from the private key.

With one pair, writers sign (private) and readers verify (public). That gives *who wrote
it*, but nothing for keeping content secret. Add a second pair for reading and every
property you asked for falls out:

```
 R  = read pair   (X25519, for encryption)    R.priv  decrypts      R.pub  encrypts
 W  = write pair  (Ed25519, for signatures)   W.priv  signs heads   W.pub  verifies
```

| Party | Holds | Can | Cannot |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Reader** | `R.priv`, `W.pub` | read everything; check that every head was signed by a writer | write: needs `W.priv`, not derivable from anything it holds |
| **Writer** (normal) | `R.priv`, `W.priv` | read and write | — |
| **Depositor** (write-only) | `R.pub`, `W.priv`* | add new content readers can open | read anything: needs `R.priv`, not derivable from `R.pub` |
| **Host** | ciphertext, `W.pub` | store, serve, refuse unsigned writes | read; forge a head (no `W.priv`); can still withhold or replay old signed states |

\* or a depositor-specific signing key the writers accept for an inbox branch (§5).

So: **two keys, neither derivable from the other, one for reading and one for writing.**
The read capability is `R.priv` (+ the public `W.pub`); the write capability is `W.priv`
(+ `R.priv` for writers who also read). A write-only depositor is the one case today's
design cannot express at all.

**Two vault modes side by side is fine.** The object store, content addressing, trees,
sync, merge, scoped clones, the path guard and the CLI stay shared. The mode decides only
three things: how keys come into being, how the data key reaches a reader, and what
authorises a write.

## 2. The architecture

```
                         owner master seed  M  (32 bytes; or PBKDF2(passphrase) for humans)
                                │ HKDF
            ┌───────────────────┴────────────────────┐
     W.priv (Ed25519)                          R.priv (X25519)
     W.pub ──────────► vault id = base32(SHA-256(W.pub))[:26]   (self-certifying, 128 bits)
                                                   R.pub
 write capability  = M                (derives everything)
 read capability   = R.priv + W.pub   (cannot derive W.priv or M)
 deposit capability= R.pub  + a signing key the vault accepts for its inbox

 vault data key  DK (random 32 bytes, generation g)
   bare/keys/dk-<g>  = HPKE-Seal(R.pub, DK)          ← readers unwrap with R.priv
   every object      = AES-256-GCM(DK, …)            ← exactly today's object format
   every ref / index = AES-256-GCM(DK, …) + Ed25519 signature by W.priv
                        over (vault_id, file_id, seq, ts, ciphertext hash)
```

**Why a data key, rather than encrypting every object to `R.pub`.** Public-key encryption
is randomised: the same tree encrypted twice gives different bytes. Today's design
depends on deterministic tree encryption in two places:
- tree ids repeat (dedup);
- a scoped clone rebuilds a spine whose ids match the whole-vault builder byte for byte.

With a symmetric data key wrapped once to `R.pub`, the object layer is **unchanged**:
`DK` simply plays the role today's read key plays. The PKI sits in two places only:
- **distribution:** `R.pub` wraps `DK`, so `DK` never travels as a passphrase;
- **authority:** `W.priv` signs heads, so no write is authorised by a bearer secret.

## 3. What each piece fixes (threat model rows)

| Row | Today | Native PKI mode |
|---|---|---|
| TM-R01 read-key holder + host forge history | by design | **closed**: heads must carry `W.priv`'s signature |
| TM-R03 refs not bound to their id | accepted | **closed**: the signature covers vault id + file id |
| TM-R29 host replays an old index (drops features) | accepted | **closed** for content (signed); freshness still needs `seq` pinning |
| TM-R13 bearer write key | by design | **gone**: the server checks a signature, so nothing replayable crosses the wire |
| TM-R14 keys in argv | H likelihood | reduced: capabilities can be handed over as wrapped envelopes (sealed-files doc §6), never typed |
| TM-R12 no read revocation | by design | **better**: rotate `R` and `DK`, re-wrap to remaining readers; old data stays readable to the removed reader (inherent) |
| Write-only contributors | impossible | **new**: depositor capability (§5) |
| Freshness for a fresh clone (SP-2) | open | partly: signed `seq` + `ts` lets a client flag a stale head; a host can still withhold |

### 3.1 Freshness, concurrent writers and the pin store (revised 10-10)

**A host that freezes.** Pinning stops a host going *back*; it cannot see a host that simply
stops showing new states (every clone keeps its last, valid view, and teammates diverge
silently). Two pieces:
1. **Signed checkpoints (heartbeat).** Every write already signs `{seq, ts}`. In addition,
   any writer's client publishes `checkpoint = sign_W(vault_id, index_seq, H(ref seqs), ts)`
   when the newest one is older than `checkpoint_interval` (default 6 h, set by the owner in
   the index gate). A quiet vault therefore still shows a fresh `ts`. `status` and `pull` warn
   when the newest checkpoint is older than `max_staleness` (default 24 h): "this server has
   shown nothing newer than <ts>; it may be withholding". The check warns and does not refuse,
   because a vault with no active writer looks the same.
2. **Witnesses (optional).** A vault can name witness URLs in the signed index: other hosts
   (a mirror, the sgit.ai site, a teammate's static copy) that store the latest checkpoint
   they saw. A clone compares the host's checkpoint with the witnesses' and refuses to *push*
   on top of a state older than one a witness holds. Withholding then requires the host and
   every witness to collude.

**Two writers, the same next `seq`.** Every signed ref and index state carries
`prev = SHA-256(previous signed state)`, a hash chain per file.
- Online, the server's compare-and-swap (`write-if-match` on the previous bytes) lets one
  writer win. The loser re-reads, merges (the index) or rebases (a ref), and writes
  `seq + 1` with `prev` set to the winner's state. This is today's index CAS loop, with the
  chain added.
- A client accepts state `n+1` only if its `prev` equals the hash of the state it pinned at
  `n`. Two valid, signed states with the same `seq` and different content are
  **equivocation**: a host that served different states to different clones, or a writer
  bypassing CAS (static hosting has none). The client refuses both, keeps its pin and reports
  the two hashes. Recovery is a deliberate owner action (`sgit vault resolve-fork`), never
  automatic.
- A clone that has been offline accepts a run `n+1 … n+k` as long as each link verifies.

**The pin store.** `.sg_vault/local/pins.json` maps `{file_id: (seq, state hash)}` for each
ref and for the index.
- **Writes:** written by the single secret writer (temp file, fsync, rename, 0600), like
  `remote_heads.json`.
- **Integrity:** the file carries an HMAC under a key derived from the read capability, which
  detects corruption and half writes. It is not a defence against an attacker who can write
  `.sg_vault/local/`: that attacker can also replace the keys.
- **Never lowered:** an update takes the per-entry maximum, so no code path can lower a pin.
  Restoring a backup merges by maximum with the pins already present, never replaces them.
  A sync tool or `cp -r` reverting the folder is covered by the next rule.
- **Fail closed:** a missing or unreadable pin file, once one has been recorded (a marker in
  `config.json`, as `remote_heads_file` is today), refuses pull and push until
  `sgit pull --accept-rewind` rebuilds it, deliberately (TM-F23's rule).
- **Backups:** `uninit` backups carry the pins.

**Fresh clones** remain trust on first use. Two optional ways to give them a floor:
- the share link or capability envelope can carry `(index_seq, index hash)` at share time;
- a witness, as above.

## 4. Mapping to the code

| Area | Stays | Changes |
|---|---|---|
| `Vault__Crypto` | AES-GCM, deterministic metadata encryption, content ids | + `Vault__Crypto__PKI`: HKDF derivation from `M`; Ed25519 sign/verify; HPKE seal/open (X25519, HKDF-SHA256, AES-256-GCM: RFC 9180 base mode) |
| Key strings | `sgit_private_vault_…`, `sgit_public_read_…` | + `sgit_pki_write_…` (M), `sgit_pki_read_…` (R.priv ‖ W.pub), `sgit_pki_deposit_…`; `Enum__Key_Kind` gains them; the prefix *is* the mode, so a fresh clone knows signatures are mandatory (no strippable flag) |
| `Vault__Components` | object store, refs, index, branches | `read_key` ← `DK` (unwrapped); + `verify_key` (`W.pub`); + `signing_key` (`W.priv`, writers only) |
| Refs (`Vault__Ref_Manager`) | encrypted `{commit_id}` | `{commit_id, seq, ts}` + signature; verified on every read path (status, pull, clone, fetch) |
| Index (`Vault__Index_Sync`) | merge rules, tags, gate | signed on every write (all writers hold `W.priv`); verified on read; `seq` monotonic per clone |
| `Vault__API` | endpoints, batch, CAS | writes carry a request signature (method, path, body hash, time) instead of `x-sgraph-vault-write-key`: **server change** |
| Commits | per-clone ECDSA signatures | unchanged (attribution: *which* writer); the vault signature answers *a writer at all* |
| Format gate | format 1/2 | `format: 3` + mode `pki`; `min_client` set at creation |
| Migration | `vault move` rewrites everything already | `sgit vault move --to-pki` makes a PKI vault from a symmetric one |

## 5. Write-only (deposit) capability

A depositor can encrypt (it holds `R.pub`) but cannot read, so it cannot read the current
tree to modify it. Write-only therefore means **append**, not edit:
- each deposit is a commit on a per-depositor **inbox branch** (`inbox/<name>`), whose tree
  holds only what that depositor added;
- its objects use a per-deposit data key `DK_d`, sealed to `R.pub` and stored beside the
  commit;
- a writer merges inbox branches into the main branch, and from then on that content is
  ordinary data.

This fits agents handing work to a human, form-style submissions, and log or report drops.
The vault accepts the depositor's signing key for its inbox branch only: the writers add
it to the signed index.

## 6. Rotation and the owner key

The self-certifying vault id (`H(W.pub)`) means a new `W` is a new vault. That is fine
for "a writer left" today (it is what `vault move` does), but heavy for teams. The clean
fix, and the same design as the threat model's "owner-signed membership":
- **vault id = H(owner root key `O.pub`)**, with `O` kept offline or in a decryption service;
- the index carries an `O`-signed **writer set** (one `W.pub` per member, or one shared);
- removing a writer = `O` re-signs the set without them. Removing a reader = new `R` and
  `DK`, re-sealed to the remaining members. The sealed-files doc's per-member envelopes
  do exactly this.

Start with one shared `W` (simple, matches today's team model) and keep the writer-set
format ready for per-member keys.

## 7. Interop and algorithms

- **Ed25519, X25519, HKDF-SHA256, AES-256-GCM** are all in `cryptography` (installed:
  49.0.0) and in current browsers' Web Crypto.
- **Test vectors.** Byte-for-byte vectors (CLAUDE.md) work for derivation and Ed25519
  (deterministic). HPKE uses a fresh ephemeral key, so its vectors fix the ephemeral key,
  the same way RFC 9180's do.
- **Post-quantum:** AES-256 content is fine. The key exchange is the exposure
  (harvest-now-decrypt-later on `bare/keys/dk-*`); HPKE has hybrid X25519 + ML-KEM suites
  to adopt when the browser side has them (TM-R20).

## 8. Effort

| Phase | What | CLI estimate |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `Vault__Crypto__PKI`, key strings, derivation, vectors shared with the web team | ~1 week |
| 2 | Signed refs and index + verification on every read path (also usable on symmetric vaults; = phase 1 of the earlier analysis) | 1–1.5 weeks |
| 3 | `DK` sealed to `R.pub`; read path via `DK`; `init --pki`, `clone` of a PKI vault | ~0.5 week |
| 4 | Server: store `W.pub`, accept signed writes (SG/Send team) | server side |
| 5 | Deposit capability + inbox branches | ~1 week |
| 6 | Owner root key + signed writer set + rotation | 2–3 weeks |

Phases 1–3 give a working native mode in which a reader cannot write and the host cannot
forge. The web UI needs the same verification and unwrap code to open PKI vaults.

## 9. Decisions for you

1. **Vault id:** self-certifying `H(W.pub)` now, or go straight to `H(O.pub)` with a writer set?
   My view: start with `W.pub`, and design the index field so `O` can be added later.
2. **Capability strings:** random 32-byte seeds only (agents and machines), or also a
   passphrase form for humans (PBKDF2 → `M`, as today)?
3. **Deposit / inbox:** in the first release or later?
4. **Server signed writes (phase 4):** ask the SG/Send team now? Until then the server
   keeps the bearer check, but clients reject anything unsigned, so forgery is closed
   either way.

---

*[Site index for agents](../llms.txt) · [HTML version](https://cli.sgit.ai/research/native-pki-vault-mode.html)*


# AC-L-001 / TM-R36 — characters outside `[a-zA-Z0-9/\_.- ]` in paths: what really happens, cli.sgit.ai

> Characters outside a narrow set in a path are silently rewritten, so one vault gets two roots and a false push conflict. What really happens, reproduced, and a fix that raises an alarm instead of rewriting.

*Source: <https://cli.sgit.ai/research/non-ascii-paths-refuse-dont-rewrite.html> · generated from the same content as the page, so the two cannot drift. Published from <https://github.com/SGit-AI/SGit-AI__CLI/blob/477d328536b04147e78281fb1f13550df1abf140/team/humans/dinis_cruz/claude-code-web/10/13/AC-L-001__non-ascii-paths__refuse-dont-rewrite.md>.*

---
# AC-L-001 / TM-R36 — characters outside `[a-zA-Z0-9/\_.- ]` in paths: what really happens

**Status:** documented, **not fixed in this push** (your call, 13 Oct). Reproduced on `dev` at
81a4176 with the Python API over the in-memory host. The fix proposal below follows your
instinct: **raise an alarm, never rewrite silently**. It is narrower than "refuse every such
character", for the reason in §3.

It is worse than the round-1 record (`review/findings/audit-context-local.json` AC-L-001) says.
Two different things share the bug: **where the vault lives** (the host path of the clone) and
**names inside the vault** (file and folder names in the trees).

## 1. The vault root: broken, and silently in the wrong place

`Safe_Str__Vault_Path` and `Safe_Str__File_Path` both use `[^a-zA-Z0-9/\\_.\- ]` in *replace*
mode: every other character becomes `_`. The working directory of the clone, pull, fetch,
push and move workflows (`directory : Safe_Str__File_Path`), `Vault__Context.vault_path` and
`Vault__Storage` go through them; other code uses the raw `str`. So one vault gets two roots.

| Step, under `/tmp/x/josé/vault` | What happened |
|---|---|
| `init` | the working copy and `.sg_vault/{bare,local}` are under `josé/vault`, **and** a second tree `jos_/vault/` is created next to it |
| `commit`, `status` | ok, `clean` |
| first `push` | **`Vault__Push_Conflict_Error`: "the branch moved on the server while this push was in flight"** — false; nothing was pushed |
| `clone` into `josé/clone` | reports success; **the whole clone is written to `jos_/clone`**; `josé/clone` does not exist |
| `pull` in `josé/clone` | `FileNotFoundError: …/josé/clone/.sg_vault/local/vault_key` |
| second `commit` + `push` in `josé/vault` | `FileNotFoundError: …/jos_/vault/.sg_vault/work/pull-…/.tmp-…` |

It is not only accents. What the type does to real folder names:

| Path | Becomes |
|---|---|
| `/Users/x/Dropbox (Personal)/v` | `/Users/x/Dropbox _Personal_/v` |
| `/Users/x/OneDrive - Acme, Inc/v` | `/Users/x/OneDrive - Acme_ Inc/v` |
| `/home/first.last@corp/v` | `/home/first.last_corp/v` |
| `/home/u/my+vault` | `/home/u/my_vault` |
| `C:\Users\Zoë\v` | `C_\Users\Zo_\v` |

**The last row needs a check on Windows.** The colon of every drive letter is rewritten, so if
any of these fields carries an absolute Windows path, every Windows user is affected, not just
users with accented names. I could not run Windows here.

Security reading: a write lands in a directory the user never named. Two roots that sanitise
alike share one store (`josé/` and `josè/` and a real `jos_/`), so one vault's objects, refs and
`work/` files can mix with another's. A local process (A6) that can create `jos_/` next to
`josé/` decides where the store goes. Likelihood M (any European or company folder name, any
Dropbox or OneDrive folder); impact H (a false "conflict", a clone in the wrong place, failures
on the next command). I have raised TM-R36 from M / M to M / H.

## 2. Names inside the vault: the core is right; the display and `--path` are not

Tree entry names are encrypted strings, not `Safe_Str` fields, so the sync path never touches
them. With `café.md`, `naïve dir/résumé.md`, `a+b@c.md`, `日本語.txt` and a `caf_.md` beside
`café.md`:

| Step | Result |
|---|---|
| status, commit, push, clone | every file round-trips byte for byte, with the exact name; `café.md` and `caf_.md` stay two files |
| edit in the clone, push, pull in the first clone | ok; content and name exact |
| `stash` / `stash pop` | ok |
| **`sgit diff`** (`Schema__Diff_File.path`) | **lists `caf_.md` and `na_ve/r_sum_.md`**: the display lies |
| **`sgit clone --path naïve`** (`scope_paths : list[Safe_Str__File_Path]`) | **records the scope `na_ve`, checks out nothing, and says nothing** |
| history file lists, publish entries, stash metadata | typed with the same class, so they rewrite the same way (not each one run) |

So "what happens if the vault creates that": another client, or the web UI, can put such a
name in a vault. This CLI clones, edits and syncs it correctly. Its listings show the wrong
name, and a scoped clone of that folder is silently empty.

Hostile names in a vault are a separate question with an existing answer: `Vault__Path_Guard`
refuses absolute paths, `..` on either separator, `.git` / `.sg_vault`, and writes through a
symlink at checkout (TM-F series). Nothing in this finding weakens that.

## 3. The decision proposed for the next push

**The rule:** a type that names a place must **refuse** what it cannot represent, never rewrite
it. A rewritten path is a silent data change: the user asked for one place and got another.
Worth a line in CLAUDE.md's Type_Safe rules.

1. **Vault roots: the alarm now, the real fix right behind it.**
   - *Stop-gap (S):* at the CLI boundary, before any command uses a vault root (`init`, `clone*`,
     and resolving the root of every other command), refuse a root the type would change:
     > `sgit cannot work in a folder whose path contains 'é' (…/josé/vault) yet. Move the vault, or clone it, to a path made of letters a-z, digits, space, '.', '_' and '-'. (TM-R36)`
   - *Fix (M):* type the host-side fields (`directory`, `vault_path`, the storage root) with
     `Safe_Str__Host_Path`. It already exists, added for `sgit serve`: any printable text,
     control characters refused, never rewritten. Then the alarm is no longer needed.
2. **Names inside a vault: do not refuse them.** They work today, other clients create them,
   and refusing would lock people out of their own vaults. That is the lock-out lesson of R1 and
   TM-F35. Instead:
   - a content-path type (Unicode allowed; NUL, control characters, absolute paths and `..`
     refused) for the display and scope schemas: `Schema__Diff_File`, history lists,
     `scope_paths`, publish entries, stash metadata;
   - `clone --path` refuses a folder that is not in the tree, rather than cloning nothing.
3. **Where an alarm is right for content: names that will not survive another OS.** Add a check
   (rule 9 puts it under `check`), and a warning at `commit` time for new names only (an alarm,
   not a refusal). It covers:
   - case-only collisions (`A.md` and `a.md` are one file on macOS and Windows);
   - Unicode normalisation twins (NFC and NFD `café`; macOS can hand back the other form, so
     status shows a delete and an add);
   - Windows-reserved names (`CON`, `AUX`, `NUL`, `COM1`…, a trailing dot or space, `<>:"|?*`);
   - control characters and newlines;
   - paths too long for Windows.
4. **Tests that land with the fix:**
   - init, commit, push, clone and pull under a root with `é`, `+`, `@`, `(` and a space;
   - clone into `josé/`;
   - `clone --path naïve`;
   - `diff` listing the exact names;
   - a `Fixed` security test that two roots that used to sanitise alike no longer share a store;
   - the check's cases.

Sizes: the stop-gap is under a day. The type change is a day or two, because the type is used by
every path field; the check is about a day.

## Where this is recorded

- Threat model TM-R36: likelihood/impact raised, this evidence linked.
- CHANGELOG `[Unreleased]` → "Known issue".
- Probe scripts were run from the session scratchpad. Their steps are in the tables above.

---

*[Site index for agents](../llms.txt) · [HTML version](https://cli.sgit.ai/research/non-ascii-paths-refuse-dont-rewrite.html)*


# Spec: pack mode for sgit (CLI-only, packs-only vaults, no server change), cli.sgit.ai

> The specification for pack mode: every push writes one zip pack, a snapshot pack compacts them, nothing is deleted, large packs go straight to S3 by presigned URL, and a gated packs-only vault needs no server change. Commands, layout, failure handling, tests and the four performance runs.

*Source: <https://cli.sgit.ai/research/pack-mode-spec.html> · generated from the same content as the page, so the two cannot drift. Published from <https://github.com/SGit-AI/SGit-AI__CLI/blob/477d328536b04147e78281fb1f13550df1abf140/team/humans/dinis_cruz/claude-code-web/10/21/spec__pack-mode.md>.*

---
# Spec: pack mode for sgit (CLI-only, packs-only vaults, no server change)

**Status:** proposal, 21 Oct 2026, agreed in conversation with Dinis; revised the same day after the review on cli.sgit.ai (*Pack mode, read closely*): decisions 1 to 5 taken as below; not built. **Scope:** a push,
pull and clone mode plus an import and a compaction command. Everything else in the CLI is
unchanged. **Server:** none of this needs a server change; the routes used are `batch`
(write/read), `presigned/initiate|complete|read-url`, `list`, `delete`, all present in
`sgraph-ai-app-send` 0.34.0 and exercised live on 20 Oct.

## 1. Goals and non-goals

Goals: a push costs one pack upload and the ref move; a pull costs one listing and the packs it
lacks; a clone costs the newest snapshot and the packs since it; large packs move straight to S3
by presigned URL; small ones through the API; nothing on the host is ever deleted by the mode;
every object is verified by id before it is written locally, as today.

Non-goals (this round): web app or static-reader support; reading packs in place without
extraction (version 2); mixed vaults (loose objects and packs written together); pruning.

## 2. Layout on the host

```
bare/packs/commits/   <epoch_s:010d>__<commit_id>__<bytes>.zip
bare/packs/snapshots/ <epoch_s:010d>__<commit_id>__<bytes>.zip
bare/packs/archive/   <epoch_s:010d>__<commit_id>__<bytes>.zip      (moved from commits/)
bare/refs/, bare/indexes/, bare/cache/, bare/keys/                   unchanged
bare/data/                                                            not written in pack mode
```

- `epoch_s` is the writer's clock at pack creation, in whole seconds (review decision 5: a listing
  shows the host each push's size and time; seconds order the listing as well as milliseconds and
  say less). It orders listings; nothing depends on its accuracy, and names stay unique by commit
  id. The security page gets one line when the mode ships: a host that can list sees, per push,
  the commit id, the size it added and the writer's clock to the second.
- `bytes` is the pack's size; the client chooses the route from it and checks it after fetch.
- A pack's member paths are `bare/data/<object-id>`, exactly as `publish --bundles` writes them, so
  extraction is a copy into the loose store.
- Zip rules as in `Vault__Publish__Bundles`: `ZIP_STORED`, members sorted by name, fixed
  timestamps, Zip64 allowed, deterministic bytes for the same object set.

## 2a. Blob compression before encryption (option for the pack trial)

Today blobs are encrypted uncompressed, and ciphertext does not compress (`publish --bundles`
measured DEFLATE making it larger). Compressing the plaintext *before* encryption is where the gain
is. Measured 21 Oct on the comms vault's working copy, per file (the way blobs are stored):

| | Size | Ratio | CPU (120 MB) |
|---|---|---|---|
| raw | 120.3 MB | | |
| deflate level 1 | 77.9 MB | 1.54× | 2.0 s |
| deflate level 6 | 76.0 MB | 1.58× | 2.9 s |
| deflate level 9 | 75.8 MB | 1.59× | 3.5 s |
| lzma level 6 | 70.3 MB | 1.71× | 34.6 s |

Images (53 MB of jpg and png) are the incompressible part; JSON goes 2.8×, markdown 2.5×, email 2×,
JSONL logs 8.8×. The store's history is the same kinds of file, so a 527 MB store would be roughly
330 MB. Rules if it is adopted:

- **Blobs only.** Trees and commits stay as they are: their encryption is deterministic so that
  rebuilt trees match byte for byte across clients, and a browser's deflate does not produce the
  same bytes as zlib. Blobs use a random IV, so determinism is not needed there.
- **Deflate, stdlib, level 6.** No new dependency; browsers decode it with `DecompressionStream`.
  lzma buys 8 % for 12× the CPU.
- **Keep the smaller.** Compress, compare, store whichever is shorter with a one-byte encoding
  flag in the blob envelope (a new envelope version, gated by `min_client` like 128-bit ids), so
  images and zips cost one fast pass and nothing more.
- **Interop vectors** for the browser: deflate + AES-GCM round trips byte for byte, as for every
  other primitive.
- **Threat model row.** Compress-then-encrypt lets the host see how compressible a file is, and
  an attacker who can place chosen bytes in the same file as a secret and watch the ciphertext's
  size can learn about the secret (the CRIME family). Sizes are already visible to the host;
  secrets are already refused at commit; a per-path opt-out (never compress under `inbox/`, say)
  and optional padding close the rest. Record it as an accepted gap with those mitigations.
- **Where to introduce it:** the pack trial vault is new and gated, so it is the cheap place to
  turn the new blob envelope on; the packs themselves stay `ZIP_STORED`.

## 3. The vault flag

The branch index gains `features: ['packs']` and `min_client: <first version with pack mode>` at
import. `Vault__Format` already enforces both: a client without the feature refuses the vault by
name; the web app and static readers refuse it the same way. A pack vault never writes
`bare/data/`.

## 4. Commands and behaviour

### 4.1 `sgit pack import <source-dir> --vault-key <new-key> [--base-url …]`

From a **full** clone of an existing vault (refuses on a partial clone, as `publish` does):

1. Re-encrypt the reachable history into the new key, reusing `Step__Move__Build_Temp_Vault`'s
   walk (blobs, then trees children-first, then commits parents-first, with the id map; signatures
   re-made with this clone's branch key, as `move` does).
2. Build one snapshot pack of every object reachable from the new head.
3. Create the vault on the server (as `init`), write the branch index with the flag and
   `min_client`, upload the snapshot (route by size, §6), write the ref.
4. Leave the source untouched. Repeatable: a second import makes a second vault.

### 4.2 `sgit push` in a pack vault

1. Collect the objects of every commit being pushed that the remote lacks, exactly as
   `Vault__Batch.collect_chain_blob_entries` plus the trees and commits do today.
2. Build one pack per pushed commit (several commits pushed at once = several packs, so a pack's
   name is always one commit id). Objects shared between them are put in the first.
3. Upload each pack by size (§6).
4. Move the ref with the existing compare-and-swap; the branch index as today.
5. Record each pack name in `.sg_vault/local/packs_absorbed.json`.

### 4.3 `sgit pull` and `sgit status` in a pack vault

1. `list bare/packs/commits/`; diff against `packs_absorbed.json`.
2. Fetch the missing packs: those under the threshold in batch reads of up to 50, those over it
   by presigned URL, 16 in flight as today.
3. For each pack: verify size, open, verify every member's id against its bytes
   (`extract_verified`), write into the loose store. A member whose id does not match is refused
   and reported per object, as fetch failures are today; the pack is not recorded as absorbed.
4. Record the pack names. Then the ref and the merge as today.
5. Status needs the ref and the index only, as today; it does not list packs.

### 4.4 `sgit clone` of a pack vault

1. Read the index; see the flag; refuse if the client is too old.
2. `list bare/packs/snapshots/`; take the last name (epoch order). Fetch it (§6; for a large
   snapshot, parallel `Range` reads of 10 MB each). Verify and extract.
3. `list bare/packs/commits/`; fetch and extract all of them.
4. Walk commits and trees locally to confirm the head is complete (the existing walk steps, which
   now find everything on disk); fetch any object still missing through the ordinary read route
   as a safety net, never as the normal path.
5. Record every pack name as absorbed; check out as today.

Scoped and shallow clones: version 1 takes the snapshot whole and keeps the scope for checkout
and later pushes. That is a step back in bytes for the agents' daily `--path <folder> --depth 1`
clone (3 MB and 13 s on the loose comms vault against the whole 430 MB snapshot; review decision
3), so: agents' working vaults stay loose until version 2, the trial measures it (run 5 in §10),
and version 2 reads the snapshot's central directory by `Range` (2.7 MB for 34k members, measured)
and then only the needed members, one `Range` each, 16 in flight. The seekable-HTTP reader that
does this is about twenty lines and was exercised on 20 Oct.

### 4.5 `sgit pack compact [--when]`

Trigger (checked on push, run on demand or by a scheduled job): `commits/` holds more than
`PACK_COMPACT_COUNT` packs (default 50, to be tuned) or their total size exceeds
`PACK_COMPACT_RATIO` (default 0.10) of the newest snapshot.

1. Build the snapshot of every object reachable from the current remote head.
2. Upload to `snapshots/`.
3. Read it back: `read-url` + `Range` of the tail to read the central directory; check the member
   set equals the expected id set. Abort on any difference, leaving everything as it was.
4. For each commit pack absorbed (every pack whose commit is reachable from the snapshot's commit):
   upload the same bytes to `archive/` with the same name, then `delete` it from `commits/`.
5. Also move to `archive/` every pack in `commits/` whose commit is unreachable from the head and
   whose epoch is older than `PACK_ORPHAN_AGE` (default one day): the pack an agent session left
   behind when its ref move lost the race and the session ended (review decision 4). Nothing is
   deleted; clones stop fetching it.
6. Old snapshots stay. Nothing else is deleted.

The move needs no download: a pack's bytes are a deterministic function of its commit (the objects
that commit introduced, sorted, fixed timestamps, as `Vault__Publish__Bundles` already builds them),
so the compacting clone rebuilds each pack from its loose store, checks the size against the name,
and uploads that to `archive/` (review note 1). A rebuilt pack whose size differs from the name is
downloaded instead and reported.

Idempotent and crash-safe: a pack present in both `commits/` and `archive/` is removed from
`commits/` on the next run after the archive copy is verified by size.

### 4.6 `sgit pack ls` / `sgit pack verify`

`ls`: the three folders with sizes and dates. `verify`: fetch the newest snapshot's directory by
`Range` and confirm the union of snapshot + `commits/` covers every object reachable from the
head (ids only, no members downloaded).

## 5. Local layout

```
.sg_vault/bare/data/              extracted objects (version 1 reads from here, unchanged code)
.sg_vault/packs/                  fetched packs kept as files (optional cache; version 2 reads by offset)
.sg_vault/local/packs_absorbed.json   names of packs whose objects are in the loose store
```

## 6. Route selection

| Pack size | Upload | Download |
|---|---|---|
| ≤ `LARGE_BLOB_THRESHOLD` (4 MB) | batch write | batch read (up to 50 packs per request) |
| > 4 MB | `presigned/initiate` + part PUTs + `complete` | `presigned/read-url` + GET, or parallel `Range` GETs |
| host without presigned (disk, memory, `serve`) | batch write (no Lambda limit there) | batch read |
| static host / folder | n/a (read-only) | plain GET |

The fallback `presigned_unavailable` is reused unchanged.

## 7. Listing when the host cannot list

A static host has no listing: `publish` writes the three folders' names into the manifest. The
local disk server answered a listing with zero objects on 16 Oct (in the SG/Send brief); until
fixed, a client on such a host falls back to the commit walk for `commits/` discovery (each pack
holds its commit, so the walk finds pack names by commit id), which is slow and correct.

## 8. Failure handling

- A pack that fails size or id verification is not absorbed and is reported; the pull continues
  with the others and the ref is not moved past what is complete, as today.
- A push whose pack upload succeeds but whose ref CAS fails leaves an orphan pack in `commits/`;
  the next push from that clone reuses it (same commit id, same bytes) and `compact` ignores
  packs whose commit is unreachable from the head (they stay, harmless, until a prune exists).
- Two writers: the ref CAS serialises them; packs never collide (names are commit ids).

## 9. Tests

Unit (in-memory API): push writes one pack per commit and nothing under `bare/data/`; pull lists
once and fetches only missing packs; a corrupt member is refused per object; clone from
snapshot + commits equals a loose clone object for object; compact verifies before moving and
moves before deleting; a crash between archive upload and delete is tidied; the flag refuses an
old client and the web-style loose reader. Integration (real server, 3.12 venv): the presigned
path for a pack over 4 MB; `Range` reads of a snapshot's directory. Live: the comms vault import
and the four performance runs in the article.

## 10. Performance runs

1. Cold clone of the imported comms vault: pack mode vs API batches; from the sandbox and from a
   laptop.
2. 100 one-file pushes: seconds and requests per push, both modes.
3. Pull after 10, 100, 1,000 pushes without compaction, then after; set the defaults in §4.5.
4. Two writers pushing concurrently for a minute: no lost packs, ref always consistent.
5. A scoped shallow clone (`--path security --depth 1`) of the pack vault against today's 13 s and
   3 MB on the loose vault, to size the version-2 work.

## 11. Later (not this round)

Reading packs by offset without extraction; scoped reads of a snapshot by `Range`; web app and
static reader support; in-place migration of an existing vault (`vault format --feature packs`
plus one snapshot, loose objects left as the archive); prune; the SG/Send `append` route for
growing a snapshot in place instead of rewriting it (the 20 Oct brief, parked; review decisions 1
and 2).

# Partial clones — a folder scope and a history depth (6 Oct 2026), cli.sgit.ai

> Cloning just the folders an agent reads and writes, read and write, plus a shallow mode, without changing the full clone: the Merkle-spine idea and the measurements.

*Source: <https://cli.sgit.ai/research/partial-clones-scope-and-depth.html> · generated from the same content as the page, so the two cannot drift. Published from <https://github.com/SGit-AI/SGit-AI__CLI/blob/477d328536b04147e78281fb1f13550df1abf140/team/humans/dinis_cruz/claude-code-web/10/06/partial-clones__scope-and-depth.md>.*

---
# Partial clones — a folder scope and a history depth (6 Oct 2026)

**Branch:** `claude/charming-babbage-5hzcxq` · **Vault measured:** `y8pwtjlw` (626 commits, 8,013+ trees, 9,404 blobs, 18,720 objects at HEAD time)
**Ask:** agents that know which folders they read and write should be able to clone just those,
read *and* write; plus a shallow (no-history) mode; and none of it may change the full clone.

## 1. The idea, in one paragraph

The vault is a Merkle tree: a commit names a root tree, a tree names its children by id. To
hold `mail/crm.riskmandate/` a clone needs the root tree, the `mail/` tree (the *spine*) and
the folder's own subtree; everything else is an entry it keeps by id ("opaque"). To commit a
change inside the folder, rebuild the folder's subtree from disk, then each tree on the spine
with one entry replaced, and keep the siblings' ids — exactly what the whole-vault builder
would produce, byte for byte, because tree encryption is deterministic (a test proves the
rebuilt root id equals the full builder's). Push uploads the new commit, the spine trees, the
changed subtree and the new blobs; the server needs nothing new. Two scoped clones in
different folders cannot conflict: out-of-scope entries are always the remote's, by id.

## 2. What was built

| piece | where |
|---|---|
| scope model (paths + boundaries, pure path logic) | `storage/Vault__Scope.py` (re-exported from `core/scope/`) |
| opaque entries in the tree builder (`build`, `build_from_flat`, `opaque=`), canonical entry order | `storage/Vault__Sub_Tree.py` |
| scoped flatten → (flat, opaque); level-by-level fetch walk that only opens held + spine folders | `storage/Vault__Scoped_Tree.py` |
| local config: `scope_paths`, `shallow_boundaries` (empty on full clones) | `schemas/Schema__Local_Config.py` |
| clone: `--depth N`, `--path F` (repeatable); depth-limited commit walk records boundaries; scoped tree walk; scoped checkout; bulk sweep skipped for partial clones | clone steps, `Vault__Sync__Clone`, `CLI__Main`/`CLI__Vault` |
| commit / write_file: scoped flatten + opaque rebuild; writes outside scope refused with the path | `Vault__Sync__Commit` |
| status: scoped diff; chain fetch stops at boundaries | `Vault__Sync__Status` |
| pull: scoped fetch (held folders only), merge within scope with theirs' opaque entries, commit walk stops at boundaries (push's implicit pull used to deepen a shallow clone to the root) | `Step__Pull__Fetch_Missing`, `Step__Pull__Merge`, `Vault__Sync__Pull` |
| push: scoped flatten, trees/blobs the clone never fetched are skipped (unchanged, on the server), cache reconcile skipped | `Vault__Sync__Push`, `Vault__Batch` |
| widen (`sgit fetch <folder>`), unshallow (`sgit fetch --unshallow`), `require_whole` | `core/actions/scope/Vault__Sync__Scope.py` |
| guard on `check fsck`, `dump`, `publish`, `vault move` | `cli/CLI__Scope_Guard.py` |
| branch switch keeps scope fields | `Vault__Branch_Switch` |

## 3. Numbers on the real vault (this session, through its egress gateway)

| clone | objects | store | files | wall |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| full (bulk sweep, unchanged) | 18,720 | 173 MB | 3,442 | 81 s |
| `--path mail/crm.riskmandate --depth 1` | 429 | 3.2 MB | 365 | **14 s** |
| `--path docs --path conductor --depth 1` | 20 | — | 15 | **5 s** |
| widen the CRM clone with `docs` | +10 | — | +8 | 2 s |

On the scoped clone: `status` in sync; `history log` shows HEAD and stops; `check fsck`
refuses naming what the clone holds and how to widen.

## 4. "No side effects on the full clone" — how that was held

- Every scope branch is behind `scope.is_scoped()` / `is_partial()`; a whole-vault clone takes
  the exact calls it took before (`flatten`, `build`, `build_from_flat`, `_fetch_missing_objects`
  without the new kwarg, `checkout`). The existing pull-step tests use a fake sync client with
  no crypto and no new kwargs, and they pass unchanged — which is the proof the full path is
  not touched.
- `Vault__Sub_Tree.build*` with no opaque entries runs the old code; with them, the entry
  order is re-established to files-then-folders by name so ids match the whole-vault builder.
- Real vault, before and after: a full clone gives the same 18,720 objects, empty scope and
  boundary in its config, and `fsck` reports the same 41 missing objects.
- `pytest tests/unit/ -n auto`: 3,932 passed (21 new partial-clone tests on two real clones
  in the in-memory API: read, write, delete, refuse-outside-scope, write_file, fast-forward
  and three-way pulls with changes outside scope, two scoped agents never conflicting, dirty
  edit survives a pull, depth-1 round trips, unshallow, scoped+shallow, widen, guards, branch
  switch, and a full-clone-unchanged check; 8 storage tests on the scoped tree).

## 5. Caveats and follow-ups

- A folder renamed by another agent silently leaves a clone's scope (names are decrypted
  along the spine). Pull should notice a held path vanishing and say so. Not done.
- Scoped clones cannot see blobs missing elsewhere; the push fix from earlier today should ship
  with this (same branch).
- `history log` on a shallow clone ends with "history stops here: shallow clone … sgit fetch
  --unshallow" instead of an `[object not found locally]` line.
- A shared, immutable object cache across clones on one machine would make every agent's
  clone after the first a local copy — the browser-style cache idea; separate change.
- `clone-branch` (thin) still walks all commits serially; with `--depth 1` on `sgit clone`
  there is little reason left to use it.

## 6. Deep review before the PR to main (same day, evening)

Two passes over `origin/main...origin/dev` after the merge: a code review (bugs, side effects)
and a security review (new exploitable issues only, >80 % confidence). CI on dev was green
first (run 37544894784 on ddee8a4).

### Security review — no new vulnerability; three hardening gaps closed

No high-confidence exploitable issue was introduced. Three pre-existing "trust the host /
trust the committer" gaps that the new fetch paths exercise more were closed anyway:

| Gap | Fix | Test |
|---|---|---|
| A batch read wrote whatever `file_id` the host answered with, and the id names the on-disk path | `_batch_read_chunk` keeps only requested ids | `Test_API__Ignores_Unrequested_File_Ids` (real local HTTP server answering with `local/config.json` and an extra object) |
| `Vault__Verified_Write.save` accepted any contained path (`local/config.json`, a working-copy file) | store-leaf allow-list `STORE_FILE_ID` + protected-dir check, before the content-address check | `Test_Verified_Write__Store_Paths_Only` |
| Pull let an untracked file be overwritten when the tree entry's `content_hash` CLAIMED the same content | proven from the decrypted blob (`blob_hash_fn`), the claim is ignored | `test_commit_whose_entry_hash_lies_cannot_overwrite_an_untracked_file` (a commit built with a lying hash) |

### Code review — 15 findings, what changed

| # | Finding | Resolution |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `Vault__Head_Paths` flattened the whole tree on a scoped clone → tracked-wins rule broke, a tracked file under an ignored dir was dropped by the next commit | scoped flatten; test |
| 2 | read-only scoped clones: status/checkout used the whole tree | scoped in `_status_read_only` and the RO checkout step; test |
| 3 | sparse push could try to load a blob it never fetched | collector skips any blob not local |
| 4 | `sgit ls`/`fetch`/`cat` on a scoped clone walked a sibling's tree and failed | `_get_head_flat_map` scoped; test |
| 5 | other commands crash with "vault may be corrupted — run fsck" on a partial clone | friendly error naming the scope + how to widen (generic, for every command); test |
| 6 | branch-only push re-uploaded the whole clone-branch history each time | stops at the server's clone head; blobs the server has are not re-sent — and the ref CAS was matching the LOCAL ref bytes, so the ref write conflicted on every push after a commit (silent on the in-memory API, a 409 on the real one): now matches the server's bytes; test checks the server ref and that nothing re-sent is a blob |
| 7 | status walked the whole local history on every call | walk stops at known-complete heads; test (0 object reads when up to date; N when N behind); the truncated-fetch case is covered by the existing lower-bound test |
| 8 | widen overwrote files already on disk under the new folder | refuses naming the clash; held folders untouched; test |
| 9 | one failing bulk-sweep chunk aborted the clone | fail-soft per chunk; test |
| 10 | sweep counters unsynchronised across threads | lock + summed futures |
| 11 | duplicate parents counted against the fetch limit | deduped |
| 12 | `CLI__Scope_Guard` duplicated `require_whole` | delegates |
| 13 | pull-step call shape | kept (the fake-client tests prove the full path is unchanged) |
| 14 | guard re-read the config | config read once in the merge step, passed through |
| 15 | `Vault__Scope` held raw `list[str]` | `Safe_Str__File_Path` / `Safe_Str__Commit_Id` with validation (`..`, absolute, non-object ids refused; nested folders collapse) |

### What the new tests then found (would have shipped otherwise)

- **Typed boundary ids broke unshallow and the status boundary stop.** `Safe_Str` hashes
  differently from the equal `str` (`'x' in {Safe_Str('x')}` is False) and `os.path.join`
  sanitises it (`/` → `_`), so once the config fields became Safe types the boundary commit
  was "not in the local store" and `--unshallow` on a scoped shallow clone fetched nothing.
  `Vault__Scope.boundary_ids()` / `folders()` hand consumers plain strings; a test pins both
  behaviours. Worth remembering for every Safe_Str that reaches a path or a set.
- The first status rewrite assumed "a local commit has local ancestors", which a truncated
  fetch (limit hit) violates; the walk now stops only at known-complete heads.
- Branch-only push's ref CAS bug above (pre-existing, invisible to the in-memory API).

`pytest tests/unit/ -n auto`: 3,953 passed (21 new review tests under `tests/unit/review/`).

### Follow-up (7 Oct): the merge of main into dev and a CI flake that was a real leak

Merging `main` into `dev` for PR #7 conflicted only on the release bot's version bumps
(dev v0.17.3, main v0.17.0; dev kept). CI on that merge then failed on
`test_Dev__Tree__Graph__Happy::test_analyse_temp_dir_cleaned_up`, which diffed `/tmp` before
and after `analyse()` and so could see any vault another xdist worker was creating at that
moment. Rewriting it to watch the `mkdtemp` calls made inside the call exposed something real:
every `sgit clone` (all five entry points) creates `/tmp/sgit-clone-*` as the workflow
workspace's root, the runner removes the workspace inside it on success, and the root stays —
one empty dir per clone, 3,881 of them in this sandbox. `_run_clone_workflow` now removes the
root in its `finally`, success or failure; a review test clones three ways and checks none of
the roots survive.
