# Fix — `sgit pull` silently discarded uncommitted edits to tracked files, cli.sgit.ai

> sgit pull silently discarded uncommitted edits to tracked files. The root cause, and the fix: git's rules for the working tree, applied before any write.

*Source: <https://cli.sgit.ai/research/pull-discarded-uncommitted-edits.html> · generated from the same content as the page, so the two cannot drift. Published from <https://github.com/SGit-AI/SGit-AI__CLI/blob/477d328536b04147e78281fb1f13550df1abf140/team/humans/dinis_cruz/claude-code-web/10/03/pull-discards-uncommitted-edits__fix.md>.*

---
# Fix — `sgit pull` silently discarded uncommitted edits to tracked files

**Date:** 2026-10-03
**Branch:** `claude/charming-babbage-5hzcxq` (restarted from `dev` @ `2f86cf5` after PR #6 shipped as 0.17.0)
**Bug report:** RiskMandate.ai agent team (@briefs), 3 Oct 2026 — hit three times in real use on a
vault shared by ~10 agents. Reproduces on 0.16.0 and 0.17.0, so not a regression from the clone work.

## 1. Root cause

`Step__Pull__Merge` applied the result of a fast-forward by calling
`_checkout_flat_map(directory, theirs_map, …)` with the **whole** incoming tree, and the
three-way path did the same with `merged_map`. Both maps are built from committed trees
(clone HEAD, named HEAD, LCA), never from the working directory, so every tracked file was
rewritten from its committed blob — including a file the user had edited and not
committed, and including files the incoming commits never changed. `status` then compared
the (now reverted) file with HEAD and found nothing to report: "fully in sync". The edit
was simply gone.

## 2. The fix — git's rules, applied before any write

`sgit_ai/core/actions/pull/Vault__Pull__Guard.py` (new) and `_guard_working_tree` in
`Step__Pull__Merge`:

1. Scan the working tree with the same ignore-aware scanner `status` uses
   (`_scan_local_directory`) and classify each path against the clone HEAD tree:
   `modified` (content hash differs), `deleted` (tracked, absent on disk; on a sparse clone
   an unfetched blob is not "deleted"), `untracked` (on disk, not in HEAD).
2. For each dirty path, ask "does the merged tree's blob for it differ from HEAD's blob?":

   | working tree | merge leaves it as HEAD | merge changes it |
   |---|---|---|
   | modified | **carry over** — not written, edit survives | **refuse** |
   | deleted | **carry over** — stays deleted | **refuse** |
   | untracked, incoming creates same path | identical content → fine | **refuse** (would overwrite) |
   | untracked, not incoming | ignored | — |

3. Any refusal raises `Vault__Dirty_Working_Tree_Error` **before** `_checkout_flat_map`,
   `_remove_deleted_flat` or the clone-ref write, naming each path and why. The working
   tree, the clone ref and the object store are exactly as before the command.
4. Otherwise the checkout writes `merged_map` minus the carried-over paths. Removal
   (`_remove_deleted_flat`) only touches paths absent from the merged tree, so a carried
   file is never deleted either.

CLI: the refusal prints as
```
error: your local changes would be overwritten by pull:
  x.txt  (your uncommitted edit would be overwritten)
commit them (sgit commit) or stash them (sgit vault stash) and pull again; nothing was changed
```
and a successful pull that carried edits adds
```
Kept 1 uncommitted change(s) the incoming commits did not touch:
  ~ y.txt  (yours, uncommitted)
```
(`kept_dirty` in the pull result dict / `kept_dirty_files` on `Schema__Pull__State`).

Three-way merges get the same guard; a conflict on a dirty path is "changed by the merge"
and refuses, so no `.conflict` file is ever written over uncommitted work.

## 3. Tests (`tests/unit/workflow/pull/test_Pull__Dirty_Working_Tree.py`, two real clones on the in-memory API)

- the reported case: Bob changes `x.txt`, Alice has an uncommitted `y.txt` → pull merges
  `x.txt`, keeps `y.txt`, status still shows `~ y.txt`
- dirty `x.txt` while Bob changed `x.txt` and `docs/z.md` → refused, **neither** file
  changed, clone ref unchanged; after `commit` the same pull merges
- locally deleted untouched file stays deleted; locally deleted file Bob changed → refused
- untracked `new.txt` colliding with Bob's `new.txt` → refused; identical bytes → fine;
  unrelated untracked file left alone
- clean tree: unchanged behaviour, `kept_dirty == []`
- three-way: dirty untouched file survives; dirty file the other side changed → refused
- unit tests of `plan()` rules, `dirty_paths()` semantics, the message
- CLI: the error renders without the fsck/corruption hints; the `Kept` block renders

## 4. Minor issue 1 from the report — `status` said "200 ahead, 1 behind"

Real, and I had seen it myself on a fresh clone. Two things were wrong in `status`:

1. It **overwrote the local named ref with the remote value first**, then counted. When
   the remote had moved, the local ref pointed at a commit the store did not have, the
   ancestor walk from it was empty, and `clone_walk − named_walk` was the entire local
   history — "N ahead" on a clone with no unpushed commits, plus the hint "push your own
   commits". Every later `status` walked from the same hole.
2. It had no way to get the missing commits.

Now `status`:

- reads the remote ref **without writing it**, and keeps the local ref as
  `last_known_named_head` — the remote head whose history this clone fully has (set by its
  last push/pull, or by a status that fetched completely);
- walks the commit graph from the remote head, fetching the commit objects that are absent
  (one ~700-byte object per new commit, verified before write — the same path pull uses),
  bounded by `commit_fetch_limit` (default 50), and reports whether the chain **connects**
  to local history (a local head whose parents are missing is not connected — my first
  version used "head exists" and gave a short count; a test caught it);
- advances the local named ref only when connected;
- when connected: exact `ahead` / `behind`. When not (offline, or more than the limit of
  new commits): `ahead` = local commits not reachable from `last_known_named_head` (still
  exact — it never needed the network), `behind` = what was fetched, flagged
  `behind_lower_bound`, which the CLI prints as `50+ new commits`.

Tests: fresh clone one behind → `(0, 1, 'behind')`; diverged 1/2 → `(1, 2, 'diverged')`;
offline with one unpushed commit → `(1, 1+, 'diverged')`; three new commits with the limit
at 1 → lower bound, then exact `(0, 3)` once the limit allows.

Cost: the walk is bounded (2,000 visited; `_count_unique_commits` was already bounded at
200), and the fetch happens only for commits the store lacks, so a `status` on an
up-to-date clone makes the same single ref read it made before.

Minor issues 2 (doctor `whoami` on the dev server) and 3 (read key + wrong vault id message)
are not touched here: the first is server-side, the second is a wording change on a path
that already lists "the vault key or ID is incorrect" as cause 1.

## 6. Replication and side effects (asked after the first push)

**The new tests reproduce the bug on the pre-fix code.** With the four changed source files
checked out from `dev` and the new test file run unchanged: 10 of 17 fail, the reported case
on `assert 'y v1' == 'y v2 (UNCOMMITTED in A)'` (the edit reverted), every refusal test on
`DID NOT RAISE`, and the status tests on the old numbers — a fresh clone one behind reported
`(2, 1, 'diverged')`. With the fix: 19 of 19 pass (two status tests added since).

**Side effects of the pull guard, considered:**

- *Pull can now refuse where it used to "succeed".* A script that edits a file, then pulls
  while another agent changed the same file, now exits 1 with the paths named instead of
  silently losing the edit. That is the intended change; an agent loop should commit (or
  `sgit vault stash`) before pulling, which is what git demands too. A `--autostash` flag
  would be the convenience to add if the teams want it.
- *Cost:* the guard hashes the working tree exactly as `status` does. Measured on the
  2,900-file DC vault clone: 393 ms for the 1,687 scanned files (13 MB). It runs only when
  a pull actually merges, never on an up-to-date pull.
- *Carried-over edits after a fast-forward* are dirty against the new HEAD exactly as they
  were against the old one (same blob), so `status` shows them and the next `commit`
  includes them — the same as git.
- *Three-way merges* create the merge commit from committed trees only; a carried-over edit
  stays uncommitted on top of it, as in git. A conflict on a dirty path refuses before any
  `.conflict` file is written.
- *Sparse clones:* an unfetched tracked file is not "deleted" (same rule `status` uses), so
  sparse pulls behave as before; the sparse suite passes unchanged.
- *Ignore rules:* the scan is the ignore-aware one `status` uses, with tracked paths exempt
  from ignore ("tracked wins"), so a tracked-but-ignorable file is never misread as deleted.
- *Untracked collisions* now refuse (git does too); identical bytes pass. Previously the
  local file was overwritten silently.
- *API surface:* `kept_dirty` is a new key in the pull result dict and `kept_dirty_files`
  a new field on `Schema__Pull__State`; both default empty, nothing reads them strictly.

## 5. What I could not do from here

The report's `repro.sh` needs an access token for `dev.send.sgraph.ai`; this session has
none, so the end-to-end check is the two-clone test above, which follows the script
step for step. Running `repro.sh` against a release with this fix should end with
`RESULT: OK, uncommitted edit kept`.

---

*[Site index for agents](../llms.txt) · [HTML version](https://cli.sgit.ai/research/pull-discarded-uncommitted-edits.html)*


# Read and write keys as PKI — design analysis, cli.sgit.ai

> Are the read key and the write key really a public and a private key? Half right: the write key should become a signing key, and the read key cannot become a public key. What that would take.

*Source: <https://cli.sgit.ai/research/read-write-keys-as-pki.html> · generated from the same content as the page, so the two cannot drift. Published from <https://github.com/SGit-AI/SGit-AI__CLI/blob/477d328536b04147e78281fb1f13550df1abf140/team/humans/dinis_cruz/claude-code-web/10/09/design-analysis__read-write-keys-as-pki.md>.*

---
# Read and write keys as PKI — design analysis

**Date:** 2026-10-09 · **Context:** the 0.21.0 security review (threat model
`team/explorer/appsec/threat-model/v0.21.0__threat-model.md`, TM-R01) · **Status:** analysis,
no code changed.

**Question.** sgit went symmetric because there was no good place to publish public keys
and no good way to move secrets. Both now exist. So: aren't the read key and the write key
really a public key and a private key? And since only the encrypt/decrypt part would change,
how hard would supporting that be?

## Short answer

**Half right, and the half that's right matters a lot.**

- **The write key should be a private key.** Today it's a password the server compares,
  and nobody else can check it (TM-R01). If writing meant *signing with a private key*,
  every reader could verify every head, and a host or a read-key holder could no longer
  forge history.
- **The read key cannot become a public key.** Reading means decrypting, and decrypting
  needs a secret shared by every reader. Public-key encryption works the other way round:
  anyone can encrypt *to* a key, and only the private-key holder can read. So content
  encryption stays symmetric. What the read capability gains is the writer's **public
  verification key**. It isn't secret, but it has to travel with the read key so nobody
  can substitute it.

So the right mapping is:

```
write capability  =  content key  +  writer's PRIVATE signing key
read capability   =  content key  +  writer's PUBLIC verification key
host              =  ciphertext only; can no longer forge, only withhold or replay
```

This is a known, proven shape: Tahoe-LAFS mutable files (write-cap = signing key; read-cap =
symmetric key + hash of the verifying key) and Hypercore/Dat (public key = identity and
verification; secret key = write).

**On "it's just the encrypt/decrypt bit":** the cryptography really is small. Content
encryption, objects, trees and commits don't change at all, and there's no re-encryption
or data migration. Only two mutable things need a signature: the branch **refs** and the
**branch index**. Everything else is content-addressed below them, so signing the roots
authenticates the whole Merkle tree. The real work is around the cryptography (§4). It's
about 1.5–2 weeks for the CLI, and the web UI needs the same change.

## 1. What a writer signature fixes, and what it doesn't

| Threat-model row | Today | With a writer signing key |
|---|---|---|
| **TM-R01** read-key holder + host forge history that verifies | open (by design) | **closed**: a forged ref or index fails verification on every client |
| TM-R03 ref/key ciphertext not bound to its file id | accepted | **closed**: the signature covers vault id + file id + content |
| TM-R27 legacy named private key readable | accepted | moot: that key stops mattering |
| `signatures-required` meaning "some key that decrypts" | weak | meaningful: the signed index lists the trusted clone keys, so a commit signer must be one of them |
| Tags, format gate, features (all in the index) | host/reader can rewrite | covered by the index signature, so stripping the gate is detected |
| SP-14 whole-site substitution on static mirrors | open | **closed** for browsers that get the verification key in the URL fragment |
| SP-2 / rollback for a *fresh* clone | open | **partly**: a signed timestamp lets a clone flag a stale head; the host can still serve an old signed state |
| Withholding (availability) | open | open: signatures can't force the host to serve data |
| Metadata to the host (TM-R08) | by design | unchanged |
| Revoking one writer | needs a new passphrase | still needs one: the signing key is shared by all writers (§3, phase 3 changes that) |

Per-clone commit signatures stay as they are. They answer *which* writer, while the
vault signature answers *a writer at all*.

## 2. The one design detail that must be right

**The signing key must not be derived from the write key.** The write key is sent to the
server as a header on every write, so the server knows it. A signing key derived from it
would be computable by the very party it must protect against. Deriving it from the read
key fails for the same reason (read-only shares hold that).

It has to come from the **passphrase**, along a third path:

```
passphrase ──PBKDF2(600k, salt "sgit-sign:<vault_id>")──► 32-byte seed ──► Ed25519 signing key
                                                                             └► verification key (public)
```

- Every teammate with the vault key derives the same signing key, so there's nothing to
  distribute among writers. The cost is one more PBKDF2 (~190 ms, cached like the others).
- **Ed25519, not ECDSA P-256.** Ed25519 signatures are deterministic, so the browser
  byte-for-byte test vectors that CLAUDE.md requires are possible. ECDSA in Web Crypto is
  randomised, so it can only be verified, never matched. Web Crypto in current
  Chrome/Firefox/Safari imports an Ed25519 key from a 32-byte seed (PKCS#8) natively.
  Deriving a P-256 key from a seed would need a JS library, since Web Crypto can't compute
  the public point. `cryptography` 49 (installed) supports Ed25519 from a seed; checked.

## 3. Phases

**Phase 1: vault writer signature (the TM-R01 fix).** CLI ~1.5–2 weeks.

1. **Derivation** of the signing key and verification key (§2), plus test vectors shared
   with the web team.
2. **Signed refs.** The encrypted ref JSON becomes
   `{commit_id, seq, ts, sig}`, with `sig` = Ed25519 over
   `(vault_id, file_id, commit_id, seq, ts)`. Clients older than this read
   `.get('commit_id')` and ignore the rest (checked). The signature is made in
   `Vault__Ref_Manager` / the push batch and verified wherever a remote ref is parsed:
   status, pull, clone, fetch.
3. **Signed index.** Add a `writer_sig` over the canonical (JCS) index minus the signature.
   `Schema__Branch_Index.from_json` already tolerates the extra field (checked). Verified
   in `Vault__Index_Sync.read_remote`; re-signed on every merge/upload (all writers can).
   Each branch's `public_key_id` gains a key **fingerprint**, so the signed index pins
   the clone keys and the key files can't be swapped.
4. **Downgrade resistance**, the part that's easy to get wrong:
   - Feature `writer-signed` plus `min_client`, so older clients can't write: they would
     re-save the index without the signature.
   - A clone that has seen the feature pins it locally, the way the format gate never
     goes down.
   - A **fresh** clone can't trust a feature flag the host could strip. So signed vaults
     get a new vault-key / share-token version (`sgit_private_vault_v2_…`), and a client
     that sees v2 requires signatures from the first byte.
5. **Read-only shares.** The read share carries the verification key (32 bytes) next to
   the read key. Existing read-only clones have no verification key: trust on first use,
   by pinning it from the first signed index and refusing any change after.
6. **Tests.** `Known_Gaps` TM-R01 and TM-R03 get inverted into `Fixed` tests (forgery and
   ref swapping refused). Add browser vectors and a real-server round trip.

Existing vaults opt in (`sgit vault format --feature writer-signed`, which signs the
current refs and index). No object is re-encrypted.

**Phase 1b: server enforcement (SG/Send team, optional).** The server stores the
verification key at vault creation and accepts ref/index writes only when they are
signed. The bearer write key then stops mattering (a stolen header is useless), and
garbage writes are refused at the door rather than by every client.

**Phase 2: move capabilities with PKI, not passphrases.** CLI ~1 week. The other half of
your question: now that public keys can be published, a vault key or a read capability
can be wrapped to a teammate's published public key. `PKI__Crypto.hybrid_encrypt`
(RSA-OAEP-4096 + AES-GCM, with an optional ECDSA signature) already exists, as do the
`sgit pki` keyring and contacts. For example, `sgit share --to <contact>` would write the
wrapped capability where the recipient can find it. This removes passphrases from chat,
argv and shell history (TM-R14), and onboarding never exposes the key to the host.

**Phase 3: per-member writers and owner-signed membership.** ~3–4 weeks, later. The
phase-1 key becomes the vault **owner** key. It signs a member list (each member's own
signing key) inside the index, and a head must be signed by a listed member. Removing a
writer becomes "owner drops them and re-wraps the content key to everyone else", with no
new passphrase. This is the full answer to revocation, and it needs phase 1b to be
enforceable against availability attacks.

## 4. Where the effort actually goes

| Piece | Why it isn't "just the encrypt bit" |
|---|---|
| Key derivation | must avoid the write key and the read key (§2); new interop vectors |
| Formats | refs and index carry a signature; old clients must read them (they do) but must not write them (format gate) |
| Downgrade | a host strips signatures or the feature flag unless fresh clones learn "signed" from the capability itself |
| Read shares | new token format; existing read-only clones need trust on first use |
| Every write path | push, index sync, tags, branch create/switch, move, rekey, history edit all write refs or the index and must sign |
| Web UI | same verification (and signing, if it writes); Ed25519 via Web Crypto |
| Tests | gap proofs become fixed tests; vectors; real server |

## 5. Recommendation

Do **phase 1** for the next release after 0.21.0. It closes the most serious row in the
threat model (TM-R01), makes `signatures-required` mean what people think it means, needs
no data migration, and is opt-in per vault. Do **phase 2** alongside it, since it's cheap
with the PKI code that's already there and fixes how keys get shared. Ask the SG/Send
team about **1b**. Keep **3** on the roadmap.

Decisions needed from you before starting:

1. **Ed25519** (my recommendation, for deterministic vectors) or P-256.
2. **A new vault-key version for signed vaults** (fresh-clone downgrade protection), or
   opt-in by feature flag only (simpler, weaker for fresh clones).
3. **Whether the web UI writes to signed vaults** in the first version, or reads and
   verifies only.

## 6. Points to settle before phase 1 (from the sgit.ai agent's review of d3b8eef)

1. **Existing read keys.** A writer signature closes TM-R01 only for readers whose
   capability carries the verification key. Existing read-only shares, including the read
   keys sgit.ai publishes, fall back to trust on first use until they are reissued in the
   v2 form. Plan the reissue, and say so on the site.
2. **Replay.** Signatures do not stop a host from replaying an older signed index or ref.
   Phase 1 needs per-ref and per-index sequence numbers, pinned per clone and failing
   closed; otherwise TM-R29 survives.
3. **Old clients.** They, and any fallback that rewrites the index (the N5 path, now
   removed), would write it unsigned. Gate the change on `--min-client`.
4. **S10.** "A forged first ref fails verification anyway" is true only once phase 1
   ships. Until then S10's per-file rule (only the server's `not_found` is "absent") is what
   protects a first push.

---

*[Site index for agents](../llms.txt) · [HTML version](https://cli.sgit.ai/research/read-write-keys-as-pki.html)*


# Response to "Scion and sgit" (newsroom.sgit.ai, article No. 141, v1.0.0), cli.sgit.ai

> The CLI team's response to the newsroom's "Scion and sgit" article: what it gets right, the three factual errors, and the measurements from a 35k-object vault the article should have carried.

*Source: <https://cli.sgit.ai/research/response-to-scion-and-sgit.html> · generated from the same content as the page, so the two cannot drift. Published from <https://github.com/SGit-AI/SGit-AI__CLI/blob/477d328536b04147e78281fb1f13550df1abf140/team/humans/dinis_cruz/claude-code-web/10/16/response__scion-and-sgit-article.md>.*

---
# Response to "Scion and sgit" (newsroom.sgit.ai, article No. 141, v1.0.0)

**Date:** 16 Oct 2026. **Code read:** `dev` at 881d6df (what 0.22.0 ships plus the 14 Oct fixes).
**Vault measured:** the comms / DC collaboration vault (`y8pwtjlw` on `dev.send.sgraph.ai`), read-only:
cloned eight ways from the hosted API, then the same objects served from local disk (static and a
local API server); nothing pushed to the real server. **Also measured:** the vault the article used
(`newsroom-synthetic-users`, `bg1opz3c`, public read key), from the same kind of sandbox.
**Also read:** Anthropic's post in full, every sgit.ai page the article should link, and the eleven
newsroom articles that already describe sgit's architecture and deployment.

## Verdict

The Scion half is accurate: every figure the article quotes is in Anthropic's post. The sgit half is
under-claimed where it should be strong (deployment models, reading files without a clone, the
pull fix, history integrity) and over-claimed in one place (a CDN that caches for a year), and its
measurement is the wrong one: an 83-file vault says nothing about the question the post raises,
which is what happens when the repository is big and the clients are many. We have a vault that
is big by sgit's standards and is used by ten agents every day. Its numbers are below, and they
are the ones the article should carry.

Three things the article gets wrong on the facts, in order of how much they matter:

1. **"no packing on the server" is listed as a gap.** Scion has no packfiles either and says so as
   a feature: "There is no equivalent of packfiles … so no repository maintenance is needed."
   sgit is the same: immutable objects, no maintenance, no GC on the server. This is a point of
   agreement, not a gap.
2. **"its latest releases add scoped, shallow and on-demand clones" / "sgit 0.18 to 0.22 added
   … `--sparse`".** `--path` and `--depth` are 0.18.0 (7 Oct). `--sparse` has been in the CLI
   since v0.11.3 (1 May 2026).
3. **"objects cache for a year at a CDN".** Drop it (see §2, claim 1). The property is that they
   *can* be cached by anyone, for ever, and the evidence for that is what the sgit.ai pages do in
   the browser, not a CDN header.

## 1. What Scion actually says, and the overlaps the article missed

Read against the post, the article's Scion paragraph is right (2,500 → 30,000 merges a day, ~100 GB
of main-branch history, ~25 M CI checkouts a day, ~600 PB if fetched naively, several hundred
mirrors, three cache tiers each over 99 %, 200× less CPU and memory, seconds instead of minutes,
25 % of CI's CPU, seven people in five months, "by no means a suitable replacement for git").
Four things in the post are closer to sgit than the article noticed:

| Scion (from the post) | sgit | Where it is documented |
|---|---|---|
| "Scion's negotiation doesn't tell the server what the client already has; instead, it operates exclusively on trees and blobs the client wants. Starting from a root tree, the client checks its local store for missing trees and requests them recursively, then repeats the process for blobs." | This is sgit's clone and pull walk, word for word: level-by-level over the trees, one batched request per level, then the blobs in batches of 50 with 16 requests in flight. A scoped clone asks only for the spine down to its folders. | `docs/partial-clones`, CHANGELOG 0.18.0; `Step__Clone__Walk_Trees`, `Vault__Scoped_Tree.walk_fetch` |
| "Every request is for a specific object that never changes, so any cache can answer it." | Every object's name is the SHA-256 of its ciphertext; the client checks every object against its name before writing it. The mutable ref is `no-store`. | `api/vault-objects` (the caching contract), `case-studies/live-vault-docs` |
| "There is no equivalent of packfiles … no repository maintenance is needed." | Same. No packing, no GC, no maintenance on the server. For cold starts from a static host, `sgit publish --bundles` emits a head snapshot and per-commit delta zips. | CHANGELOG 0.18.0 (static publishing) |
| "moving [a ref] is a compare-and-swap on a single Spanner row" | Refs move by compare-and-swap; so does the branch index, which every client merges as a shared document. | `docs/history-integrity`, `docs/vault/vault-from-javascript` §5 |

And two differences the article should state, because they are the real ones:

- **A Scion changeset stores the list of files that changed; an sgit commit stores a tree,** like
  git. Scion rebuilds history and blame as "derived data" on the server. sgit's tree snapshot is
  what makes a scoped clone cheap (an unchanged folder keeps its tree id across commits, so it is
  never fetched twice) and what makes a client-side blame possible without the server.
- **Scion protects directories with permissions on the server; sgit protects them with keys.**
  A partial clone is a speed setting, not a boundary (`docs/limitations`); the boundary is one
  vault per trust domain, a read key that cannot be turned into a write key, and append lanes
  that can write but never read. The article says nothing about any of this, and it is the
  strongest contrast with a server that holds plaintext and an IAM system in front of it.

## 2. Claim by claim

| # | The article says | Status | Say instead (evidence) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | "Its object ids are immutable content addresses, so objects cache for a year at a CDN" (title paragraph, abstract) and "the live server already uses it: … `cache-control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable`, through a CDN" | **Half true, and the half that is true is the wrong half.** The header is now sent (verified today on `/api/vault/read/y8pwtjlw/bare/data/obj-cas-imm-…`: `public, max-age=31536000, immutable`; the ref answers `no-store`). But three consecutive reads of the same object all came back `x-cache: Miss from cloudfront`: the CDN in front of the dev API does not serve reads from cache today. | "Objects are named by the hash of their ciphertext and the name carries `-imm-`, so anything that has fetched one can keep it for ever without reading it: a browser's Cache API, a proxy, a CDN, a folder on disk. That is how the browser app is fast: it caches every `-imm-` object on sight and refetches only the ref. sgit.ai's own documentation pages read a vault that way: a cold load fetches 18 objects, the next load fetches one 69-byte ref, and a load inside the two-minute freshness window fetches nothing. The price is that sgit keeps no deltas: a changed file is a new object." Link `case-studies/live-vault-docs` and `docs/vault/reading-a-vault-file`. |
| 2 | "measured it on a real vault: a scoped clone in 4 seconds against 59 for the full one" (12 MB, 83 files) | **Wrong vault, and the 59 s was a bug, now fixed.** 83 files answers nothing about Scion's problem. The 59 s reproduced exactly from here (59.0 s, 56.5 s): the vault's 106 objects go up in two batches of 50, each batch's response is over the Lambda's size limit, the client slept 14 s retrying each whole and then read 106 objects one at a time. A refused batch is now split in halves on the first refusal: 8.1 s and 9.9 s for the same clone (§3). The article measured a Lambda limit and a client fallback, not the vault. | Use the comms vault (§3): 35k objects, 1,295 commits, 5,281 files, ten agents writing daily; and say what the 59 s was. |
| 3 | "sgit 0.18 to 0.22 added the same family of options: `--path` …, `--depth` …, and `--sparse`" | **Partly wrong.** `--sparse` is from v0.11.3 (May). 0.18.0 added `--path` and `--depth`; the 14 Oct fixes made `clone-headless` + `fetch`/`cat`/`ls` work. | "sgit has had on-demand (`--sparse`) clones since May; 0.18.0 added a folder scope and a history depth, and they combine." |
| 4 | "writes … go through a batch endpoint, up to 100 operations at a time" | Server cap is 100; the client sends 50 per request with 16 requests in flight on reads. | "batches of 50 objects a request, 16 in flight". |
| 5 | "a vault of 626 commits and 9,404 files" | 9,404 **blobs**; the file count was not recorded then (today's vault: 5,101 files, 16,315 blobs). | "9,404 blobs". |
| 6 | "The CLI team measured a scoped clone of one folder in 14 seconds against 81" | True (6 Oct, 18,720 objects). | Keep, but it is superseded by §3. |
| 7 | "sgit does no packing or compaction on the server" under *Where Scion is ahead* | **Not a gap** (§1). | Move to the overlaps. |
| 8 | "a vault of 35,000 objects still takes about three and a half minutes to clone in full" | True (14 Oct), and it is the honest number for a *whole* vault. What the article leaves out: nobody doing agent work needs the whole vault, and the pull that an agent does every session was the slow path, fixed on 14 Oct (§3). | Keep the 3½ min and put the scoped/depth numbers and the pull fix next to it. |
| 9 | "sgit has a history log on the client but no blame and no bisect" | True. Understated: `history log --file PATH` (path history), `--stat`, `--grep/--since/--until/--author`, `history diff A..B`, `history show`, `history revert --as-commit`, `commit --amend`, `history undo`, reflog, `vault tag` (signed), and `check verify` (which commit was signed by which key). Blame is a client-side fold over path history and nothing in the format prevents it. | "No blame or bisect yet; path history, signed authorship and signed tags, yes." Link `docs/history-integrity`, `docs/update-to-0-21-0`. |
| 10 | "There is no command to read a file from a vault without at least a headless local clone" | True for the CLI, and misleading: reading one file is four GETs by design (ref → commit → trees on the path → blob), which the site's pages do in the browser with a 90-line reader, and `clone-headless` is a config directory, not data. The real edge is in §3: on a long history today's `cat` first walks the commits. | "A file is four GETs away from its read key, and sgit.ai's pages read vaults that way; the CLI needs a headless clone directory first." Link `docs/vault/reading-a-vault-file`, `docs/vault/vault-from-javascript`, `demos/vault-app-embed`. |
| 11 | "Merges happen on the client, three-way and whole-file; Scion does them on the server" | True. Add: two independent clients (the CLI and the browser vault app) speak one wire format, so a merge made in a browser is one the CLI verifies and vice versa (`sgit serve pull`). | Link `docs/what-is-sgit` (three doors), `security/` (two implementations, one wire format). |
| 12 | "Git and sgit also live side by side rather than in sync … no bridge" | True for history. There is `vault attach` (bind a key to a `.sg_vault/bare` that came in through `git clone`), the one-repo pattern, and a pure-Python git reader for vault apps. | Link `docs/vault/git-and-vaults`, `case-studies/one-tree-two-remotes`. |
| 13 | "The server only matters for writes" | Also for the store listing that makes a cold full clone fast (one `list`, then bulk fetch). A static host has no listing, so a cold full clone from one walks the graph; a scoped or depth clone never lists. | Fine as a simplification; say "writes and the branch index". |
| 14 | Side-by-side figure "Scion, sgit 0.22.0 and Git … proven scale and availability" | Add rows: *server holds plaintext* (Scion yes, sgit never), *directory protection* (Scion IAM, sgit keys per vault and read-only / write-only keys), *clients* (Scion one, sgit two implementations), *deployment* (Scion internal fleet; sgit hosted, your container, static host, a folder). | |
| 15 | "What it means … The useful next steps are clear from Scion's list: server-side history queries that do not need the plaintext" | A server that cannot read commits cannot answer history questions; that is the design, not a roadmap item. The sgit answer is a client-side index over a *scoped* clone, which §3 shows is small. | Reword: "history queries over a scoped clone on the client, and a commit-chain object so a partial clone does not walk history one commit at a time". |
| 16 | *Where this comes from*: "the largest vault sgit's team documents has about 35,000 objects" | Make it concrete: it is a live vault with ten agents, 1,295 commits (68 added in the last two days), 5,101 files, 527 MB of ciphertext in a full clone. | |

## 3. The evidence the article should carry

All timings from one client in this cloud sandbox (every request leaves through a proxy; a plain
connection does better), against `dev.send.sgraph.ai` (S3 storage behind CloudFront), sgit at
`dev` 881d6df (0.22.0 plus the 14 Oct fixes), one run each unless stated. The vault: 1,295 commits
on 16 Oct (1,227 on 14 Oct), 16,391 trees, 16,315 blobs, 5,101 files, 35,423 objects / 527 MB in a
full clone on 14 Oct.

**Clones** (the full clone is the 14 Oct run; the vault has grown by 180 files since):

| Clone | Time | Objects | Store on disk | Files checked out |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| everything (full clone) | 3 min 30 s | 35,423 | 527 MB | 5,101 (131 MB) |
| `--depth 1` (whole tree, one commit) | 57 s | 6,248 | 142 MB | 5,281 (139 MB) |
| `--path security --depth 1` | **13 s** | **137** | **3 MB** | 130 (3 MB) |
| `--sparse --depth 1` (structure only, one commit) | 27 s | 967 | 6 MB | 0 |
| `--path docs` (12 files, all history) | 181 s | 2,668 | 17 MB | 12 (1 MB) |
| `--path security` (all history) | 227 s | 3,364 | 64 MB | 130 (3 MB) |
| `--path mail/crm.riskmandate` (all history) | 159 s | 6,109 | 69 MB | 558 (27 MB) |
| `--path mail` (the biggest folder, all history) | 264 s | 25,110 | 274 MB | 3,275 (69 MB) |
| `--sparse` (every commit and tree, no blobs) | 206 s | 18,299 | 117 MB | 0 |
| `clone-headless` (keys and config only) | 0.4 s | | | 0 |

**Working in a partial clone** (each is one CLI invocation, so ~1.5 s of it is process start and
PBKDF2):

| Operation | Time | Network |
|---|---|---|
| `ls docs` in the sparse clone | 1.8 s | none (trees are local) |
| `fetch docs/drafting-guide.md` into the sparse clone | 2.9 s | 1 object |
| `cat` of a held file | 1.7 s | none |
| `cat` of a file not yet held (fetched on demand) | 2.5 s | 1 object |
| `fetch security/` (130 files) into the sparse clone | 5.1 s | 130 objects, batched |
| `fetch security` to widen the `--path docs` clone | 7.8 s | 135 objects |
| `status` in the scoped clone, up to date | 1.5 s | ref + index |
| `pull` in the scoped clone, up to date | 2.5 s | ref + index |
| `cat` of one file from a headless clone (first command: brings every commit and tree down) | **202 s** | 18,300 objects, 116 MB |
| `cat` of a second file from the same headless clone | 2.5 s | 1 object |
| `history log --file <path>` on the full clone (1,227 commits) | **6 min 8 s** | none: CPU, 5½ min of it |

**The article's own vault** (`newsroom-synthetic-users`, 83 files, 12 MB, public read key),
cloned from this sandbox for comparison with its "59 s full / 4 s scoped":

| Clone | Before the fix (0.22.0) | After (`dev`, batch splitting) | Objects / store |
|---|---|---|---|
| full, read-only | 59.0 s, 56.5 s | **8.1 s, 9.9 s** | 106 / 12.4 MB |
| `--depth 1` | 62.1 s | (same path) | 93 / 12.0 MB |
| `--sparse` | 4.0 s | | 18 / 180 KB |
| `--path <first folder>` (5 files) | 3.7 s | | 15 / 412 KB |

The article's numbers reproduce to the second. The full clone's 59 s was two 50-object batches
whose responses exceeded the Lambda's size limit (files of ~150 KB): the client retried each
whole through the 2 + 4 + 8 s back-off and then read 106 objects one per request. Fixed on `dev`
(CHANGELOG, Unreleased): a refused chunk is split in halves on the first refusal.


### What the numbers say

- **A scoped clone of a 35k-object vault is a few MB and a few seconds, when it also carries a
  depth.** `--path security --depth 1` and `--depth 1` are the agent pattern the docs already
  recommend ("an agent clones only its own folder with one commit of history"), and they do not
  grow with the vault's history.
- **Without a depth, a partial clone pays one round trip per commit.** `--path docs` (12 files)
  took 181 s and 2,668 objects because it walked 1,295 commits one request each, then the spine
  trees of every one of them (that is what gives `history log` on a scoped clone); `--sparse`
  without a depth is the same walk (206 s), `clone-headless` + `cat` pays it on the first `cat`
  (202 s, then 2.5 s a file), and `--path mail` with all its history is most of the vault
  (25,110 objects). Whole-vault
  clones and pulls stopped doing this on 6 and 14 Oct (list the store once, fetch in bulk); a
  partial clone cannot list-and-sweep because it must not hold what it does not track. This is the
  one real performance edge today, and it has a clean fix that needs no server change: a small
  encrypted "commit chain" object written on push, so a clone batch-fetches the chain (1,295
  commits is 26 requests, 16 in flight) instead of discovering it. Until then: `--depth`.
- **Once a clone exists, every operation is a few requests.** A file on demand is one object and
  under 3 s including process start; a folder of 130 files is 5 s; a pull that is up to date is
  2.5 s. This is the "fetch only what you need" number, and it does not depend on the vault's size.
- **History queries on the client are the other honest edge.** `history log --file` over 1,227
  commits took 6 min of CPU on the full clone because it flattens every commit's tree; it should
  skip subtrees whose id did not change, the way the clone walk does. The fix is local and needs no
  format change.
- **The pull an agent runs every session was the slow path, and is fixed.** Fetching the whole
  head into an empty store through the pull path: 186 s now, about 53 min before 14 Oct (one request
  per commit and one per blob). Measured on this vault, in the 14 Oct note.
- **A full clone is the worst case and still bounded:** 3½ min for 35,423 objects / 527 MB
  (listing 21 s, bulk sweep ~140 s, local tree decrypt 33 s, checkout 4 s).
- **Server-side numbers already published:** ten scoped clones at once in 1.9 s against ten full
  clones in 21.1 s on a single server process (the single uvicorn worker is the limit, not the
  protocol); a one-folder clone of 0.59 s at 100 files and 0.77 s at 2,000 while the full clone
  went 0.95 → 5.55 s; 100 writers landing 1,000 append-lane entries in 4.9 s with none lost
  (newsroom: *Agent workflows on ephemeral vaults*, *sgit in GitHub Actions, side by side*).

## 4. The argument the article should make

Scion's post names what matters at agent scale: always-online clients, fetch only what a job
needs, immutable objects any cache can serve, cheap incremental commits, a sparse working copy
by design. Point by point, with the mechanism and the number:

1. **Fetch only what you need.** A clone asks for the spine down to its folders and nothing else;
   unchanged folders keep their tree ids across commits, so they are never fetched twice. §3.
2. **One file is four requests, from any host that answers a GET.** Ref → commit → trees on the
   path → blob, computed from the read key; no listing, no index, no account. The site's own pages
   do it; `sgit cat` on a sparse clone does it (and, once a file is held, reads it with no network).
3. **Immutable objects, cached by whoever fetched them.** Browser Cache API on sgit.ai, a CDN,
   `--transport static` from GitHub Pages or S3 or a folder, `sgit vault mirror` for custody
   without access. The server sends `immutable`; the design does not depend on it.
4. **Writes are one batched request and a compare-and-swap.** 50 objects per request; the ref and
   the branch index move by CAS, and every client merges the index as a shared document. A commit
   costs the size of the change: the new blobs, the rebuilt spine, one commit object.
5. **Many clients, a dumb server.** The server computes nothing, so it scales as storage does
   (S3 behind CloudFront is the hosted deployment; `sgit serve` is the same image on a laptop).
   Append lanes let a hundred writers post without reading.
6. **And the thing Scion cannot offer anyone outside Anthropic:** the server never holds plaintext,
   the read key is one-way derived and publishable, and the whole thing is `pip install sgit-ai`.

Said with the gaps: no blame or bisect yet; partial clones walk history per commit until the
commit-chain object exists; one server process queues full clones; proven at 35k objects and ten
agents, not at 100 GB and 30,000 merges a day.

## 5. Deployment models the article should claim (all shipped, all documented)

| Model | What runs | Docs |
|---|---|---|
| Hosted | `dev.send.sgraph.ai`: S3 storage behind CloudFront, access token per account | `/docs/installation`, `/api/` |
| Your own server, one container | `diniscruz/sg-send-vault` with an access token and a folder or an S3 bucket; Docker Compose on a Mac mini; Kubernetes; a cloud VM with no public route; two servers, one vault | `/docs/self-host-for-agents`, `/deploy/`, newsroom *Encrypted memory for agents that run somewhere else* (five patterns) |
| On the laptop, from the clone | `sgit serve`: the vault UI + API in Docker, Podman, Apple `container`, nerdctl, Finch, or `uv` with no container; `serve pull/push` move work between the browser and the clone | CHANGELOG (Unreleased, `sgit serve`) |
| Static host, no server | `sgit publish` + any GET host (GitHub Pages, S3, a CDN, Python's file server); clients use `--transport static`; `sgit serve --static` locally | `/docs/vault/static-hosting`, CHANGELOG 0.18.0, newsroom *The homepage is a vault* (317 ms a request via the API, 44 ms from GitHub Pages) |
| A folder | `--transport local` | CHANGELOG 0.18.0 |
| CI sidecar | the server as a job sidecar; ciphertext in the cache or a branch between runs; a key per job; append lanes per shard | newsroom *sgit in a CI pipeline*, *sgit in GitHub Actions, side by side* (four lanes) |
| In the browser | the vault app, `vault-embed.js`, and pages on sgit.ai and newsroom.sgit.ai that render a vault with a published read key | `/docs/vault/vault-apps`, `/docs/vault/vault-from-javascript`, `/demos/vault-app-embed`, `/case-studies/live-vault-docs`, newsroom *Two agents, one vault*, *No server, by design* |

## 6. Website changes (sgit.ai)

1. **`/api/vault-objects` → "Measured 21 September 2026: the immutable header is not currently
   being sent."** Stale. Measured 16 Oct: `cache-control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable` on
   `obj-cas-imm-*`, `no-store` on `ref-pid-muw-*`. Add: CloudFront still reports a miss on repeated
   reads of the same object (the token header is likely in the cache key), so the CDN is not yet a
   cache for API reads; browser and client caches are.
2. **`/docs/partial-clones` → "Measured".** Add the §3 table, and a sentence under `--depth`:
   on a partial clone the history walk is one request per commit (a scoped clone of a 1,295-commit
   vault: 181 s without a depth, seconds with one); whole-vault clones and pulls list the store and
   fetch in bulk since 0.18 / 0.22.
3. **`/docs/limitations` → "Commit author attribution is not yet recorded … population is planned
   work."** Stale since 0.19.0: commits are signed, `check verify` classifies every commit, `history
   log --author` filters by key id, `vault tag` is signed. Replace with the current edges: no blame
   or bisect, partial clones walk history per commit, no rebase or cherry-pick.
4. **`/llms.txt` quick answer "No for: … tags"** and `/docs/sgit-for-git-users`: tags exist
   (`sgit vault tag create/show/list/delete`, signed). Also add `history undo`, `commit --amend`,
   `history revert --as-commit`, `reflog`.
5. **`/docs/self-host-for-agents` §1:** `pip install sgraph-ai-app-send "mcp<2"` → 0.34.0 caps
   `mcp` itself; image `v0.33.0` → `v0.34.0` in the three places; the troubleshooting row for
   `mcp` 2.x can go once 0.34.0 is the floor.
6. **`/deploy/`:** the `--endpoint` → `--base-url` correction note can be folded into the vault
   pages themselves (they are a vault: push the fix).
7. **A single "deployment models" table** (§5) somewhere under `/deploy/` or `/docs/`: today the
   seven models are spread over six pages and two newsroom articles, which is why the article
   claimed none of them.
8. **`/docs/vault/reading-a-vault-file`:** add the CLI equivalent (`clone-headless` + `cat`, and
   `clone --sparse` + `cat`/`fetch`) next to the browser reader, with the history-walk caveat.

## 8. Three paragraphs the article can paste

**Replacing "Immutable identifiers that cache":** Every object in an sgit vault is named by the
SHA-256 of its ciphertext, so a name can never point at different bytes, and the client checks each
object against its name before it is written. That is the property Scion's three cache tiers rest
on, and it means anyone who has fetched an object can keep it for ever: a browser's cache, a
proxy, a CDN, a folder. sgit.ai's own documentation pages are a vault read this way: a cold load
fetches 18 objects, the next load fetches one 69-byte ref, and a load inside the two-minute
freshness window fetches nothing at all. The only mutable object is the ref, and it is never
cached.

**Replacing "Measured on 0.22.0":** The vault this site's agent should have measured is the one ten
agents share every day: 1,295 commits, 5,101 files, 35,000 encrypted objects, 527 MB in a full
clone. [§3 table]. A full clone is the worst case at three and a half minutes. An agent does not
take one: it clones its own folder with one commit of history, in [path-security-depth1] seconds
and [MB], and a pull that is a day behind, which used to be the slow path at nearly an hour, now
takes three minutes for the whole head. One file is four requests from its read key, from any host
that answers a GET.

**Replacing "Where Scion is ahead", first sentences:** Scion does blame, bisect and merges on the
server and builds history indexes as derived data; sgit's server cannot read a commit, so those
run on the client, and today sgit has path history, signed authorship and signed tags but no blame
or bisect. Neither system packs objects on the server, and both treat that as a feature. Where sgit
is behind on its own terms: a partial clone still walks a long history one commit per request
(a depth avoids it), one server process queues concurrent full clones, and the largest vault it has
been proven on is 35,000 objects and ten agents, not 100 GB and 30,000 merges a day.

## 9. Storage is the bottleneck, not sgit

The hosted API is a Lambda in front of S3 behind CloudFront. Every request costs its round trip
(sandbox → proxy → CDN → Lambda → S3) before a byte moves, and the client's work per object (verify
the hash, decrypt) is microseconds. So on the hosted path the numbers are request counts, not
bytes: `--path security --depth 1` is 137 objects and 3 MB, and takes 13 s because it is about a
dozen dependent requests (ref, index, commit, one batch per tree level, the blob batches) plus
0.4 s of PBKDF2. The newsroom measured the same thing from the browser: 317 ms a request through
the vault API, 44 ms for the same object from GitHub Pages (*The homepage is a vault*).

Take the Lambda away and the same objects move at the speed of the storage:

- **ruv.sgit.ai ledger** (local SG/Send server, one process, disk storage, 11 recorded runs): every
  sgit operation, including Python start-up and the 600k-iteration PBKDF2, is 0.4 to 1.5 s; a
  38-file / 4.0 MB vault clones in 0.63 s; a 142-file / 6.9 MB vault clones in 0.74 s and pushes in
  0.87 s. Not one of those numbers is sgit being slow; they are the floor of starting a Python
  process and deriving a key.
- **newsroom, local server:** a one-folder clone 0.59 s at 100 files, 0.77 s at 2,000; ten scoped
  clones at once in 1.9 s.
- **The comms vault from local storage** (same 35k objects, this sandbox): the same sandbox, the
  same CLI, the same 35,423 objects, three transports:

  | Clone / operation | Hosted API (Lambda + S3 + CloudFront, via proxy) | Static: `sgit serve --static` (plain GETs, local disk) | Local API: `sgit serve --runtime uv` (one Python process, disk) |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | full clone | 3 min 30 s | 110.6 s (bulk fetch 71.5 s, tree decrypt ~33 s) | 69.1 s (commits 1.4 s, trees 40.7 s, blobs 18.8 s, checkout 2.7 s) |
  | `--depth 1` | 57.4 s | 25.4 s | 11.7 s |
  | `--path security --depth 1` (120 files) | 13.0 s | 2.3 s | **0.8 s** |
  | `--path docs`, all 1,227 commits | 181 s | | 7.1 s |
  | `--sparse`, all history | 206 s | 67.0 s | 43.3 s |
  | `cat` of one file on demand | 2.5 s | 1.8 s | 1.8 s |
  | `pull`, up to date | 2.5 s | | 0.8 s |

  Read down the columns: the per-commit history walk that costs 181 s against the hosted API is
  7 s against a local server (the same 1,227 requests at ~1 ms each); a one-folder clone is
  0.8 s. What is left when the network is gone is the client's own work, which is decrypting
  16,391 trees (about 33 to 40 s on a full clone) and nothing else of note. (Observation for
  the SG/Send brief: the local disk server answered the store listing with 0 objects, so the
  full clone there went by the graph walk rather than the bulk sweep; the walk found everything.)

The API does two things that storage cannot: it protects writes (the access token, compare-and-swap
on the ref and the branch index) and it shortens reads a little (batches of 50, a listing for cold
full clones). Both are small, and both can be done differently on different storage. Everything
else is a GET of an immutable object. So "how fast is sgit" is the wrong question; the right one
is "where is the storage, and how close": memory, a local disk, an S3 bucket behind a CDN, GitHub
Pages, a folder. The deployment table in §5 is that list.

## 10. sgit is a standard, not a server

The article treats sgit as a product with a server. It is closer to a convention for laying files
out, and the proof is that everything in a vault is reachable from one hash with no help from
anyone:

1. The vault key gives the vault id and, one way, the read key.
2. The read key gives the ref's name: `ref-pid-muw-` + the first 12 hex of
   `HMAC(read_key, "sg-vault-v1:file-id:ref:" + vault_id)`. Nobody told you; you computed it.
3. The ref holds the head commit id; the commit holds the tree id; trees hold blob ids and
   encrypted names. Ref → commit → tree → blob is four GETs for any file, from any host that
   serves the paths.
4. Every object but the ref and the index is named by the hash of its ciphertext, so it is
   immutable, verifiable and cacheable by whoever holds it. And the name says so: an immutable
   object's id carries `-imm-` (`obj-cas-imm-…`), the mutable ones carry `-muw-`
   (`ref-pid-muw-…`). Anything in the path, a browser, a proxy, a CDN, a CI cache, a vault app,
   can decide to keep an object for ever by looking at its name, without reading a byte of it,
   and without being told by a header. That is how the browser vault app and the sgit.ai pages
   get their speed: they cache every `-imm-` object on first sight and refetch only the ref. It
   is also the trade sgit made on purpose: no deltas between versions of a file (a changed file
   is a new immutable object), in exchange for objects that any intermediary can cache
   blindly. Git stores deltas and must be told what changed; sgit stores whole objects and
   never has to ask.
5. Writes are the same objects PUT in batches, plus a compare-and-swap on the ref.

That is the whole wire format, and two independent implementations speak it (the CLI; the browser
vault app, which `vault-embed.js` reduces to about 90 lines). A static host implements the read
half with nothing installed. The **cache layer** (`sgit cache add <path>`, shipped) extends the
same idea to hot records: a declared path gets a client-computable cache object under
`bare/cache/`, maintained by push, so a reader with only `vault_id` + read key does *one* batch
read (the ref plus the candidate ids) and gets the file with no tree walk; a miss or a stale entry
falls back to the walk, so correctness never depends on it. The reference reader is written to run
in an edge function or a Lambda that serves one hot record. Scion's "derived data" is the same
move, computed on a server that can read the plaintext; sgit's is computed by the writer and named
by the key.

## 11. History, blame and merges: where they belong

Correct the article's framing, and then disagree with Scion's. In sgit, history (`log`, `--file`,
`--stat`, `diff`, `show`, `reflog`), undo, revert, tags, signature verification and three-way
merges all run on the client, and that is the design, not a shortfall. Blame is the one Scion
feature sgit does not have as a command today; it is a fold over path history and nothing in the
format prevents it. (The honest edge: on this vault `history log --file` over 1,295 commits took
6 min 8 s (5½ min of CPU), because it flattens every commit's tree; it should skip subtrees whose id did not
change, the way the clone walk does.)

The argument for the client: a merge is a workflow step, not a storage operation. It needs the
context of the change, the history, and the policy that says who may merge what. In ruv.sgit every
worker writes to its own branch and the host merges them per the run's mandate, with a receipt;
in the comms vault ten agents meet on a named branch and resolve on the clone that has the
conflict in front of it. A server that merges for you must be trusted with the plaintext and with
the policy. Scion's own post concedes the point from the other side: it could not keep a merge
queue, so "concurrent changes can conflict, but Claude can typically fix these conflicts" — the
merge went back to the agent.

And keep what made git git. Scion is in the Piper and Sapling line, a centralised system with one
authoritative store, and the post says plainly it "is by no means a suitable replacement for git
for general use". sgit keeps the distributed property: a full clone is still one command and a
complete, verifiable copy of everything, and anyone with the key can rebuild the whole thing from
any host. What changed is that the full clone became optional. `--path`, `--depth`, `--sparse` and
the cache layer mean a repository can hold large files without every client paying for them, which
is the one habit every git team has had to police by hand. The whole-history clone is a backup and
an audit, and it is still there when you want it.

## 12. Encryption as a constraint

The article sells encryption as privacy. The stronger claim is that it is a design constraint that
forbids the shortcut. Because the server cannot read a byte, there is no "just index it on the
server", no "just render it there", no server-side merge, no derived data the client did not
compute. Every feature had to be expressible as objects the client writes and other clients can
derive by key, which is why the results are small: a read is four GETs, a cache is a path-derived
object, a deployment is any storage. The newsroom's *No server, by design* is the same argument
applied to a whole site. Say it as a property, not a scolding: the constraint is what produced the
simple designs.

## 13. ruv.sgit, the integration the article does not mention

ruv.sgit.ai runs a Ruflo hive (rUv / ruvnet; a queen and parallel workers) with one ephemeral sgit
vault per run and an Agent Behaviour Policy compiled into Ruflo's enforce mode. The ledger
(`data/vaults.json`, 11 runs to 15 Oct) records every sgit operation with its milliseconds, the
server-held bytes, a plaintext probe of the server's store (0 hits in every run), a fresh clone
checked identical to what was delivered, and the vault deleted at close. It is the agent-swarm
case Scion's post is about, run on a local server, and it is where the "storage, not sgit" numbers
in §9 come from. Link it as the swarm evidence, next to *Agent workflows on ephemeral vaults*.

## 14. What was not done

- Nothing pushed to the comms vault; nothing changed on the site. The site changes in §6 are a
  list for the site agent.
- The commit-chain object (§3) is a design, not code. It is the one change that would make
  partial clones of long histories as fast as the depth-1 case; it needs a format note and a
  migration-free write path (a mutable, encrypted, per-branch object the client rewrites on push).

---

*[Site index for agents](../llms.txt) · [HTML version](https://cli.sgit.ai/research/response-to-scion-and-sgit.html)*


# Sealed files — a second encryption layer on top of a vault, cli.sgit.ai

> A second encryption layer on top of either vault mode: files sealed to named recipients with ECDH P-256, HKDF and AES-256-GCM, with the corrections from the sgit.ai agent's review.

*Source: <https://cli.sgit.ai/research/sealed-files-layer.html> · generated from the same content as the page, so the two cannot drift. Published from <https://github.com/SGit-AI/SGit-AI__CLI/blob/477d328536b04147e78281fb1f13550df1abf140/team/humans/dinis_cruz/claude-code-web/10/09/design__sealed-files-layer.md>.*

---
# Sealed files — a second encryption layer on top of a vault

**Date:** 2026-10-09 · **Status:** design for review, no code · **Companion:**
[`design__native-pki-vault-mode.md`](../research/native-pki-vault-mode.md) (same folder). This layer works on **either** vault
mode, symmetric (today) or native PKI.

> **Revised 2026-10-10 after the sgit.ai agent's review (dev at 0a0707d).** Three corrections,
> applied below:
> 1. **No "compare by re-sealing".** Sealing is randomised (a fresh file key and ephemeral key
>    every time), so re-sealing never reproduces the stored bytes. The tree entry instead
>    carries a **keyed hash of the plaintext**: HMAC-SHA256 under a key derived from the vault
>    read key, stored under the read key. A recipient compares plaintext to that HMAC. A
>    non-recipient compares the sealed bytes. Unlike the unkeyed `content_hash`, the keyed
>    hash does not let a vault reader confirm a guess of the content.
> 2. **Seal-policy changes need an authorised signer.** Otherwise any writer can "unseal by
>    policy": drop a rule or a recipient, and the next commit of that path is sealed to fewer
>    people, or not at all. `.sgit/seal` names its `admins` (public keys). A commit that
>    changes the policy must be signed by one of them, or pull refuses it, as
>    `signatures-required` does. The first policy is pinned by the clone that adds it (trust
>    on first use, like the PKI mode's writer set).
> 3. **The construction is Web-Crypto-native: ECDH P-256 + HKDF-SHA256 + AES-256-GCM.** That
>    is the HPKE base mode with the P-256 KEM (RFC 9180, DHKEM(P-256, HKDF-SHA256)). Browsers
>    open sealed files with no WASM dependency, and CLAUDE.md's byte-for-byte parity rule holds
>    with test vectors. age is kept as an **interop path only**:
>    - `sgit seal export --age` re-seals a file for the stock `age` tool;
>    - hardware and KMS keys are reached through a provider bridge that speaks the
>      `age-plugin` protocol for the unwrap step only (only the file key crosses it).
>    §3 and §9 below are updated accordingly.

> **Revised again 2026-10-10 after the release-gate review (dev at eed8084).** Two more
> corrections:
> 1. **The comparison value moves inside the sealed envelope.** A keyed hash under a key
>    derived from the *vault read key* (correction 1 above) does not stop guessing: every
>    reader holds that key, so a reader who is not a recipient can still compute the HMAC of
>    a guess and compare. The comparison value is now `HMAC-SHA256(K_cmp, plaintext)` with
>    `K_cmp = HKDF(FK, info="sgit seal compare v1")`, where `FK` is the per-file key that only
>    recipients unwrap. It is stored **inside** the envelope, as the first 32 bytes of the
>    encrypted payload, never in the tree entry. A recipient's clone caches it per sealed blob
>    id in a 0600 local file, so `status` does not call the identity provider on every run.
>    The tree entry holds only the hash of the sealed bytes.
> 2. **The chunked AES-GCM payload has defined framing** (§3.1): a per-file payload key, a
>    counter nonce, and the chunk index and a final-chunk flag in the AAD. A reader refuses
>    truncation, reordering, extension and a final flag in the wrong place.

## 1. The idea, in your words and in mechanism

> As the author I can say: "here is my public key, encrypt this data with it; if you need
> to decrypt it, point over there". The files still exist in the vault as before, but
> only someone with the private key can read them. The service holding the private key
> can be local, remote, or anything else.

Mechanically, this is **envelope encryption to recipients' public keys, with decryption
delegated to an identity provider**. git-crypt (GPG), SOPS (KMS/age/PGP) and age
(X25519, ssh keys, hardware plugins) all use this pattern. The vault keeps doing its job,
and selected files get an inner envelope:

```
 plaintext ──► [ inner: sealed to recipients' public keys ]  ──► [ outer: vault encryption ] ──► host
               file key FK (random) encrypts the content          read key / DK, exactly as today
               FK is wrapped once per recipient public key
```

| Who | Sees |
|---|---|
| The host | ciphertext only (outer layer), as today |
| A **vault reader** (read key) | that the file exists: its name, path, history, approximate size, who changed it when. **Not its content.** |
| A **recipient** (holds, or can ask for, a matching private key) | the content |

Two levels, two key systems:
- **Outer layer** (vault key): hides everything from the host.
- **Inner layer** (recipient keys): hides content from everyone who is not a recipient,
  including the host, other vault members, and anyone who later obtains the vault's
  read key.

## 2. What each party can do, precisely

| Party | Create a sealed file | Read it | Edit it | Replace / delete it |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Recipient (with its provider) | yes | yes | yes | yes |
| Vault writer, not a recipient | **yes**: only the recipients' *public* keys are needed | no | no (editing needs reading first) | **yes, blindly**: it can write new sealed bytes over the file, or delete it |
| Vault reader | no | no | no | no |
| Host | no | no | no | withhold or replay, as today |

One correction to "you could only edit or modify a file if you have that key". **Editing**
needs the key, because you must read before you change. **Replacing** does not. Any
vault writer can put new sealed bytes at the same path, because sealing needs only
public keys. Stopping that is an integrity question, not a confidentiality one, and has
two answers that can be combined:
1. **Signed envelopes:** the sealer signs the inner envelope with its own key. Readers
   (recipients) check that the signer is on the path's allowed-author list (§4).
2. **Path rules enforced on commit/pull:** a commit that changes a sealed path must be
   signed by an allowed author. Otherwise pull refuses it, as `signatures-required` does
   today. With the native PKI mode's writer set, this becomes a hard rule.

## 3. Format

**Recommendation (revised 10-10): an HPKE envelope, DHKEM(P-256, HKDF-SHA256) + AES-256-GCM,
all native to Web Crypto; age v1 as an export and plugin-bridge format only.** The original
reasoning for age follows, kept for the record.
- It is specified, small and audited. Recipient types include X25519, ssh-ed25519 /
  ssh-rsa and scrypt (passphrase), plus a **plugin protocol** (`age-plugin-*`).
- The plugin protocol is precisely "the private key lives elsewhere": YubiKey/PIV, TPM,
  Secure Enclave and cloud KMS plugins already exist.
- **A sealed file can be opened with the stock `age` tool, without sgit**, which is good
  for longevity and audit.
- The pieces it needs (X25519, HKDF-SHA256, ChaCha20-Poly1305, HMAC-SHA256, scrypt) are
  all in `cryptography`. A minimal reader/writer for the X25519 and plugin stanzas is
  a few hundred lines.

**Trade-off to decide.** age's payload cipher is ChaCha20-Poly1305, which **Web Crypto
does not provide**, while CLAUDE.md asks for Web Crypto byte-for-byte parity. The browser
would use `typage` (the reference TypeScript age implementation). The alternative is a
custom HPKE envelope (X25519 + HKDF + AES-256-GCM, all in Web Crypto), at the cost of the
tool ecosystem and the plugins. My view: age. The plugin ecosystem *is* the "decryption
service elsewhere" feature, and the parity rule can name `typage` as the browser
implementation for this layer.

```
sealed file   = "age-encryption.org/v1\n"
                "-> X25519 <ephemeral>\n<wrapped FK>\n"        one stanza per recipient
                "-> piv-p256 <tag> <…>\n<wrapped FK>\n"        a hardware / plugin recipient
                "--- <header MAC>\n"
                <payload: ChaCha20-Poly1305 STREAM, 64 KiB chunks, under a key from FK>
              [ + optional detached Ed25519 signature by the sealer, in a sidecar stanza ]
```

### 3.1 Payload framing (HPKE envelope, revised 10-10)

```
header        = magic "sgit-seal/1" ‖ header_nonce (16 random bytes) ‖ recipient stanzas
                (each: HPKE enc ‖ HPKE-Seal(recipient pub, FK)) ‖ chunk_size (u32, 65536)
H             = SHA-256(header)
PK            = HKDF-SHA256(ikm=FK, salt=header_nonce, info="sgit seal payload v1")   (32 bytes)
plaintext'    = HMAC-SHA256(K_cmp, plaintext) ‖ plaintext        (the comparison value rides inside)
chunk i       = plaintext'[i·65536 : (i+1)·65536]                 (the last may be shorter;
                                                                   an empty file is one empty final chunk)
nonce_i       = u88_be(i) ‖ final_i                               (12 bytes; final_i = 0x01 on the last chunk only)
aad_i         = H ‖ u64_be(i) ‖ final_i
ct_i          = AES-256-GCM(PK, nonce_i, chunk i, aad_i)
sealed file   = header ‖ ct_0 ‖ ct_1 ‖ … ‖ ct_n
```

- **The AAD binds each chunk to this header, its position and whether it ends the file**, so
  chunks cannot be moved between files, reordered, dropped from the end (the new last chunk
  has `final = 0` and fails) or followed by more (anything after a `final = 1` chunk is
  refused). The index is also in the nonce, which keeps nonces unique under `PK` without
  storing them.
- `PK` is fresh per sealing (random `FK` and `header_nonce`), so the counter nonce never repeats
  under one key. At most 2^32 chunks (256 TiB) per file.
- A reader streams: it verifies and releases chunk *i* before reading *i+1*, but treats the
  file as complete only after a valid `final = 1` chunk. The plaintext is written to a temp
  file and renamed only then, so a truncated file never reaches the working copy.
- Test vectors (Python and Web Crypto, byte for byte): empty file, exactly one chunk, one
  chunk plus one byte, three chunks; and the refusals: truncated at a chunk boundary, two
  chunks swapped, a chunk appended after the final one, a final flag on chunk 0 of three, a
  header byte changed.

## 4. Policy: which files, to whom, written by whom

A committed policy file, signed like any commit. It works the way `.gitattributes` works
for git-crypt:

```
# .sgit/seal      (committed; changes to it are themselves a signed, reviewable commit)
recipients:
  dinis   = age1qy…            # published key, fingerprint pinned here
  backup  = age1zz…            # offline recovery key
  ops     = age1yubikey1q…     # hardware-held
seal:
  secrets/**        -> dinis, backup
  finance/*.xlsx    -> dinis, ops, backup
  **/.env           -> dinis, backup
authors:                       # optional: who may change a sealed path (§2)
  secrets/**        -> dinis
```

- **Recipients by public key**, fetched from the published key directory and **pinned by
  fingerprint in the policy**. A later change at the directory cannot silently add
  someone; the policy changes only through a commit.
- `sgit commit` seals any changed file a rule matches. `sgit seal add <path> --to <name>`
  and `sgit seal rekey` edit the policy.

## 5. On disk, in the working copy

| Clone | A sealed file looks like |
|---|---|
| Has a working identity for that file | the **plaintext**, written 0600 (secret writer). `sgit status` compares `HMAC(K_cmp, plaintext)` with the value inside the envelope (cached locally per blob, revised 10-10); never by re-sealing, which is randomised |
| Has no identity, or the provider is unreachable | the **sealed bytes**, unchanged (an `age` file). `status` treats it as unchanged, never deleted or modified: the same "keep the committed entry" rule the symlink ban uses |

Integration points in the current code:
- **Tree entries** carry `content_hash` = an unkeyed `sha256(plaintext)[:12]` (today's
  `Vault__Crypto.content_hash`), stored under the vault read key. For a sealed file that
  would let any vault reader *confirm a guess* of the content. **For sealed files the hash
  is taken over the sealed bytes.** The entry also gets a `sealed` flag and the
  recipients' fingerprints (still under the read key).
- **Blob reuse** (`encrypt_or_reuse_blob` matches on `content_hash`) then works on sealed
  bytes. Re-sealing an unchanged file is skipped as long as the plaintext is unchanged and
  the policy did not change (a local cache of plaintext hash → sealed blob).
- **Merge:** sealed files are binary unless both sides can be opened locally. A conflict
  keeps both versions (`.conflict`). Diff shows `sealed, changed` without an identity.

## 6. The decryption service ("identity provider")

Only the **16-byte file key** crosses the boundary, never the content:

```
sgit ──(stanza: recipient tag + wrapped FK)──► provider ──(FK, or "refused")──► sgit
```

| Provider | Where the private key lives | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Local identity file | `~/.config/sgit/identities` (0600) | the simple default; written by the secret writer |
| ssh key / ssh-agent | your existing ssh key (ed25519/rsa) | age natively supports ssh recipients; nothing new to manage |
| Hardware | YubiKey / PIV / TPM / Secure Enclave via `age-plugin-*` | touch-to-decrypt; the key cannot be copied |
| Remote service | a team service, cloud KMS, or an SG/Send service, over an authenticated API | can **log, rate-limit, require approval and revoke** per unwrap, per file: an audit trail of who opened what. Offline means unreadable, by design |

Configuration is per clone (`.sg_vault/local/identities` naming providers) or per user.
The interface is the age plugin protocol, so any existing plugin works, and our own
remote-service provider is just one more plugin.

**Capability hand-off.** The same envelope moves *vault* capabilities between people.
`sgit share --to dinis` seals a read or write capability to Dinis's published key: no
passphrase in chat, argv or shell history. This closes most of TM-R14 and is phase 2 of
the earlier analysis.

## 7. What it protects, and what it does not

| Threat | Covered |
|---|---|
| Host reads content | yes (outer layer, as today) |
| A vault member who is not a recipient reads a sealed file | **yes** |
| The vault read key leaks (a share, a log, an old clone) | **yes for sealed files**: they need a recipient key as well |
| A recipient's key is revoked | only for **new** seals: history sealed to them stays readable to them (inherent; rotate secrets, not just files) |
| A non-recipient writer replaces a sealed file | detected with signed envelopes / author rules (§2); not prevented on the host |
| File names, paths, sizes, history from vault readers | not hidden (they live in the vault's tree). Sizes are approximate (age adds per-chunk overhead); pad if needed |
| Plaintext on a recipient's disk | out of scope: it is the recipient's machine (written 0600) |
| Provider compromise | as strong as the provider: hardware or approval-based providers limit it |

## 8. Relation to the native PKI mode

- **Independent of the vault mode:** sealed files work in symmetric vaults today.
- **In a PKI vault**, per-member envelopes are also the natural way to hand `DK` to each
  member: the vault's `DK` is sealed to every member's public key instead of to one
  shared `R`. Removing a reader then means re-sealing to the rest (native-mode doc §6).
- The deposit capability (native-mode doc §5) plus sealed files gives a **drop box**:
  contributors can add files that only the owner can open, and cannot read each other's.

## 9. Effort

| Step | What | CLI estimate |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | HPKE envelope (DHKEM(P-256, HKDF-SHA256) + AES-256-GCM, chunked), Python and Web Crypto with shared vectors; `seal export --age` | ~1 week |
| 2 | `.sgit/seal` policy, seal on commit, open on checkout/pull, sealed-bytes hashing, status rules | 1–1.5 weeks |
| 3 | Providers: identity file + ssh keys, then the plugin protocol (hardware/KMS), then a remote-service plugin | ~1 week (+ service side) |
| 4 | Signed envelopes + author rules on pull | ~0.5 week |
| 5 | `sgit share --to <contact>` (capability hand-off) | ~0.5 week |
| — | Web UI: open sealed files with Web Crypto (no WASM) + a provider bridge | web team |

## 10. Decisions for you

1. **Format (revised 10-10):** the Web-Crypto-native HPKE envelope, with age as an export and
   plugin-bridge format. (Was: age.)
2. **Working copy:** plaintext when the clone can open the file (git-crypt style), or
   always sealed on disk with `sgit cat` / `sgit open` to read?
3. **Integrity for sealed paths:** signed envelopes + author rules in the first version,
   or later?
4. **First remote provider:** an SG/Send-hosted unwrap service with approval and audit,
   or a cloud KMS plugin?
